I sea leave humbly to approach your Most Gracious Majesty, to express the high sense of gratitude I entertain for the honour of being permitted to dedicate the present work to your Majesty.

I have, since my affliction, been indebted to your Majesty’s benevolence for most essential benefits, and now, with that condescension which so peculiarly adorns your Majesty, you deign tv gild the produce of my humble toil with your exalted patronage, and thus confer upon me a distinction most gratifying to my feelings and ambition.

_ My powers of personal exertion have been too much curtailed, to allow me to offer — your Majesty in return, more than a heart replete with loyalty and gratitude, otherwise I would be proud in devoting the remainder of my existence to prove the ardour of my zeal and attachment. :

With the sincerest aspirations to heaven, that your Majesty may long continue to rule over that free and. enlightened nation, which, der ‘your paternal government, has risen td a transcendant height of glory,

‘Were any individual, gifted with the full and ordinary powers that it has pleased the Creator to confer upon the human race, to undertake a journey into'a ‘strange and almost unknown country, there could be no reason why he should not collect, and communicate, a fund of curious and interesting particulars relative to the scene of his travel, its inhabitants, and productions; but that one circumstanced like the Author of the present work, under a total deprivation of that most important of the senses for acquiring a knowledge of external objects—the vower of visioneshould, in the first place, meditate and attempt sucha journey; and, secondly, venture to obtrude its results upon the public, must be deemed viii PREFACE. That he should intrude upon the public the narrative of his journey and adventures, requires a farther explanation. With his great disadvantages, he has no right to presume that he could add much to what was previously known respecting the immense Russian Empire, or, with much authority, illustrate the manners, customs, or character of its inhabitants; the field, however, is a wide one, and one which has not frequently been trodden, so that numberless of its indigenous produedons, both natural and moral, remain to be discovered. Whether the Author has succeeded in collecting,—to carry forward the metaphor,—any of its original plants, or of the latent seeds, or springing flowers of the recent civilization of this country, he leaves to the reader, after the perusal of his pages, to determine. He is, however, willing to admit, that in sending forth his narrative, he is not a little influenced by the wish to be regarded as.. member, however humble, of the literary world, in which feeling he is, to a degree, encouraged by the favour-

ablé manner in which his former production was received by the public. Those who may be inclined to censure his “presumption in this respect, he trusts will not deny some indulgence to his peculiar situation, or refuse to admit, however much the work itself may ‘fail in interest, that the innocent gratification he has derived from its composition is some excuse for the publication.
Before closing his introductory: remarks, the Autbor is particularly anxious to do away

.with any impression, which the public may be likely to entertain, with respect to the fidelity _ of his descriptions, and the opportunities. which were afforded him of acquiring information during his journey.

A late interesting traveller, (Captain Cochrane,) whom the Author had the pleasure of meeting at Moscow, previous to setting out for Siberia, in commenting upon this intention of visiting’ that remote part of the Russian empire,* has thrown out insinuations injurious to
* See a Pedestrian Journey through Russia, &c. by Capt. J D. Cochrane.

the authenticity of. the present publication. After ridiculing the Author’s scheme of travel, ina vein of combined pity and sarcasm, this gentleman proceeds to state, that “ any information he (Mr. Holman) may receive.can only proceéd: from exiles and criminals ; and, consequently,. is not implicitly to be relied on, particularly ' Situated as he is, possessing hardly a sufficient knowledge of the Russian language.to appreciate the-value of such hearsay information.” ft might be easy to remark on the inconsistency of this passage ; in which Captain C. . accuses the Author of gaining his hearsay- in- - formation from a people whose language he asserts him not able to comprehend. The Author hopes that he shall be able to disprove this insinuation, and which, he hegs to remark, if it is to be received as designating the manner in which Captain C. “procured his own information, must be considered as decidedly fatal to the veracity of that gentlemdn’s late publicétion. ” _ Physically blind as the Author is, he cannot but be sensible of the mental obscurity of
Captain C., and might, without impropriety, address him im the words of the Roman satirist,
“ Cur tu lippus aliorum vitia tam cernis acutus.”*

It is with feelings of honest pride and satisfaction, that the Author is enabled to assert, that the information detailed in this work, was collected, generally, under the most unexceptionable circumstances, and from the purest and most authentic sources. On entering Russia his introductions led him immediately into the most respectable,society, comprising many of the highest characters of St._Petersburg; from thence he passed forward through

* the country, from one individual point to another, until he reached the ultima Thule of his journey, with an uninterrupted chain of | friendly intercourse with the most elevated and dignified persons of the empire, the highest officers of his imperial majesty’s government
“not being excepted; during more than four months’ residence at Irkoutsk he was received into the family of his excellency the governor- ¢

general of Eastern Siberia, the virtuous and patriotic Alexander Lavinski,- with a confidence and kindness which rather indicated the affectionate regard of a brother, than the _ cold attentions that would be looked for by an unknown and accidental stranger.

It was from these unexceptionable channels, and not from the spurious, doubtful, and sur4 charged accounts of “criminals and exiles,” that his subject matter has been derived; and ° after such an exposition, he confidently ventures to throw himself upon the candour of the public, to decide whether he has not triumphantly repelled the unjust and unmerited anticipations of Captain Cochrane.

One painful subject remains to be noticed— the abrupt and hasty manner in which ‘the Author was conducted from out of Siberia, and the Russian empire, by the particular mandate of the imperial Alexander, a measure for which he is totally at a loss to assign any satisfactory reason,‘and which prevented’ him from completing the more arduous and interesting part of the arrangement for travel which he had sketched out for himself. | t

The reason advanced, of the Emperor’s anxiety for the personal safety of the Author, is evidently more specious than real, since it is contradicted by the unnecessary harsh treatment, and strict surveillance which were extended over him during his conveyance as a state prisoner to the Austrian frontier. Had this motive really existed, it is reasonable to infer that he would have been left at St. ' Petersburg or Moscow, in the bosom of his friends, instead of being dragged out of the empire, and left on‘its borders, a still greater stranger than even in Siberia itself.

The Author feels it due to himself to state, that he is neither conscious that he could have given private personal offence to his imperial majesty, nor have excited the suspicion or jealousy of the government, by any of his proceedings or enquiries; in short, he neither felt himself prompted by his powers or inclination to interfere with, or animadvert upon, the government, even so far as to pass the slightest censure upon the many glaring faults which could not fail to be observable to the eye of a free-born Englishman.

To conclude, his chief motives, in undertaking this arduous journey, have been to interest himself with human nature, and by comparing it under its different circumstances, to glean a harvest of amusement and information.
And all the teeming regions of the south Hold not a quarry to the curious flight
Of knowledge, half so tempting, or so fair, As man to man.”

He begs to add, that if the facts he has accumulated shall be deemed deserving of the perusal and attention of his countrymen, or contribute to their gratification, his object in publishing them will have been fully accomplished.
On the 19th of July, 1822, I embarked in the Saunders-Hill, schooner, commanded by
Docks, and bound for St. Petersburg, with the
ostensible motive of visiting the Russian empire; but the real one, should circumstances VOL. 1.. B

2 " THE AUTHOR’S MOTIVES, &c. prove propitious, of making a circuit of the. whole world: an intention, however, which, as will be seen in the sequel, was frustrated by causes over which J had no controul. My motives for concealing so important a part of these views, it will not be difficult to ex- - plain: they are attributable to the opposition my kind friends have always been inclined to make against what, under my peculiar deprivation, they are disposed to regard as Quixotic feelings; a feeling on their parts which I am desirous to suppress, since, on various occasions, I have to charge it with the disappointment of my most anxious wishes. Alas! how little are they able to appreciate my true sentiments and powers, as developing themselves in an intense desire to occupy the mind, toacquire solid information, and triumph over those difficulties which others might deem insurmountable! That my views are not chimerical, may be inferred from the success which, as far as my innate powers are concerned, has hitherto attended my exertions. * Where the mind is properly constituted, the diminution of one faculty naturally calls others iy GRAVESEND. 3 into-more extensive action. In my case, the deprivation of sight has been succeeded by an increased desire for locomotion; nor, little as the world may imagine me adapted for its indulgence, am I conscious of having ever ' over-rated my abilities in that particular: in short, there ‘are few obstacles which man’s perseverance may not enable him to overcome, if he will but rightly exercise those faculties with which the beneficence of his Creator has endowed him.

Aftér a delay of many hours, occasioned by the captain not being on board, and other causes, our vessel dropped down to Gravesend, where, however, we did not arrive until seven o’clock on the following evening, and were then detained until lcte in the succeeding day. Soon after leaving this place, the wind being adverse, at five o’clock we anchored in the Lower Hope. Here, about midnight, an acci-

dent occurred, which proved the cause of a mortifying detention. A- large and clumsy collier contrived to run foul of us; and this accompanied by so great a shock, as not only to induce us to think our vessel split in two, but actually to snap the cable, loosen the scroll, or figure-head, and.carry away some of our rigging; we soon, however, disengaged ourselves, and got down another anchor. ‘As this accident was’ occasioned by the carelessness of the other party, who were coming up the river with a fair wind, our captain determined to compel them to compensate the damage he had received; to effect which, and repair our injuries, we were. obliged to return to Gravesend ; which was the more mortifying, ‘as the wind soon after became favourable for our progress down the river.

During the confusion which attended this accident, I was happy in being able to make myself useful by taking the helm, and complying promptly with the-captain’s ‘ starboard’ and ‘ port.’ The best of it was, that he was ignorant of having a blind helmsman, until the fray was over, when, observing some one f ° THE MOUTH OF THE THAMES. | 5 en chemise blanche, (for 1 had turned out of my birth in this state at the moment of alarm,) he at first mistook me for his wife. He was, however, so well satisfied with my nautical skill, as afterward: to permit me to steer the vessel in a fresh breeze.

On the 24th, having repaired damages, we once more quitted Gravesend, and, the wind being fair and the tide in our favour, we soon cleared the mouth of the river. Our rapid progress towards the ocean led me into a train of reflections ; during which the lines of Denham, addressed to the Thames, occurred to.
- me, and. particularly the couplet in which he describes it as
‘ Hastening to pay its tribute to the sea, Like mortal life to meet eternity.”

My meditations, however, were interrupted by what had nearly proved a fatal illustration of this allegory, and of the uncertainty of human life. One cf our sailors, havifig carelessly taken hold of a loose rope, fell overboard from the fore-yard.arm ; being, however, a good swimmer, he was picked up without injury.

My only companions in the cabin were the captain, his wife, and child, a little: girl of about two years of age, whose fretful temper proved no slight annoyance to her parents and myself. Soon after getting out to sea, the lady began to suffer from sickness; the child, however, continued well and troublesome during the voyage.

Although I have never myself experienced the distressing sensation of sea-sickness, I have witnessed so much of its effects as to fancy that I am not incapable of suggesting a variety of means for preventing or relieving it; these I am induced to detail, hoping they may prove’ useful to some suffering voyager. As I believe the affection is generally accompanied by an undue biliary secretion, it appears desirable, for some days before embarking, to put the digestive organs into the best possible state of health. With this view, the diet and other regimen should be plain and unirritating, every thing being:avoided which has a tendency to give rise to acidity on the stomach ; at the same time a gentle dose or two of calomel “may be taken, to clear out the biliary f° MODE OF TREATING IT. 7 passages. ‘The best private stock of provision will comprise plain, unsweetened biscuit, the lean of ham,- hung beef, and a little good brandy ; but tongues, butter, honey, and sweetmeats, should be avoided. On first going on board, the individual should keep quiet, and on no account, however well he may feel, indulge himself in walking on deck, viewing the surrounding objects, or the rigging of the vessel, until he has become habituated to the motions of the latter. He should, as much as possible, divert his mind from noticing the _ motions of the vessel, by occupying it with some amusing or interesting subject. The first meal ought to be particularly sparing, both as to quality and quantity. If it be breakfast, let it consist of a single cup of coffee or tea, with a small quantity of sugar only, and no milk, accompanied by a piece of biscuit or dry bread. If hunger becomes urgent between breakfast and dinner, relieve it with a portion of biscuit; and if thirst is troublesome, allay it with a little weak brandy and water, or a glass of soda-water. At dinner, the most proper food will be a little plain

boiled or roasted meat, without fat of gravy, with a boiled potatoe, or bread ; such vegetables as contain ‘much saccharine principle, and particularly greens, being abstained from; and asa beverage, weak brandy and water, or soda-water, may be taken. If wine be desired, Madeira, or Teneriffe, is preferable to other kinds. In the evening, the tea or coffee, as in the morning, may be repeated; and when disposed to retire to rest, let care be taken to lave as much free air as possible, the confined air of the vessel being one of the most powerful exciting causes of the indisposition. If, notwithstanding, symptoms of sickness come on, I would recommend, on the first approach of giddiness, to assume a horizontal position on deck, if possible, for the advantage of the refreshing air, and to take occasionally, particularly after each effort of vomiting, a little sodawater. By attending to the above directions, the attack may, throughout the voyage, either be prevented, or, at least, materially alleviated.
For the succeeding three days our progress was favourable, but on the 29th a squall car-

ried away the fore-top gallant-mast ; we soon however got the wreck cleared, and another substituted, and in the evening of this day the coast of Jutland began to make its appearance ;-on the following day we came in sight of the Swedish coast, passed the Castle of Marstrand, and in sight of the wings beacon at the entrance of Gothenberg, and by evening arrived at the entrance of the Categate. On the Ist of July we made the Island of Zealand, ‘and ‘passed the Castle of Cronberg, built by Christian the Fourth, where the unfortunate Matilda, Queen of Denmark, and sister to our late king, was detained a prisoner. In the evening we anchored in Elsinore roads. On Tuesday, July 2nd, we landed at Elsinore, and ‘breakfasted with our hospitable consul Mr. Fenwick. The wind being fair, Captain Courtney, anxious to get forward, as soon as his necessary business with the port was transacted, to enable him to pass the sound, hurried me away, co that I had no time to visit the interesting objects of the place, some of which would have afforded "ne considerable satisfaction, particularly the Castle of Cron-

berg, and the palace and gardens where Hamlet’s father is reported to. have been murdered and buried. This palace is said to be a large square stone building, standing on the foot of a hill, which gradually rises beyond it, and which is ascended by serpentine walks planted with trees, whose ample foliage affords an agreeable shelter from the scorching heat of the noon-tide sun, and leads to the famed spot immortalized by Shakspeare, in the following passage, as the scene of poor Ophelia’s fate.
*¢ There is a willow grows ascaunt the brook,
That shows his hoar leaves in the glassy stream ; Therewith fantastic garlands did she make
Of crow-flowers, nettles, daisies, and long purples, That liberal shepherds give a grosser name,
But our cold maids do dead men’s fingers call them : * There on the pendent boughs her coronet weeds Clambering to hang, an envious sliver broke ;
Fell in the weeping brook. Her clothes spread wide ; And, mermaid-like, a while they bore her up:
Which time, she chaunted snatches of old tunes ;
As ong incapable of her own distress,.
Unto that element: but long it could not be,
Till that her garments, heavy with their drink ~ Pe'l’d the poor wretch from her melodious lay
Independent of the poetical interest it excites, the spot itself is highly picturesque and

The houses of Elsinore are generally large, lofty, and well built, and at the same time ex- ‘ceedingly neat and clean; the streets are however narrow, ill paved, and without footways, while the windows of the basement story project so much into the street, that the pedestrian is in constant danger of being driven over by the carriages.

_At one o’clock in the afternoon we again got under weigh; at two, past Tycho Brach’s Island, the wind being light and variable ; and at half ° after ten in the evening anchored off the Crown Battery at Copenhagen. I anxiously wished for an adverse wind to prevent our sailing, so as to allow me time to visit the city of Copenhagen ; but after a stormy and rainy morning, the weather became so fair about noon, that we left our anchorage and procecded on the voyage. After cdasting all day along the Islands of Zealand and Drago, in the evening we entcred the Baltic Sea, steering straight for the Island of Born-

holm, which we made early the next day, and from whence we were visited by a boat laden with poultry, eggs, and milk. On the following morning we saw the Island of Gothland, where General Norby retired with the Danish fleet from Calmar, on receiving accounts of a general insurrection in Denmark ; the consequence of which movement was the siege and capture of that city by Gustavus Vasa. During the two next days we had boisterous weather and rough seas, but on the following day, July 7th, the weather proved very fine, and at ten in the morning we found ourselves off the Light-house on the Island of Dagho, which lies at the entrance of the Gulf of Riga. There is a passage on each side for shipping, but the western one is the deepest and largest. Some years back the proprietor of this island, Baron » built a house on an elevated situation, crowning it with an octagonal tower, in which large mirrors Os plate glass were eisposed to reflect the light so as to resemble the light-house ; this
- room he occasionally caused to be illuminated, while the proper light-house was kept in

darkness; deluded by the artifice, many vessels were wrecked on the coast, with the loss of numbers of their crews ; the cargoes were then seized by this monster, and appropriated to the gratification of his infamous cupidity. At length the captain of a vessel, who had been a sufferer in consequence, ventured to wait upon the baron, intending to upbraid him with his treachery: it happened that a person who had officiated in the family as a tutor, had experienced a fit, and was supposed to have died, so — that his corpse had been laid out in one of the apartments of the castle. Into this room, the baron conducted his victim, and there dreading a disclosure of his villanies, murdered him with an axe. At this juncture the supposed corpse recovered its sensibility,eand witnessed the cruel scene, but had the prudence to continue motionless until the inhuman monster had left the apartment, when he availed himself of the opportunity to escape to Riga, and gave that informaticn which terminated in the wretch’s perpetual banishment amid the savage wilds of Siberia; there @ prey to conscience and remorse, he dragged out the misera-
ble remnant of an existence, already too near its close to allow time to expiate a life of such dreadful depravity.

We now entered the Gulf of Finland, and commenced an intricate and dangerous navigation, which, however, is facilitated by different coloured flags placed on the various shoals, and a number of light-houses, for which the Russian government do not exact-any dues. Towards midnight we had much thunder and lightning, followed by a heavy squall of rain. At three in the afternoon of the 10th of July, we approached the guard-ship off the harbour of Cronstadt, who fired a shot to compel us to come to an anchor in these roads, which, as it was a strong gale, the captain would gladly. shave avoided; for he even apprehended this measure would have occasioned the loss of his vessel, and was desirous to run straight into harbour ; he was obliged however to attempt a compliance, and the consequence was, that his cadle broke and parted from the first anchor, while the vessel drifted so far with the second anchor,*as to have been very nearly on slidre ; this result, however, would have been
a matter of perfect indiffererice to the commanding: officer of the guard-ship ; at length the weather became more moderate, and enabled us to lie secure. |

Early on the following morning, the guardboat visited us, with her crew in a state of evident intoxication, in consequence of their previous yisits to other vessels, from each of which they invariably expect to be treated _ with liquors; a point of discipline widely different from what is observed,in the British ‘service. Our captain was unwilling to increase their exhilaration; but as soon as the officers descended into the cabin, they desired their crew might be furnished with brandy. The captain was then given to understand that he must pay for the shot that had been fired over him: this is said to be a perquisite of the captain of the guard-ship. I am, however, much mistaken, judging from the sound, if there was any shot really fired over us; be this as it may, it appears hard enoug}i to Le | obliged to pay for the instrument df one’s own punishment, like a boy at school, who is charged for the birch that tickles him.

A singular feature in the manners of these gentry is a system of begging any, or every, article which happens to take their fancy, | and this in a way that neither expects, nor admits of, adenial; nay, such was their rapacity and meanness, that one even asked the captain to give him needles, thread and tape, for the use of his wife; and which, to keep him in good humour, were promised on the next voyage. I afterward heard many luvdicrous instances of the extent to which they sometimes carry their begging system. A.”

- lady of my acquaintance came over when a child, and brought a doll for her amusement: one of the custom-house fellows took it into his head to long for this plaything, and, with yapturous admiration, made his petition accordingly ; nor could the poor child’s tears, nor the captain’s entreaties, induce him to forego his covetous demand. At length the child’s unwilling and faltering consent was © gained, by a promise of Lringing her a better one next voyage. Cold, indeed, must be the. hearts of such.nen!
Of course this system is not sanctioned by
the government; it is only submitted to by

the captains of foreign vessels to preserve the complacency, and prevent the ill-will and annoyance of these fellows in the arrangement of their port duties. On the contrary, an instance occurred not long since, where, on a threat of complaint to the government, the officer, in the most abject manner, returned the articles he had received, and entreated that the affair might not be noticed. In our instance, their cupidity received a material check, on finding that there was a British officer on board; and, as they have a wonderful respect for military rank, from that moment all begging ceased.

I trust that these unpleasant traits of Russian character will be softened down on a more intimate acquaintance. They could not, however, fail to excite an unfavourable impression at the very moment of entering the country; nor am I unaware of the injustice of drawing general inferences from the peculiar manners and customs of a sea-port. How incorrect would be the opinion of a foreigner with respect to our own country, were he to

take his estimates of its character from the impressions he might receive on his first landing at our sea-ports! He would necessarily fail to discover any of that genuine solidity and integrity of character peculiar to our country, which developes itself so gradually as almost to close the door against the admission of friendly intercourse with strangers; but which, once admitted, evinces more purity, and permanence, than attaches to any other people in the world.

We were now for some time detained by the necessary arrangements with the customhouse, during which I preferred remaining on board the vessel to entering the inns of Cronstadt, whith, by report, are little better than * ale-houses; and I was not permitted to proceed to St. Petersburg until my passport was regulated, and which could not be effected filess than twenty-four hours. On the following afternoon, however, I was induced to go on shore, by the receipt of a polite invitation from the Rev. Mr. B——, an English clergyman resident at this place, who had heard of me through the medium of the press.

Our captain and his lady accompanied me; and with them I visited a large shop, where we were presented with tumblers of tea, prepared with lemon-juice, as a substitute for cream, as is their custom during the time of a fast. After this, I had the pleasure of passing amost agreeable evening in the company of Mr. B—— and his sisters, where I could not avoid noticing a peculiarity in the tea, as if it had been made from aromatic herbs. It was of a fine quality, but scented with the flowers of a Chinese shrub, (the olea fragrans ; named by the Chinese qguaz-fa,) a small quantity of which is placed at the top of each chest. The tea thus perfumed is then termed “ flower-tea,” and is in particular estimation among the Russians.

Mr. B a Greek church during the time of service, was kind enough to take me to and afterwards to a new chapel of his own, at present in an unfinished state, and which will be a most important accommodation to the numerous British seamen who enter this port. In the evening I returned on Loard.
On the following morning I again went on

shore, to call on our worthy consul, Mr. Booker, and was taken to examine his lifeboat, which was made of wicker-work, covered with leather, with two skates under it, running the whole length of the boat; the advantage of which structure is, to enable it to be used in crossing the Gulf of Finland, either in the water or on the ice, as. circumstances may require. Mr. Booker, whose house is the very temple of hospitality, kindly invited me to pass the remainder of the day with him; but as my passport was now ready, I was desirous of proceeding immediately to St. Petersburg.

At five o’clock I took my passage in the steam-boat to St. Petersburg, distant, from Cronstadt about fifteen miles, or twenty-two Russian versts, for which I paid five roubles.* I was not, however, allowed ta take my luggage, unless I would consent to pay a cus-

* The Russian rouble corresponds with the French franc, being (according to the present rate of exchange) equal to ten-pence of English money. For a particular account of the moneys, weights, and measures of this country, the reader is referred to Appendix B.

\ * ARRIVAL AT ST. PETERSBURG. 1 tom-house officer for accompanying it; and therefore contented myself with a sufficiency for immediate purposes, leaving the remainder to be forwarded to the customhouse at St. Petersburg with the vessel’s cargo. ;

In this short voyage I had the advantage of being accompanied by one of Mr. B.’s clerks ; who, on our arrival at the imperial city, about eight o’clock, kindly procured a droshka, and conducted me to the abode of my old and particular friend, Mr.C—l1—b—k, the gentleman whom I have so frequently mentioned in my late Travels through France and Italy.

WueEn I arrived at St. Petersburg, our ambassador and consul, as well as the principal part of the English merchants, were enjoying their summer country residences, at a distance of'from five to fifteen miles from the city, chiefly in the direction of the Peterhof road, which may be regarded as the court side of the town. The kind offices of my friend C—, and the many letters of introduction with which I was provided, soon, however, enabled me to avail myself of numerous invitations, so that it was not long before I found mvself immersed in all the gaiety of this animated metropolis, and its neighbourhood.

One of my first concerns was to procure a servant, and I had the good fortune to meet with an intelligent Russian youth of eighteen, well acquainted with the French language, and consequently qualified to act as an interpreter in my various transactions with his countrymen.

For some days I was occupied with visiting my friends, and delivering my letters of introduction. On the second day I had the pleasure of accompanying Mr. C—— to the country residence of a gentleman six miles out ot town on the Peterhof road ; while here a most tremendous thunder storm came on, which killed a horse,'and melted part of a metal inscription over the portico of the residence of our ambassador in this neighbourhood. These convulsions of nature, I soon learnt, are frequent in this country during the summer season.

In the course of this morning, my friend took the opportunity of enquiring the christened name of my ‘ather, in order that his servant might know how to address me with due respect. It is peculiar tu this country, that no one thinks of addressing his superior

with a title correspondent to our Mr.,:but by an addition of his own to his father’s christian name ;—for instance, my father’s name being John, I was called James the son of John ; unless there be two of a name the surname is considered superfluous. A still more respectful manner of addressing elderly peo- - ple is to call them “ father” or “ mother,” while amongst the lower orders, they address all of nearly their own age as “ brother” or * sister.” On the 20th, I had the gratification of dining at our consul-general’s, in company with some of. the members of our embassy, as well as other distinguished persons, among whom was the celebrated general of engineers, Betancour. ‘In a few days afterward I was also honoured with an invitation to the country residence of our ambassador, where I had the pleasure of meeting a large party, comprising among others, some of the foreign ministers, Sir R. K. Porter, and other brother travelers. On th@.ist of August, while driving on the Peterhof road, we had the gratification of being passed by the emperor in his caleche,

drawn by four horses abreast, and who was on his way to our ambassador’s to stand sponsor for one of his children. His majesty was dressed in the uniform of his guards, green, with red cuffs and collar. The coachman was in the costume of his country, that is, he wore a long caftan tied round the waist by a red sashs a black velvet cap fastened close round his head, square at the top, and ornamented with a tassel on the centre; and_on his hands, a large pair of military gloves that passed over the cuffs of the caftan. Only one feld-jager, in’ full uniform, followed the carriage.

This I am told is his majesty’s usual style of travelling in the neighbourhood of the city; in the city itself, however, he drives only a ‘pair, and sometimes a single horse. IIe is always, remarkably condescending in his manner, returning every salute either with a bow, or by touching the corner of his hat; and he not unfrequently stops and enters into conversation with such persons as he is acquainted with. Several of niy friends have had this honour. °

In about a week after this time, his imperial majesty reviewed his fleet, which was lying at Cronstadt, and which is fitted out every summer. for a three months’ cruize in the Gulf of Finland, for it seldom ventures into the Baltic; so that this part of the Russian navy may fairly be termed “ fresh-water sailors,” as the water in this gulf is scarcely brackish, even at its upper part, near the Baltic ;—it contains in short, so little saline principle, that I could with advantage use it with soap to wash with. Perhaps, I should not be carrying the accusation too far to term them also “ fair-weather sailors ;” since, on an indication of foul weather, they immediately make for port.

The constitution of the Russian navy is widely different from that of England, as. their sailors are formed into regiments, and occupied for more than half the year as garrison soldiers. These regiments, termed equipages, rank with the guards; one, however, is more particularly called “ the guard equipage,” and employed in the personal service of the emperor. Three of these regi-

ments form a brigade, commanded by a rearadmiral; while each individual regiment is under the controul of a captain of the first rank, which is equal to that of a colonel in the army, with a proportionate number of subordinate officers, who are all educated as cadets for the service, and regularly exercised in nautical tactics, having -a hull of a ship built.on shore, which is masted and rigged for that purpose, as well as yachts, to enable them to acquire a practical knowledge of their profession,, by cruizing in the Baltic.

Promotion in these corps goes by seniority, excepting that any distinguished service, or the pleasure of his imperial majesty, may authorize a deviation from the general rule. It may be questioned whether this system is favourable to the character of the Russian navy. On the one side, it may be urged, that the length of time required to reach the higher ranks, must afford every opportunity of gaining a due proficiency ; while, on the other hand, the sti- Mulus for exertion may be diminished, by the certainty of attaining promotion as a mere

matter of course. We have, however, an instance, in the super-eminent abilities and distinguished conduct of our artillery and marine corps, that this latter principle does not necessarily operate to produce such a result.

On the llth, I accompanied some friends to visit the Sarskoe-Selo and Pavlosky palaces. We were, however, disappointed in seeing the interior of either of them, as a part of the imperial family were occupying them as summer residences. I purpose, however, to avail myself of a future opportunity of describing them. We were, notwithstanding this disappointment, much gratified with the beauty of the gardens, and returried highly delighted with our day’s excursion.
° On the 16th, the emperor quitted his capital for Warsaw, with the intention of proceeding from thence to the congress of Verona.

On the following day, I had the gratification of being introduced as a visitor to’the English club, with respect to which excellent establishment I shall have many observations to make on.a fuinte occasion. After dinner, several of the members retired to the bowling-

green, where I ‘was vain enough to attempt a participation in their amusement; and, what is more, to fancy that there was not any material difference to be found between those who could,.and those who could not see.

Early on the morning of the 11th of September, the guns of the fortress burst forth tidings of joy; which, on inquiry, proved to be the annunciation of the birth of a princess, the fourth child of the Grand Duke Nicholas. The day was, however, a propitious one for other reasons, being no less than the anniversary of the emperot’s names-day, and that of St. Alexander Nevsky, who is also the patron saint of Petersburg. On the latter account, there was a grand procession of ‘the clergy, from the Casan Church to the monastery of St. Alexander Nevsky, where his mortal remains and mysterious relics are deposited, and which the empress and other parts of the imperial family, with thousands of pious or curious persons, accompanied.
I did not attend this procession; such ceremonies being by no means congenial with my feelings and sentiments, as they partake

too much of the important’ nothingness of this world to interest me. Above all, I pity the man whom circumstances compel to a life of monastic seclusion, or who has hisenergies and active benevolence cramped by the dull and monotonous observances of forms and ceremonies, It is from the spirit of rational liberty, the study of men and manners, and contemplating the unaffected simplicity of nature, that I derive my highest gratifications.
“Thou, Nature, art my goddess; to thy laws My services are bound! Wherefore should I Stand in the plague of customs ?”

And yet, without doubt, such ceremonials operate powerfully on the minds of men, and become important, if not necessary, engines in their political management; and at the same time, serve essentially to demonstrate the tone of national character.
In the evening, the imperial yachts on the river were illuminated.
Soon after this time, the variability of the weather began to indicate that the summer
‘was rapidly drawing to a close, and to announce the approach of winter. This is a subject, however, which I am induced to ‘ reserve for an exclusive chapter.

On the 17th of October, the ship Kitty, Captain Warren, arrived at Cronstadt, after the short passage of ten days from London, having been only thirty-five days from this port, during. which time she had delivered her cargo in the London Docks. This is her fourth voyage to St. Petersburg during the present summer; and, if she returns safe to London, is more than any vessel has before accomplished. She had, however, a narrow escape this time from being wrecked on the Island of Dagho, in consequence of being deceived by a false light, that of the proper light-house having been extinguished, whether by accid2nt or design, as in the anecdcite previously related in my voyage to this country, Thad no opportunity of ascertaining. I have since learnt that she eventually reached London in safety.

a gentleman who was singular enough to drink salt and water instead of wine, and who, I am informed, is a great projector, having. presented the government here with a variety” of plans of proposed improvements; one of which was, to form a water communication, in a direct line, between Lake Ladoga and the Gulf of Finland, which would not only shorten the distance one-third, but ensure a safer and more ready communicaiion than by the Neva, the rapid current and shoals of which river prove extremely dangerous to its navigation. The government. however, is said to have declined embracing any of his speculations, but have accorded so far with his personal interests, with respect to one ‘of them, as to have made him a grant of a tract of land in Finland, with exclusive privi- . leges, to enable him to work a mine there, which he pronounces to be exceedingly rich in copper ore. “
Now we are on the subject of speculation, I will take the opportunity of noticing a threatened disappointment in a speculation of another kind, which occurred about this

time, and excited much conversation in St. Petersburg. A gentleman and lady, accompanied by a large party of friends, presented themselves, one morning, at the door of the english chapel, with the view of being linked together in the happy chain of matrimony, when, to their great consternation, it was announced that the clergyman was absent in the country, and not expected to return before the important hour of twelve, after which it was conceived the ceremony could not be performed. Independent of the annoying jocularity of their friends, other serious objections to the delay started up: all the preparations for the day were in advance; the apartments prepared, and the cooks busily employed in the necessary arrangements for the marriage-feast, and the subsequent ball in the evening. What is to be done? are these operations to be suspended, or are they to proceed? At three o'clock, however, the clergyman returned,’and kindly consented to marry them at four. The bride recovered . from her fainting fits, the bride&room’s spirits were re-assured, and the day concluded with — VOL, I. D

additional hilarity and happiness. The dilemma arose from a neglect in not duly advertising the clergyman of the day of marriage ; the fault, however, lay with the clerk, who, on being applied to, informed the gentleman that it was quite unnecessary to pre-cngage the clergyman, as he always remained at home until after one o'clock.

A still more ludicrous disappointment happened during the present summer, at the same chapel. A wedding party had assem-, bled, and were waiting for the clergyman, when the bridegroom, whispering to the bride that he wished to step out for an instant, quitted the church. The clergyman soon made his appearance, but the bridegroom was not to be found; and, after waiting for nearly two hours, the party were obliged to return to their homes without the ceremony being performed. It proved that the gentleman had gone out with the view of asking an old and particular friend to be father to his bride; but, b¢éing a broker, had unfortunately, instead.of entering at once upon the subject of his visit, commenced with a point of business, which so absorbed him, as to entirely put the more immediate concern out-of his head; so that he literally forgot his bride and all the promised happiness he had been so near realizing. ‘The ceremony was, however, performed on the following day, to the surprise of many of the ladies, who declared that, after such neglect, they would have rejected such a husband in toto.

We now arrived near the close of the year, and this without any permanency of that rigorous frost which so usually characterises - a Russian winter, but of which We were yet destined to have a specimen. The river did not close permanently until a few days before Christmas. The days now attained their shortest length; and the season, owing to this cause, and the uncertainty and variability of the weather, became a most disagreeable one ; numerous sources of occupation and amusement were, however, still open to me; and’ what between the pleasures of society, and * the pursuit of information respecting thosé parts of the empire I was so’ soon to travel through, and which I gleaned not only by personal inquiry, but also from the best authors on the subject, whether ancient or modern, I had no reason to’complain that the hours hung, heavily or unpleasantly, on my hands. Occasionally I occupied myself in studying the geography of Russia, tracing my intended route with the finger. I beg to observe, however, that I was always particularly cautious in divulging my real plans; on the contrary, I rather endeavoured to keep them concealed, by appearing to show a greater interest with respect to parts that I least contemplated visiting. This reserve appeared to be neces+ sary, to avoid fruitless argument, and prevent my being accused of wild and chimerical views, and which the world are too fond of giving me the credit of.
I had the gratification of celebrating the happy festival of Christmas a PAnglois, with a party of my countrymen.

On the following evening the whole city was in agitation, from an extensive fire breaking out, the light from which, in consequence of the clearness of*the atmosphere, was so vivid as to illuminate every part of the town.

All the inhabitants imagined it in their own heighbourhood ; whereas it proved to be in the suburbs, a quarter of a mile from the Peterhof Gate. It originated in an immense wooden building, used as a cloth manufactory ; and, notwithstanding the prompt and energetic exertions of the well-regulated fire-police, was soon entirely consumed. Fires are here always more formidable in winter, on account of the greater difficulty in procuring supplies of water.

This being the holiday season, our dinner parties were unusually numerous ; and, as far as the most sumptuous cheer, and rational and brilliant conversation could effect it, were in the highest degree interesting; so that we seldom separated without regret.
“ "Tis pain to depart in the luminous hour
Of wine and of wit, when the heart is in flower, Which shoots from the lip, under Bacchus’s dew, In blossoms of thought, ever springing and new.”

Nor was the softer’and fascinating converse with the fairer sex neglected, or undervalued, by us; for few evenings passéd without engagements to balls or musical parties, in which they shone most conspicuous.
Oh, woman! whose form and whose soul Are the spell and the light of each path we pursue! Whether sunn’d at the tropics, or chill’d at the pole, If woman be there, there is happiness too!”

On the Ist of January, 1823, I had the pleasure of dining with a party of English at Mr. L——’s, in order to welcome. the new year; which holiday is, by most foreigners. doubly celebrated in this city, some keeping the new style, while others adhere to the old.

On the fourth of this month, in company with my friend C, I visited the market of frozen provisions, «where the produce *of no less than two thousand sledges are exposed for sale, the whole of which were nearly disposed of. ie

year’s-day, on which the inhabitants make it a rule to call upon, or to send: cards of congratulation to all their friends. * On the 18th, the grand ceremony of blessing the waters of the Neva took place, of whiclr I have given a full description in another place.

On the 2ist, I accompanied a friend to thd Gustinoy-Dwar, or quarter for shops, with a view of making purchases. These shops are ‘comprised in two square buildings of immense extent, the one contained within the other, the inner constituting a body of warehouses, from which the retail shops, situated in the outer quadrangle, draw their supplies. The latter is two stories in height, and ornamented with a colonnade around both of them.
On the 2d of February, the emperor made his first appearance in St. Petersburg, after his return from Verona, and was received with évery indication of juy by his subjects.
On the 14th of this month I had the honour, with some other friends, of being introduced, by Sir James Wylie, to the Grand Duke

Michael, who, in the most condescending manner, was pleased to conduct us over the Artillery School, which is under his especial patronage. The great order and regularity of this institution afforded me the highest gratification. I was particularly interested by two boys from Iceland, and several young’ Cossacks, who were educating in this school. His royal highness afterwards was pleased to accompany us to the Artillery Hospital, and from thence to the hospital of the imperial guards, in both of which every attention appeared to be paid to the cleanliness, comfort. and welfare of the patients. There was one poor fellow who, under the delirium of a fever, had fractured his own skull with a hammer; he was, however, in a fair way of recovery.

I feel myself highly indebted to Sir James Wylie’s kindness for various other attentions, and particularly for the active interest he took in my defect of vision. He not only personally examineé my eyes, but introduced me to some of the most eminent oculists of St. Petersburg. Unfortunately, however, the result only afforded a confirmation of the
many previous opinions that I had been favoured with on this subject; all agreeing that, until some change took place in the state of the organ, an operation was not likely to prove beneficial. ;

On Tuesday, the 18th,"I paid a visit to the first house that was inhabited in this city by its founder, Peter the Great; a gratification of niy curiosity which I had frequently before been anxious to indulge, but could not induce any of my friends to fix a time for accompanying me. I have often been impressed by the indisposition, or, perhaps, more properly speaking, habit of procrastination, which Many acquire with respect to points that admit of being effected at any-time; and shave been compelled to goad them, as it were, to gratify themselves with what they have long proposed to, accomplish, but had never undertaken, because they considered it at all .times within their reach. For my own part, however, I never wish to jose sight of the old proverb—* Carpe Diem.”
This interesting hut, still in good preservation, is built of larch wood, to which its great

durability is attributed: it is, however, protected by a temporary building. It comprises only three small rooms, one of which was the ynonarch’s bed-chamber. In the corner of the latter was a priest’s cloak, hanging on a peg, an image, and a censer, intended for the use of a clergyman who performs some religious ceremony here at stated periods; such is the veneration in which this almost sacred building is held by the Russians, who regard it as the germ from which their magnificent city originated.

There is also a boat preserved under the same temporary roof, which was built by this extraordinary man: it is a kind of Dutch yawl, clinker built, with the head and stern alike, and is now in a very decayed state.

Thursday, the 27th, was a day of high gratification to me, as I had the honour of dining a la Cossaque, with the celebrated General Yefremoff, at the village appropriated for the quarters of the Co§sack troops stationed at St. Petersburg, and which is situated about a mile beyond the Nevsky Ménastery. Our % party was received by the general in the most
warm and friendly manner. JI was, I believe,

the only stranger present; but his polite attentions soon banished all reserve. He had even the condescension to bring me his helmet, and a variety of other articles, which he thought might interest me to examine. He also ordered in some of his soldiers, that

ments. How gratifying to receive such attentions from such a man! and how unjust, to designate, as barbarous, a hation, one of whose members, risen from the rank of a common soldier, can shew so much sentiment and sensibility to an apparently unfortunate individual like myself! ° :

Previous to dinner being announced, we were tempted to whet our appetites with caviare, dried fish from the Don, cheese, &c. with brandy and various other liquors, including a peculiar spirit, made in the country of the Don Cossack, in which the buds of the birch-tree had been infused, that made it so bitter as to be quite nauscous.
-At length dirner was served up—if in order,
in a very reverse one to what I had been

accustomed. The first dish.was corned beef, followed by sturgeon, which, in its turn, was ‘succeeded by soup; after this we had a varicty of made-dishes and of game, while roasted meats brought up the rear.

We had a great variety of wines, comprising Madeira and French wines; but these were neglected for the more agreeable ones from the general’s own estates, in the Don Country. Most of these were very sweet and effervescent, like champaigne and’ cyder, agreeable to the taste, but, at the same time, highly treacherous, and sure to give a severe headache next day if indulged in, particularly when drank, as is usually done here, out of tumblers.

As soon as dinner was concluded, we retired into an adjoining room, to take coffee; about an houy after which a most sumptuous dessert was introduced. The glass now again circulated with freedom; and, as there was no escaping the vigilarfte of a Cossack geheral, Tam afraid few of our party could hope to escape the penalty of the succetding morning. Our good host was the life of his company: :
nor do I recollect when I ever spent a more animated and happy day.

While taking our wine, some Cossack children occasionally ran into the room, one of whom, a little girl of about three years of age, I took into my arms, and presented with wine, which she appeared to take with much relish ; in short, she was so contented with her situation, as to be unwilling to leave me.

The novelty of our entertainment was, however yet to come. A dozen strapping Cossacks now entered the room, and began to entertain us with a variety of their national songs, the whole singing together, but each taking separate parts. After this had proceeded for a time, all on a sudden, they caught

«up one of our party, laid him out on their arms, and began tossing him into the air, thus making him dance to the tune of their song; this was repeated in succession with each individual, and considered a great compliment, which was returned by a present of money. It was practised upon the general himself
_28 Well as his Visitors. A single individual of our party alone escaped this dance in the air:
he was one of the imperial chamnberlains, and so bulky, that the Don amateurs were actually shy of amusing themselves with his person.
I shall conclude the above account, with a few historical anecdotes of our noble host.

At the period of the battle of Leipsic he had attained only the rank of colonel, and had then the honour of saving his emperor from falling into the hands of the enemy. He was advancing at the head of three hundred cossacks, when’ he met his imperial majesty, closely pressed by a body of French cavalry. He was ordered by the emperor to charge the French with the view of allowing him time for escape ; this, notwithstanding the great disparity of force, was effected in the most gallant manner; the clouds of dust which their advance occasioned prevented the enemy from ascertaining their numbers, while the horrid yell which always accompanies the charge of these troops, struck such terror into the hearts of their adversaries, that they speedily retreated. ” For this important service, Colonel Yefremoff received from the empcror’s hand, on the ficld of battle, the order of St. George, of which he is more proud than of all the other laurels won by him during the war. The rank of general soon followed, and he now stands next to the hetman.

During the retreat of the French army, his gallant conduct attracted so forcibly the attention of Murat, who commanded the French -cavalry, that he sent him a valuable watch, accompanied by a flag of truce, with the request that it might be presented to the gallant officer who commanded the cossack troops, as a mark of his esteem, for the activity and bravery he had so often witnessed. What an honourable testimonial to receive from an enemy!

Sunday, March 9th. The weather is now become so much milder that the snow is fast disappearing in the streets, and I consequently become anxious to expedite my departure for Moscow, under the apprehension that I might otherwise lose the advantage of the snowroads, which is considered, beyond comparison, the most pleasant and expeditious mode of travelling in this country. I determined, therefore, to limit my remaining residence in this city to three or four days more at farthest; on enquiry, however, I had the mortification of learning, that the Moscow diligence, in which I proposed to take my place, was already on its wheels, in conse- “quence of a deficiency of snow for more than a hundred versts from St. Petersburg; ,but that after proceeding thus far, we should again meet with snow,which would carry us more than four hundred miles in a S. E. direc- ‘tion. This proves, what, however, I believe, all philosophers have admitted, that the inte- | rior of a country is colder in winter, in proportion to its latitude, than ‘those parts which are nearer its coasts; and it appears also, that it is in the same ratio warmer in summer: for instance, the degrees of cold in winter, as well as of heat in summer, are much greater at Moscow than at St. Petersburg, notwithstanding its latitude is nearly five degrees more southerly. The reason of this is, that the surface of the earth, which is solid and opaque, attains the temperature of the atmosphere, sooner than the surface of the sea, which is constantly changing its particies, “until its whole depth is brought to a similar tempera- VOL. I. E ture; consequently it is longer in cooling during winter, and warming during summer.

I recollect having frequently experienced an illustration of this principle, when sailing southward, in winter time, from North America. We always knew when we were within the influence of a current (or gulf-stream, as sai-_ lors term it, from its coming from the Gulf of Florida, whence it runs northward along the coast of America,) by.the increase of atmuspheric temperature arising from the warmer exhalations of this current, the water of which always proves, on examination, to be comparatively warm.

BeroreE taking leave of St. Petersburg, it will naturally be expected that"I should make some remarks concerning this city and its neighbourhood. My notices of these points, however, must necessarily be very incomplete, and, possibly, in some instances, from the peculiarity of my situation, inaccurate; I profess, therefore, to con‘ine myself to such facts, as either became more expressly the subjects of my own enquiries, or accidentally fell in my way.

To preserve consistency in my remarks, I shall comprise them under a variety of heads: and, in the first place, shall attempt to convey the result of my observations,.respecting the situation, localities, and neighbourhood of this interesting capital.

* by its immortal founder, Peter the Great, is, in consequence of its neighbourhood to the Baltic sea, and its communications with the interior by water, by no means ill adapted to be the capital of this immense’empire, whether we lock to the facility afforded to intercourse with its own distant provinces, or with those nations of Europe, with whom it may maintain political, or commercial relations.
In bringing this city, however, to its present grandeur, many disadvantages, both of situation and climate, were to be contended against.

little better than a morass, and, perhaps, affords, at this time, one of the most glorious instances of the rapid triumph of art over nature; since the industry of man has, in little more than a century, clothed its naked marshes

BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE CITY. 53 with superb palaces, embellished by scenery of the most interesting description. In short, St. Petersburg, previously an insignificant village, and comprising only a few fishermen’s huts, is now become one of the most extensive, populous, and magnificent cities in the world.

It is situated, more immediately, on the banks and islands of the Neva, a considerable river, which receiving its waters from the Ladoga Lake, after a course of forty miles, pours its rapid and chrystalline stream into the Gulf of Finland. 7

This city stands upon a considerable extent éf.¢round, which, however, is not yet wholly occupied by building, but comprises many extensive gardens. According to the latest accounts, its population consists of more than two hundred and fifty thousand souls, comprising natives from almost every civilized part of the world. Its streets are broad, and well-built ; its few squares elegant and spacious; its architecture rich and varied; and its churches, palaces, and public buildings, numerous and magnificent. It is im- . possible to describe the gratification which,
notwithstanding my loss of vision, I derived from my frequent contemplations df the various objects of interest it contains.

The reader will, probably, wonder how I could derive, in this wey, any actual gratification, or correct ideas of the objects themselves. As this is an universal objection, applicable to my whole scheme of travel, I shall avail myself of the present opportunity of explaining and defending myself.

The various organs of sense are the mere instruments by which the impressions of external objects are conveyed to the mind, which then reasons upon, and draws its inferentyg respecting, the nature of these objects. The conclusions thus arrived at, are, consequently, mere tdeas, and yet they comprize all we can really know, respecting the appearances, forms, and qualities of whatever is external to us; and in this sense our whole knowledge of the external world is but ideal.

Now, so as ideas are excited in the mind respecting the existence of external things, it matters not through what senses the impressions from which they are derived are r) EXPLANATORY OBSERVATIONS. ft)

transmitted ; whether through the medium of sight, touch, hearing, or any other sense ; and although the eye be the more generally appropriate one for this purpose, yet all the others admit of being put into requisition as auxiliaries to it, or, when vision is denied, as substitutes for it; and it it well-known what extensive powers they acquire under such circumstances. But it will be urged, that the knowledge thus attained, cannot be depended upon as strictly correct. This I admit; but it matters not as to the ultimate effect, as regards the feelings of the "individual ;—the gperations of his mind may be called forth with equal force, and, aided by the power of imagination, and the recollections of pre-existent analogies, or other information acquired previous to his loss of the organ in question, its conclusions may, notwithstanding many inaccuracies, be equally decided, and, perhaps, equally agreeable, as under ordinary circumstances. Hence the opinions I am led to form, of the countries through which I travel, afford me ineffable delight. There "is, however, _«probably, another advantage,—that the atten-
tion being chiefly directed to the more grand and interesting features, the meaner ones are in a proportionate degree excluded. ‘

The reader will, probably, now comprehend the 'manner in which I arrive at what, perhaps, may be termed an zdeal knowledge of the places I visit. Accompanied by an intelligent friénd, or some other guide, I examine every place of interest;—touch what I can, and hear of all; and then combining the in-

‘formation thus gained with previously ac- -quired knowledge of the subject, and some portion of imagination, a picture is produced, comprising, in my mind, a strong impression of reality, and answering the purpose to me, almost as well as if I had actually seen it. How far my descriptions of such pictures correspond with the actual lineaments of the objects themselves, I must leave to others to determine..

I shall now attempt a brief, but, I fear, very imperfect, account of the more ‘remarkable palaces, or other magnificent public buildings with which tais metropolis, and its environs, abound. The approach from Germany is by

one of the most magnificent roads that can be imagined, and which, from its leading to thé imperial palace of Peterhof, is termed the Peterhof Road. It consists, for a distance of twenty versts, of one continued line of elegant villas, which are the summer residences of the nobles, and more wealthy merchants. To the westward ‘of this road, in the direction of Cronstadt, is situated the palace of Oranienbaum, formerly the favourite residence of Peter the Third, whence he was forcibly conducted to Roptsha, previous to his imprisonment and death. This palace, which commands delightful views of the Gulf of Finland, Cronstadt, and the Finnish coast, is still kept up, although the imperial family never reside at it; occasional visits are, however, made to its gardens, when the court is at Peterhof. A colony of Germans has been established, by government, in its immediate vicinity, who derive much emolument, in the summer season, from letting their houses to the citizens of St. Petersburg.
At the extremity of the Peter‘nof Road, and at the distance of thirty versts from St. Peters-
58 CHATEAU OF STRELNA. @ burg, is the Palace of Peterhof, situated on

‘the brow of a hill, sufficiently elevated to admit a view of the Gulf of Finland and port of Cronstadt, over the tops of the trees which surround it. It was built by Peter the Great, in the year 1711, from a plan of the celebrated Leblonde. Circumstances did not admit of my Visiting the interior of this palace. The gardens are elegantly laid out, with innumerable fountains, or jets d’eau, and which, being illuminated by thousands of variegated lamps, during /étes, which are occasionally given here, produce one of the most magnificent spectacles that can be conceived. The multitudes of people who throng to enjoy these spectacles are incredible; the city becomes a comparative solitude: every horse, carriage, and boat, is put into requisition ;— nay, such is the crowd on the Peterhof Road; that the dust from the carriages is said to resemble the smoke of a furnace!
In this neighbourhood, the stranger will be much interested by the elegant Chateau of Strelna, the occasional residence of the Grand Duke Constantine, and where he, some years

GATCHINA—THE PAVLOSKY PALACE. 59 since, entertained the English residents in the most sumptuous manner. Adjoining, is the celebrated monastery of the same name, and which has a fine appearance as you sail along the coast.

Gatchina, where tlie empress mother resides during a part of the year, is another of the more distant palaces which deserves the attention of the traveller. It was once inhabited - by, the Emperor Paul.

. About.thirty versts from the city, is the Pavlosky, a truly charming place; perhaps as much indebted to nature, as to art, for its various beauties. This was the late emperor’s favourite summer residence, and is, in consequence, equally prized by his widow, who makes it her chief abode. This lady, who is ofa cheerful disposition, here assembles around her all the beauty and fashion of the country.

The grounds of the Pavlosky are very extensive, beautifully laid out and wooded, and with numerous walk’, tastefully disposed. The flower-beds, however, appear to be singularly arranged, each species having‘ a parterre to itself; for instance, there was a large bed of
carnations, another of-tulips, a third of mignionette, and so forth, in succession, throughout its whole Flora.

Somewhat nearer to the city is the superb Palace of Sarskoe-Selo, (or, in English, the imperial village,) where Catharine the Second _ principally resided, and acted many of those scenes which have procured her, from the world, the most adverse epithets. This palace, however, is chiefly indebted to the reigning emperor for its present magnificence, and who has left nothing undone which could contribute to its beauty and splendour.

I had the pleasure of spending a most delightful day with a lady who resides at this palace, and who, in the most obliging manner, ‘conducted me through its various apartments. To attempt a minute description of all that is capable of interesting the reader, would require a tedious detail; I shall, therefore, only advert to the more remarkable points of attraction.,
In- the first place, we were shewn the apartments which had replaced that portion of the palace that was burnt down last year, and

which has now been restored, in every re- Spect, to its original state, even silks of similar patterns having been expressly sent for from China. The fire in question broke out in the chapel, and was chiefly arrested by -the judicious conduct of the emperor, who attended in. person, and ordered an intermediate part of the building to be pulled down, to stop the progress of the flames. "The most beautiful apartments in this palace are, the amber room, the pear] room, and the Chinese room. The walls of the first are covered with amber, with festooned pannels, in the centres of some of which are various ornaments, in pietra dura. The amber which decorates this room,» was presented to the Empress Elizabeth by Frederick II. of Prussia.

The pearl room is so called from its floor and walls being richly inlayed with motherof-pearl: the doors, which are of the rarest woods, are also stiperbly ornamented with the same material. In this room are four valuable tables of lapis lazuli."

rine’s audience-chamber, where she received her own and the foreign ministers. It is adorned with numerous pagodas and Chinese figures, and has an unique appearance. The ceilings of the whole of these rooms are beautifully painted.
‘The ball-room is of immense size; nearly two hundred feet in length, and eighty in breadth, with thirteen windows on each side of it.

After being entertained at the palace with a most sumptuous dinner, we were taken in an equipage, drawn by four horses, termed a linea,* through the park to the village of Bablova, where the emperor has a set of baths. One of these, which has not yet been fitted for use, consists of an enormous circular basin, cut out of a single block of granite, about eighteen feet in. diameter, and seven in depth.

* This linea -may be compared to two long sofas placed back to back, sufficiently capacious to accommodate eight person on each side, with a regular coach-box in front, and a place for the footman behind.
delightful in the extreme, although entirely artificial.

Among other objects deserving of notice ‘here, is a superb building, which serves the purpose of a farm-yard, being occupied by * various breeds of cattle, which the emperor has caused to be imported from different parts of the world: among these are English cattle, from Teeswater. The luxurious accommodation of these animals, forcibly reminded me ‘of Caligula’s marble stables and gilded oats. The celebrated lamas, brought from Lima, succeed here, and are very’ picturesque objects in the grounds. Attached to the farm is a cottage, elegantly plain in its exterior, but internally handsomely fitted up, for the occasional reception of their majesties; the walls are decorated with eight small paintings, in old-fashioned frames, one of which is said to have cost a hundred and seventy-five thousand roubles!!
On our return to the palace in the evening, a fine military band was playing to the inhabitants in front of it. The concluding piece was the Evening Hymn, and so exquisitely
fine, as almost to ravish the soul from ‘its earthly tenement..

At the distance of about three miles from St. Petersburg, is a small, interesting.island of the Neva, named Kamenoi-Ostrof, which has a palace, that is occasionally visited by © the emperor and empress.

His imperial majesty has, however, lately built one’ of the most: magnificent chateaus in the world, for the residence of his mother’, on_ another of: the cluster of these islands of the Neva, named Yellagin Island.

The above islands, in the immediate vicinity of St. Petersburg, to which they are connected by handsome bridges, may be regarded almost as fairy scenes, and are flocked to by all ranks, as favourite places of summer resort. The empress mother frequently takes excursions about them in elegant gilded barges; when the characteristic costume of her party, and the melody of accompanying music, accordant with the measured cadence of the ‘oars, combine to produce almost the effect of enchantment..
It was formerly a custom in Russia, and

indeed is still observed as such in some parts of the- empire,.to make excursions on the water, in boats elegantly fitted up for the occasion, accompanied by bands of vocal and instrumental music; the performers were chiefly ‘slaves, well skilled in that delightful science. What, however, surpassed every other kind, is a horn music, peculiar to this country, the mellow tones of which are exquisitely and indescribably harmonious.

“In cadence sweet, now dying all away, Now swelling loud again, and louder still, Clear and sonorous.” Mg Hlavirig given an account of most of the imperial palaces situated in the vicinity of St. Petersburg, I will not weary my reader with descriptions of the various noble residences comprised more immediately within the city itself, although many of them are well worthy of attention; but shall conclude the present chapter with a brief notice of the citadel, or fortress, arid a few of the principal churches. The fortress is situated on what is named Petersburg Island, and contains a church VOL. I. F

within it, in which are deposited the remains of some of the czars of Russia, and various banners, keys of towns, and other trophies, chiefly taken from the Turks. There is one English flag, which we must charitably suppose to have been captured in battle, although I am credibly informed it belonged to a cutter that was cast on shore during the war. You are shewn here, as a curiosity, a boat, said to have been built by the hands of Peter the Great.
The mint, where the national money is coined, is also comprised within the walls of the fortress; also a manufactory of verdigris. |

St. Petersburg is by no means deficient in churches. The Empress Catharine erected great numbers, the principal of which was the one dedicated to St. Isaac, but also known as the Marble Church. What is singular, this church (with the exception of the Grand Duke Constantine’s palace) was very lately the only stone building in the whole city. It is now, however, taken down, the emperor having selected its site for a splendid new

‘ THE ISAAC CHURCH. 67 church, to be built upon the plan of a French architect. Unfortunately, however, after an immense expence incurred, the foundations have been found inadequate to support the inass of the new intended superstructure; so that the new building is at a stand, until either some plan is devised for strengthening the foundation, or a new spot selected. In whatever way this point may be decided, one thing is certain—that a church must be reerected on the site of the Isaac, since it is a superstitious custom amongst these people, that where a church his once been, a church must continue to be;—nay, if one is taken down, with a view of rebuilding it, some portion of the old edifice must remain; and this is the reason why the foundations of the Isaac Church have not been entirely razed.
A law exists in Russia, which must materially obstruct the building of churches by the noble or wealthy, which is, that they are ever after obliged to maintain an officiating clergyman..

In the chapel of the Nevsky Monastery is a rich shrine of St. Alexander, made of silver, and surmounted by a canopy of the same. Various relics of the saint, presented by the Emperor Alexander, are shown on a silver stand, covered by glass. In the buryingground lies the famous Suvaroff, and many of the principal nobility of Russia.

In the Catholic Church, the stranger will probably be interested by the simple tablet erected to the memory pf General Moreau. This tablet, which is encircled by a small iron railing, that extends scarcely six inches from the wall, bears the following inscription :- “ General Moreau, born at Morlaix, August,. 1763; died September 13, 1813.”

Tue literary character of Russia is at present in its infancy ; it is, however, under the patronage of his imperial majesty, in a state of progressive growth, which will, probably, lead to a respectable maturity ; although it is not likely, for the present, to rival the vigour and strength of the other leading European nations, or of the United States of America. -
There cannot be a stronger evidence of the present extent of Russian literature, and at the same time of the attention paid to promote it, than what the Imperial Library affords.

This noble institution, situated in the Nevsky Perspective, adjoining the French, Theatre and the Anitshkin Palace, the residence of the Grand Duke Nicholas, is a handsome quadrangular building, three stories in height, and containing no less than three hun- - dred thousand volumes, of which only seven ‘thousand are in the Russian language, being the whole produce of its literature, and those principally on ecclesiastical subjects; the number of English works is about the same, the great bulk of the collection being French, Latin, and German.

The manuscripts, however, form the more interesting part of the collection; a number of which are extremely valuable; some of these I had the pleasure of examining,— and amongst them a quantity brought from France, during the late revolution, by M. Dubrowsky, who was attached to the Russian embassy at Paris, comprising many original letters from crowned heads, their ministers, and chief nobility; amongst the rest, is a remarkably curious, highly-illuminated missal,
bound in purple velvet, which belonged to Mary Queen of Scots, and contains original verses, and other remarks, as well as her signature, in her own hand-writing.*

Among other curiosities, preserved in the same room with the manuscripts, is a copy of the standard of Posharsky, in red silk ; also, a portrait of the Virgin Mary, the lines of which consist of minute writing; and a slate, on which the last lines of the poet Dershavin are preserved, as written by his own hand.,

There is also a considerable collection of shinese books and charts; and I had the pleasure of being introduced to Dr. Henderson, a missionary, who was a daily visitor to the library, for the purpose of studying the Ethiopian language.
This library is thrown open to the public every Tuesday; but, by especial permission, may be scen on any other day, excepting Sundays and holidays,
