The Konskamara, or Museum, contains an immense number of interesting specimens of the works of nature or of art, many of them truly objects of great curiosity. It is impossible to enumerate all that is capable of exciting, in the highest degree, the attention of a visitor; but the following will, perhaps, more particularly be deemed deserving of his regard :—

In the first room, on the ground floor—a mass of native iron, which is said to have fallen from the clouds, weighing one thousand three hundred and sixty-eight pounds, and brought from Siberia by Professor Pallas; -also, a variety of specimens of porphyry, petrifactions, &e.
In the second room—an immense number of mineralogical specimens; with models of the furnaces made use of in the mines of Siberia..
In the third room—a large collection of different shells and fossils; and an orrery, twelve feet in circumference.
The fourth room comprises — anatomical preparations, and a number of insects and

reptiles preserved in spirits, the more curious of which are, a child with two heads, encircled by a serpent; the dressed skin of Peter the Great’s giant, seven feet three inches and a half in height, stuffed with hair; also that of his dwarf, prepared in the same manner, the hands and feet of which terminate in two forked points, instead of common fingers and toes ; the skeletons of both these. preparations are also preserved here. In this room a boa-constrictor serpent, twenty feet in length, is to be seen.

In the first room after ascending the stairs— is a stuffed elephant, and the'skeleton of one of those stupendous animals, the mammoth, a name first given, by some Russian peasants, to the remains of an incognitum dug up in Siberia. The present animal was discovered, by a Tungoose chief, in 1799, with his flesh upon him, embedded in a mass of ice, through. which a small part of the animal only was visible, and which then continued gradually to develope itself, until, at length, fhe Tungoose was enabled
. to cut off all his flesh and tusks, with the former of which he fed his dogs. It?was not until _ Seven years after its first discovery, that

Mr. Adams saw it, and caused it to be conveyed to St. Petersburg. Some have brought forward the perfect state of this animal as an argyment of the present, or late, existence of the genus, but we have no- other authority for giving credit to the supposition ; and the probability is, that the high state of preservation in which it was found, is attributable to its inclusion in frozen matter, and that its had lain in that state for many ages.
The following extract from Jepherson’s Virginia, relative to this animal, may not be uninteresting to the reader :—
“Ist. The skeleton of the mammoth bespeaks an animal of from five to six times the cube volume of the elephant, as M.de Buffon has admitted.

“2nd. The grinders are five times as large, are square, and the grinding surface studded with four or five rows of blunt points ; whereas those of the elephant are board and thin, and their grinding surface flat.
“ 3rd. I have never heard an instance, and suppose there has been none, of the grinders of an elephant being found in America.

“ 4th. From the known temperature and constitution of the elephant, he could not have existed in those regions where the remains of the mammoth have been found. The elephant is a native of the torrid zone and its vicinities : if, with the assistance of warm apartments and warm clothing, he has been preserved in life, in the temperate climates of Europe, it has only been for a small portion of what would have been his natural period, and no instance of his multiplication in them has ever been

‘known. But.no bones of the mammoth have ever been found further south than the salines of the north Holston, a branch of the Genissee, in about thirty-six degrees and a half north latitude, while they have been found as far north as the Arctic Circle.”
These observations conclusively prove the total distinction between this animal and the elephant.
A variety of other animals are to be seen in the same room with ‘the mammoth, and about four hundred specimens of birds.
In a gallery that leads from this room, are
~ costumes of all the eastern nations subject to

Russia ; among which are two wax figures, as large as life, representing Kamstchadale sorceresses, habited in the dress in which they practise their art. Around them hangs a string of rings, intermixed with pieces of iron; the left hand holds a musical instrument, resembling a rude tambourine ; and the right a flat piéce of wood, intended to beat it with. This room contains, also, a very neat Kamstchadale dog-sledge, and its model in ivory..

‘The second room above stairs contains— Peter the Great’s turning lathe and working - tools, and a chest-of-drawers made by himself, as well as various models of barges and ships ; there is, also, the favourite horse he rode at the battle of Narva, and his dog, both stuffed. The room itself is ornamented with representations of his battles, in basso-relievo.
The third room contains —an -exquisitely beautiful carving, in ivory, of Abraham on the point of sacrificing his son Isaac..
In the fourth is—a beautiful chandelier, made, in ivory, by Peter the Great ; and several specimens of his works‘in brass.
The next room has—a figure of Peter him-
self, the hands and face in wax, habited in the identical suit he more ordinarily wore; the whole said to be a most perfect representation.
In the sixth room, the medals, many of which are very valuable, are deposited; they were, however, not exhibited.
In a room below stairs, there is a curious musical desk, containing many secret drawers, the work. of an artist at Vienna, and which ‘cost the Empress Catharine forty thousand roubles.

The Academy of Arts is well deserving attention, although as yet in too infant a state to enter into competition with the more celebrated schools of Europe. + It contains, at present, about a hundred and seventy pupils, who are instructed in the arts of drawing, painting, sculpture, and engraving. The productions of the academicians are exhibited twice every year; they possess, however, so small a share of merit, that the only advantage which is hence derived, consists in the emulation which may be excited, and the gratification of their friends. * i On entering the hall, the first room on the

right is the saloon, where the president and professors. meet. It is ornamented with a full length portrait of the emperor, copied by one of the academicians from a French painter : there is also a picture of Peter the Great at the siege of Narva.
The two rooms on the left are oceupied with statuary, and a series of casts from the Elgin and other marbles.

In a small recess, between the two, nextrooms, is a splendid statue of Napoleon, by Canova, of a colossal order, and which is the bijou of the academy. It was originally intended for the city of Hamburg, from whence it was sent to St. Petersburg, at the time the Russians were in possession of that place, in 1814, after which it lay for two years in the warehouse of a Russian merchant, previous to being received into the academy.

The pedestal of this statue was so high, that I could only reach the knees of.the figure ; but this was sufficient to satisfy me of its exquisite character. The knee-pan, the heads of the bones of the leg, the muscles that form the calf, the ancles, the contractions of the

toes, from the supposed weight of the body resting upon them, were all inimitable, so. beautifully had the chissel written its delinea- . tions on this marble. My gratification on touching it was such, that I could with diffieulty withdraw my hand; and had the leg béen clothed with a real shoe and stocking, and of a natural temperature, I might have imagined it real.

In this room is a model representing the manner in which the immense block of granite, that forms the pedestal of the celebrated equestrian statue of Peter the Great, was transported over the morass to the water side, in order to be conveyed to St. Petersburg.
In another room were ten students, busily employed in drawing the human figure, from a living model.

Another establishment from which I derived a high gratification, was the Mint, where the various processes of separating the metal from its ores, forming it*into bars, and the subsequent stamping of it into coin, the latter effected by machinery moved bY the powerful action of the steam-engine, were explained by

the superintendance of a respectable old Ger-~ man, eighty years of age, who refused the remuneration offered him for his trouble, with a disinterestedness by no means common jn this ‘country; indeed, he was a rara avis. We were afterwards shown.a fine collection
‘of national medals struck at this place. |

It may be expected that I should explain the nature of, the interest I take in a visit to such a place as the present; for it will scarcely be admitted that the ]:ss of sight can, on such an occasion, be compensated by the mental powers. Few who have the blessing of sight, give themselves time to consider what ideas they would entertain of external objects, if they were deprived of this sense, or how, much pains they would take to compensate such deprivation. Indeed, it is scarcely possible for any one to have a right conception of the confidence which a person, who has been long afflicted with blindness, acquires, with respect ‘to his various intercourses with the world.: time and experience must prore POWER OF DISCRIMINATION. SL duce it, but reflection and judgment alone can bring it to perfection.. There are, -however, some points, particularly those which relate to personal intercourse, which may be more instantaneously acquired, as if by a principle

‘of perceptive instinct; this, at least, my experience indicates ;—for instance, when any one is conversing with me, I conceive myself to see the expression of countenance as the words are pronounced, almost as if ‘I actually saw it, and, in ordinary cases, receive a similar kind of satisfaction. This may be accounted for from a combination of causes—as the tone of voice, the manner of speaking, and other circumstances, which excite in my mind an ideal picture of the features, personal qualities, manners, nay, even the character of the person conversing with me, particularly when aided by associations derived from my own experience. I thus satisfy myself, at least, with a representation according to my own conception, although my ideas, connected as they + are with remembrances of what I have formerly seen, cannot have the same originality aS
would be the case with persons who have been blind from their birth.

I am only actuated by any intense desire to see, when I meet with some one who excites more than ordinary interest in my- feelings, or with any extraordinary productions of nature or art; it is then the imagination takes fire, and my desire to see increases with the difliculty, nay, impossibility, of gratifying it; then my feelings are worked up to such a pitch, that I become truly restless and impatient, when nothing but a change: of place, or thé introduction of a new subject sufliciently powerful to constitute a counteracting influence, can restore me to calm reflection.

If it be inquired how I can understand the structure and action of machinery, I would ask how the machinery in question came to be originally invented ; doubtless, it would be replied, “ By man’s imagination.”. If so, how much easier may it be for my imagination to comprehend what has been reduced to prac: tical demonstration, so evident, that a mere operative mechanic can execute it, from description only.

With respect to the different chemical processes carried forward in this establishment, as they all depend upon the well-known laws of chemical action, I could have no great difficulty in comprehending them. They chiefly relate to the separation, principally by means of acids, of the more precious metals, which always arrive from Siberia, or other mines, in & more or less impure state.

The College of Mines, or, as it is more commonly termed, the Mine Corps, is a very interesting place, situated on the right bank of the Neva, in the quarter of the town named Vasili-Ostroff. It was founded originally by Peter the Great, who, amongst the other benefits conferred on his country, has the honour of having laid open a new source of wealth to it, by causing researches to be made for metallic treasures in various parts of his empire. Mines were consequently opened in different governments, under the direction of this college, and particularly in Siberia: he also established a chief office for mines at Ekatarinenberg, a town which he built, and named after his empress.
The College of Mines contains a splendid collection of minerals, among which is one piece of malachite (oxyde of copper) said to weigh three thousand four hundred and fifty six pounds, English.
There is one large room appropriated to models of every description, connected with mining; as, a beautiful representation of the section of a mine, steam-engines on various plans, &c. &e. ;

Under the garden, -behind the college, an artificial mine has been constructed, which has the parts, windings, and different passages, that a real mine is supposed to possess, with different stratifications of rock, earth, veins of metal, &c. &c. The whole is most ingeniously executed, so that you might almost imagine yourself in a real mine.

A number of cadets are regularly instructed at this college in the science of mineralogy, and all the various operations connected with intning 3 after which they receive appointments to the different governments of the empire.
The paper manufactory, ereeted in 1750, by the Empress Elizabeth, and situated in the

neighbourhood of the Peterhof Palace, merits the inspection of the curious. Its beautiful and compact machinery was procured from England. One part of the building is appropriated to the purposes of the imperial lapicides, or polishers of precious stones. [res were exhibited a great variety of beautiful porphyries, jaspers, agates, &c. elegant vases, tables of malachite, and variegated marbles, as well as sothe curious ornamented pyramids, made by order of Catharine the Second, and intended one for each government in Russia, being specimens of the marble or other more valuable stones that they produce.

The government glass manufactory shoutd not be passed over, where seven hundred and fifty workmen are kept constantly employed, half of them in cutting, grinding, and polishing this useful material. Yet, although many splendid specimens are produced, the Russian glass is not of equal quality with that of England or France, being more brittle, less sonvrous, and not so exempt from colour. Their mirrors are some of them of greaf magnitude ;
the largest they ever made, I believe, measurin,
fourteen feet by five feet ten inches. I examined one which had just been cast, eleven feet by four, the price of which would be about forty pounds sterling. :

I also: visited the iron-foundry, situated at dhe fourth verst on the Peterhof Road, under the superintendence of Mr.’ Clark. I was here shown, amongst other interesting things, the model of a cast-iron dam and locks, an invention of that gentleman’s for. the use of canals, and which it was imagined, would come into general use, on account of its durability, economy,’ and less liability to be affected by frost. I was also much pleased with a neat iron spiral staircase, which had been cast for the Belvidere Lodge of the Sarskoe-Selo Palace, built after the model of the one in Windsor Park.

Public institutions may be regarded as the: hobby-horses of the imperial family; and where they are conducted, as here, under the full controul of despotic power, must necessarily, with the great attention paid to them, - evince the greatest degree of order and regularity, if not of perfection, so as to reflect y ZAM ARS |

THE FOUNDLING HosPITA te sy" 187) the highest credit on their Feapactive patrons. af An instance of the truth of this, remark is met,’ with in the Foundling-Hospital, under the ims mediate protection of the dowager empress; the extent of which is such, that no less than three thousand five hundred orphans are.an+ nually admitted. Only, however, five hundred ° of these are a¢commodated in the house, the remainder being sent into the country. ©

The little pensioners are immediately placed in charge of a number of nurses, kept in the house on purpose, from whom, as they ine crease in age, they are progressively transferred through the different departments of the esta» blishment, appropriately constituted for their reception.

The system observed is intended to encout rage industry, and with this view a routine of active employment, accordant with the age of the individual, is provided, so as to remind one forcibly of the three first of Shakspeare’s seven ages.

A certain number of the girls receive accomplished educations for the purpose of being sent out as governesses, including the French and German languages, music, dancing, &c.; and are occasionally married from the institution, in which case they receive a small portion from the empress. Many of the boys, also, are taught various languages, mathematics, &c.; while others are educated in the
“mysteries of different trades, according to their
abilities or genius. It is from this source that the theatres are principally supplied with their performers.,
There is no distinction of religion observed, except that if a child has not previously been christened, it is brought up in. the Greek church. Every child is vaccinated as soon as admitted.

If any person wishes to place a child for a time only in this institution, he may do so on paying a hundred roubles, and designating it by some particular name ; and any one may be taken from the institution, by giving a satisfactory security for its constant protection.
It will naturally be conceived, however, that I took still greater interest in a visit to the asy: - lum for the blind, an institution which appeared to me excellently well regulated.

I found its poor, afflicted inmates all very usefully, or agreeably, occupied ; some with music, reading, and other literary pursuits ; others, in the manufacture of different works of art, as baskets, mats, ropes, &c:

The mode in which the art of printing was carried on, struck me as particularly interest ing. The different types being arranged; alphabetically, in a box, aie then transferred, with great expedition, (acquired by habit) into the grooves of a frame of wood, a proper portion of the subject in question having thus been composed, a damp sheet of ‘paper is laid over it, and pressed with a cushion, after which, it is dried by a gradual and moderate heat, and in this way the surfaces of the letters are sufficiently elevated to be easily distinguished by the finger, by the assistance of which the correctness of the gomposition is ascertained. In accomplishing this both hands are used; one passes over the surface first, with a view of gaining a general idea, and is then immediately followed by the other to confirm it, the whole being effected with a celerity which surprises the stranger.

They all appear to have some: knowledge of music, at least so far as toto take part in a hymn, which is sung before sitting down to dinner, and again on finishing the repast. We had the gratification of being present at this interesting ceretnony ; and after its conclusion, were entertained with an instrumental]

We visited their‘bed-chambers, where each individual had a clean’comfortable bed, with every other convenient accommodation. In short, I left the place highly gratified, and deeply impressed‘with the benevolence of the Emperor, under whose especial patronage it is conducted.
There is, also, in this city, an interesting

_ deaf and dumb.asylum, which unforeseen circumstances prevented my visiting ; and I ine tentionally omit noticing a variety of other institutions, fearing that the detail would be wearisome to my readers; as, for instance, various cadet corps, and inany public semina+ ries for the education of the different classés of -

Amon the places of public entertainment, the theatres, of course, hold the first rank. There are few civilized countries in which the drama has not constituted a favourite amusement, and even been highly instrumental in forming, or evidencing, the national taste and character. The Russians may be regarded as considerably attached to it.

There are, however, at this time, only two theatres of any note in St. Petersburg; the great stone theatre, exclusively the property of government, where both Russian and German performances. are exhibited; and the small
* theatre, built of wood, in the Nevsky Perspective, occupied, for the present season, by a French company.,

Prince Shafofsky is the pr ical writer for, the Russian stage, and some of his tr anslations of the English and French pieces, and, particularly Ivanhoe, have been very’ success- ; ful. He has failed, however, in his.attempts to translate the Scottish pieces of our great unknown, betraying the greatest ignorance both, of the costume ‘and national ‘character of that people.* ~ ». ff

The prevailing taste of a Russian audience; however, at this time, is pantomime, accompa~ nied by martial music, noise, smoke, and fighting. Incredible expence is lavished in the decorations of these pieces; and the orchestra yields to none in the world in strength, and to few in taste.

_ sounded from the stage, I, one evening, visited the Russian theatre; the performance was a translation of Schuler’s Joan of Arc, in which the heroine, instead of the ignominious fate recorded in history, is made to receive a more glorious death in battle-field. The friends ° who accompanied me used every kind endea- "your to make me comprehend the action of the piece, but I cannot say that I derived much gratification from the oratorical powers of the performers.

I must, however, candidly confess, in consequence of repeated trials, that, since my misfortune, theatrical amusements interest me much less than might be imagined; indeed, I recollect very few instances in which I have not been wearied out before the conclusion of the piece; Iam, in general, far more pleased with a happy recitation in the closet, possibly, in some measure, because my mind is then less abstracted from the mcidents of. the piece, and more at liberty to clothe them with ideal scencry, and other embellishments, than it can do amidst the noise and confusion necessarily attendant upon a living representation on the stage; so that the intellectual gratification is diminished in proportion to the force of external, impressions.

There appear, however, other redsons for this diminished gratification. 'It is only from the voice that I can draw my inferences of the powers of an actor, and unless his emphasis and intonations be perfectly correspondent with the sentiments of the piece, and which is too seldom the case, my imagination is at once broken in upon, and then adieu to all congenial sympathy, or decorative mental imagery. To hear a fellow chop his part, mechanically, into lame sentences, accompanied by improper emphasis, reminds.me of the tide acting against the wind: In short, I cannot force my imagination ‘to operate in contradiction to my senses, or prevent my ears, probably too nice in this respect, from detecting that hesitation, falsity of intonation, or indescribable something, which indicates that the feelings of a performer on the stage are seldom dérived from the heart.

‘The German stage was originally an amateur theatre,’ where merchants, and various other respectable. individuals, used to perform with great eclat. It is now in little estimation, although Angeli, who is both an excellent actor
and writer, is attached to it. Among other pieces, he has brought out Kenilworth, ina very creditable manner..

The feeling.of inveterate hostility towards the French which succeeded the invasion of 1813, has, until very lately, prevented a French theatre from being opened in this tity. A company of that nation has, however, not long since been imported, and, as the Russian nobility are all acquainted with the language, is receiving great encouragement, notwithstanding few of the actors are above mediocrity. They get up, however, small pieces, or vaudevilles, with much taste.

Some twenty years since, St. Petersburg had its Italian opera, the speculation, however, did not answer; this is, perhaps, a matter of surprise, as the Russians are so passionately fond of music, that in many of their houses — they are entertained with it during dinner. ‘On Sundays, and all the principal holidays, bands of music are stationed in the public gardens, and do not fail to attract a great number of people. °
I shall avail myself of this opportnnity of

making some remarks on the subject of Russian music, which possesses a considerable degree of character; nay, many of the national airs well merit the epithet of beautiful : besides, the language much resembles the. Greek or Italian, as comprising a great. number of. vowels, and is therefore well adapted for harmony. | The singing heard at the court festivals affords a particular instance of the fascinating power of Russian vocal music. The aged General Partnensky, who has the direction of - the emperor’s choristers, was sent to Italy, by Catharine the Second, expressly to perfect himself in the science of vocal music. On his return, he was directed to select the finest voices the empire could produce, and his band, without doubt, constitutes as perfect q set of vocalists as can be met with. With the exception of the misereres at Rome, I never derived so high a gratification from sacred music as it afforded me; one bass voice, in particular, I thought exceeded any thing I had heard in the latter place. Catalani, whem at St Petersburg, is said to have been moved
to tears by their magic expressions; and this is no uncommon occurrence with other’amateurs. i i

Among the more popular amusements of the Russians, may be named the enjoyment of the many delightful promenades and gardens with which this city abounds. Among the former, the most conspicuous are, the English Quay, the Admiralty Boulevardes, and the Nevsky Perspective. The latter comprise thiefly the imperial pleasure grounds of Kamenoi-Ostroff, Kreslofsky, the Summer Gardens, situated in the city, and those of the principal nobility, which, particularly on Sundays and holidays, are thrown open for public accommodation. Here all sorts of amusements are provided for the people, as music, fire-works, puppet-shows, swings, summer wooden and winter ice hills, &c. &c.

The summer hill consists of an inclined wooden plane, along the grooves of which you are launched forward from an eminence, in a ear just large enough to hold two persons, with their feet projecting on either side; the

The ice hills, used in winter, are constructed upon. similar principles. A wooden frame is first erected, and floored with slabs of ice, in the manner of a pavement; water is ithen poured over it, in order that, when frozen, it may fill up the interstices, and give a smooth surface.

Independent of the ice hills, the young men also amuse themselves during the winter by skating. The skating-ground on the Neva, in front of the English line, during my residence here, comprised a space of.five hundred and twenty-five ‘feet long, by two hundred and forty-five broad, which, being planted round with fir-trees, had a picturesque appearance. It is kept up by subscription, and men are constantly employed to keep it clear of snow, and to water it every night, so as to give a new surface in the morning.
The English residents amuse themselves also with their national diversions of hunting and horse-racing.

The establishment ‘of the British Hunt, so called from having been first formed, and chiefly supported, by our countrymen, is at the village of Garilla, about twelve miles distant from the city, where they keep their dogs, and have accommodations for refreshment and lodging, after the sports of the day are concluded. It consists of about thirty couples of hounds, who chiefly hunt the hare, of which two species are met with in this country; the one somewhat less than our English hare, the other very large, and so strong as to give the dogs a hard chase. They occasionally fall in with a fox, who seldom fails to knock up the pack for the day. After partaking of the sports of the field, the members of the hunt, amongst whom are our ambassador, consul-general, and many respectahle English and German merchants, return to Garilla to enjoy themselves in still more substantial pleasures, and talk over the feats of the day. I had once the pleasure of par-
taking of their festivities, and can bear ample evidence to the goodness of their cheer, and the conviviality, hilarity, and loyalty with which it was expended.

One circumstance is much complained of with respect to this hunt—that its meetings are generally held on a Sunday. The arguments against the propriety of this, however, have been rebutted by the merchant members, - on the plea that,. being confined to their * counting-houses for six days in the week, the seventh only remains in which they can enjoy that pleasure and relaxation which is so important for the preservation of their health.

Horse-races are held repeatedly during the summer, generally on a new course which the empcror has lately presented td ‘the public, situated between the Sarskoe-Selo and [eterhof Roads, at the distance of about three miles from the city.
There is a house of entertainment on the Peterhof Road, about five versts from the city, named Krasnoi-Coback, or the red house, to which numbers of the inhabitants resort, under

the pretext of eating a peculiar kind of pancake,.named waffle, which is in the form of an oblong square, made in a mould, and is extremely light and agreeable in its flavour. This house has an exclusive privilege of selling liquors duty free, which was conferred upon it by Peter the Great, in consequence of his being in the habit of refreshing himself there when on his way to and from Cronstadt. The Empress Catharine IJ. also passed the night here, on her way to Peterhof, after assuming the reins of government on the imprisonment of her husband. The original house is yet standing; the business, however, is conducted in a more modern building, immediately adjoining to it.
I shall avai] myself of the present opportunity of introducing my readers to some of the very respectable club-houses which exist at St. Petersburg.

There are two clubs -more particularly celebrated, to both of which I had the honour of being admitted a visitor. The first, situated on the Moika Canal, between the red and blue bridges, and is named the English club, in

consequence of its having been originally established, more than fifty years since, by some of the English gentlemen employed in the counting-houses- of the merchants: here, with a view of benefitting the adverse fortunes of a Mr. Gardner, an eminent ’merchantj whom they constituted their econome or manager. It is now limited to three hundred and fifty members, natives as well as strangers, many of the first persons in the empire being enrolled among the former. Such, indeed, is the respectability attached to this society, and consequent desire to be amongst its mem-~ bers, that it generally takes three years to effect an admission.

Lord Cathcart, when ambassador at this court, was one of its earliest and warmest patrons. An anecdote is related with respect to this nobleman, that on the occasion of his health being drank at an anniversary dinner, at which he presided, a gentleman opposite, in the enthusiasm of the moment, fore getting he had not emptied his glass, while in the act of waving it over his head, discharged its contents full in his lordship’s face, who og bore: the salutation with such stoicism, as called: forth the remark that “ his lordship stands fire well.”.

, Ag the club acquired extent and reputation, aicode of Jaws for its government became indispensable ; copies of which, in the English, German, and Russ languages, lie constantly: on the table of the reading-room.

The management is vested in seven directors, of whom three are Russians, two Germans, and two English, one of the latter of whom is invariably the treasurer, and one of the first a person of the highest distinction.

The subscription varies from four to six guineas per annum, according to the state of their finances. A considerable, additional revenue, however, is derived from other sources, as wines, cards, the billiard-room, &c.; that from cards alore being estimated at ten thous sand roubles per annum.

Dinner may be had here any day at a regular charge of two roubles and a half: ‘the sum, however, is doubled on particular occasions ;—wines, of course, are hot included, these being charged according to their qua-
lities. There are, However, regular dinners only three days in the week.. f

Every member is allowed to introduce a friend ;.but if the general number of these visitors exceeds twelve, each is éxpected to pay five roubles to the poor’s fund. Strangers in St. Petersburg may be admitted for six months with all the advantages of members, excepting that their names must be inserted in the book by a member on each day of admission. After this time they are no longer regarded as strangers, but renew their alienship at any time, by residing six months out of St. Petersburg. At table, the gentlemen of each nation generally arrange themselves together. A variety of newspapers and other periodical works, constantly lie on the table of the reading-room. ;

The next club in estimation is termed the German Club, or, as being entirely composed of commercial men, the Commercial Club. Indeed, this character is so fully preserved, that no officer can be admitted, either as a member or visitor.

sion, far more extensive than the purposes of the society require, and therefore the superfluous part is let out in lodgings. Here a most extensive variety of newspapers may be seen; and such is the resort of the mercantile world to this place, that, during the time of the Neva being impassable, it is used as.a substitute for the exchange. It also contains’ an apartment used as a public ball-room.

The dinners given here are unusually large and splendid ; and even the cabinet ministers occasionally participate in the hospitalities of the place. The one I partook of was on an ordinary occasion, and yet the champaigne

‘corks flew about abundantly. I believe, however, that our countrymen, whether it is from want of taste or not, are less passionately fond of this beverage than other foreigners, particularly the Russians, the latter of whom not unfrequently drink it from tumblers.

AmonesT the public accommodations of a large city those are most important to the stranger, which contribute to his personal. comforts. In these respects St. Petersburg is certainly defective; as its hotels and other places of entertainment of this kind, are very far from being equal to what are met with in London, Paris, and other capitals of Europe.
There are in this place some large hotels, although few, if any, merit the denomination of “ good.” Demont's, situated on the Moika canal, has the reputation of being the best ;

‘but, perhaps, the more agreeable one, is the London hotel, in the Nevsky Perspective, which is the Bond Street.of St. Petersburg. The locality of the Hotel de Europe, near the Stone Theatre, is, also, by no means unpleasant, although it is not equally convenient, as being less central. At all the hotels, apartments are to be hired, without the tenant being expected to board in the house.

The only hotel I was myself in the habit of frequenting, was Page’s, and which much resembles a boarding-house in the United States of America, being intermediate to a house of that description and an inn. Here you may have board and lodging combined; or, if in private apartments, partake of the advantages of anexcellent table @’héte, in the English style, at the rate of three francs per head, where an agreeable mixed society, of consuls, offigers, merchants, men of genius, travellers, &c. &c. may always be met with. It is singular that the Russian officers, of all ranks, seem to take a particular pleasure in dining here. For board and bed-chamber, the charge is
ten roubles per diem; wines, beer, coffee’ after dinner, &c. are paid for as extras.

The eating-houses and coffee-rooms are not numerous in St. Petersburg, and chiefly found in the neighbourhood of the Gustinoy-Dvar, or shops, being frequented by the Russian merchants and tradesmen. Although the accommodations they afford are but indifferent, you will find in constant readiness, or preparation, a great variety of dishes, particularly fish, and this more especially during the fasts, which are numerous with the Russians ; but you may, even at these times, order chops, steaks, or other fleshmeat, if you desire it.
Tea-houses are particularly numerous for ' the accommodation of the native merchants and lower orders, who are remarkably fond of that beverage.
Private lodgings are scarce, and consequently dear.
Next to his personal accommodations, one of the chief points of interest with a stranger, is the facility afforded him of visiting his

friends, or the various interesting objects that may call forth his attention. The great extent of this city and the hospitality of its inhabitants, make it desirable that he. should, avail himself of some conveyance or other.

For this purpose, boats are constantly in readiness, for plying on the river. By land, numerous carriages, named droshkas, which are the hackney coaches of the place, await your orders, the fares of which, barring imposition, are not exorbitant, except that on Sundays and holidays, which are here so humerous as to comprise nearly a third part of the year, you are compelled to pay a considerably increased rate.

Perhaps, on the score of economy, the best way for a stranger is to have his own equipage. A droshka, drawn by one horse, and a coachman included, may be hired at the rate of about five pounds per month ; or acarriage, with foug horses, for from fifteen to twenty pounds. In effecting an arrangement of this kind, it is necessary to use much circumspection, and to

have every point clearly understood, and evi. denced by a written agreement, I was present at a dispute on this subject, between an English, gentleman and the proprietor of a carriage he had hired, which, through the firmness of the, ’ former only, in resisting the imposition, termi+ nated eventually in his favour. Every convenience is now afforded in this ‘ city, for the accommodation of the pedestrian, its streets-being kept remarkably clean, and, in most parts, well paved with flagstones. For the introduction of the latter convenience, the inhabitants, it is said, are indebted to the Emperor’s visit to England, at least, soon after, or even before, his return, a. peremptory order was issued, that each householder should, within a given time, lay flagstones down before his house, for the purpose of forming a foot-way. Such was the consequent requisition, at the time, for the necessary — materials, that I am afraid of stating the im- Tense sums which many are reported to have paid for complying with the order. - Another consequence is, that walking in

_ the streets has become fashionable here; even the Emperor himself, not unfrequently, condescends to be thus visible to his people, ‘on which occasions he is particularly affable, especially to the Jadies. This has proved no small inducement to them to become pedestrians.
Police of St. Petersburg—Pervades all societies, in disguise—

and circumnspection—Anecdote of two English gentlemen

In order to provide for public security and protection, and, at the same time, to guard against the discussion of, and interference with, the measures of government, an active police pervades every quarter of St. Petersburg. *

So great is the vigilance and art of these gentlemen, that it is necessary to observe the strictest caution in conversing with strangers, as they, not unfrequently, assume every variety of disguise, in order to detect such persons as may be adverse or obnoxious to the

government. I have heard of a gentleman, who having business with the master of police at the early hour of seven in the morning, took the opportunity of making an enquiry respecting the - probability of finding him at ‘home, from a peasant-like man whom he met on approaching his house. This person immediately conducted him to the house, which, to thesurprise of the gentleman, he entered, sans ceremonie; and immediately proceeding to an inner apartment, threw off his peasant’s dress, and stood forth the master of police himself; after which, he exhibited a great variety of dresses of the different characters he was in the habit of assuming.

In these various garbs the police frequent all public places. During the reign of the Emperor Paul, it was not unusual for an unfortunate being to be hurried away to the wilds of Siberia, in consequence of a heedless expression. The following ludicrous instance of the zealous feelings of these police géntlemen, and the whimsieallity of the above monarch, is spoken of :—
Two English gentlemen, am&asing themselves with an excursion to Lake Ladoga,

having ascended a hill that overlooked the Fortress of Schlusselberg, were accosted by a person who approached them with an-enquiry as to their business there. Not pleased with the intrusion, they carelessly replied, that they were taking a view of the fortress. Now the word expressing this in the Russian language, as well as in the English, signifies taking a sketch. The man immediately declared himself a police officer, and with much mystery, conducted them, under arrest, to St. Petersburg, where they were taken before the governor and the master of police, who gave them to understand, that the affair was so serious as to make it necessary to report it to the Emperor. After consideable suspence, they were placed in separate kabitkas, and driven away, without the least annunciation of the intention of the government with respect to them ; the affair, which at first they treated lightly, now began to assume a serious aspect. At length they found that they had arrived at the very fortress, in the neighbourhood of which they nad been arrested; Paul having determined, as they were afterwards informed,
that, they should have an opportunity of inspecting the inside as well as the outer one.

The governor at first treated them civilly, and even ordered tea, but, unfortunately, before it could be served up, having read his orders, instead of participating of the expected refreshments from the hands of a smart footman, two ferocious gaolers were introduced, who immediately conducted them to separate cells, where they were kept for a considerable time, in solitary confinement, on bread and water; and so ignorant were they of their future fate, that when the hour of release arrived, one of them, who was ignorant of the Russian language, knew not whether to hail the opening of his cell as the harbinger of death or liberty. :

The police regulations for preserving the public peace, and keeping order in the streets, are very strict, and some of them not a little peculiar: for instance, both the self-pleasing art of whistling, as well as indulgence in smoktng, are interdicted. A friend of mine one day received a check as he was amusing himself in the former way during his walk. How
annoying such regulations must be to bakers’ boys and Germans,—the former might, in consequence, be compelled, to chink, the ‘Jattér prevented from doing so.

The following occurrence, witnessed‘ one day in the street by a friend of mine, serves to instance the dread entertained by the lower classes of getting under the power of the police. As he was passing the Isaac bridge, a droshka suddenly stopped before him, when the driver leaped-down, and,-with every symptom of con+ sternation, took his passenger from off the seat of the vehicle, and laid him on the road; he then hastily remounted his box, and drove away with all possible speed. The passenger had been seized with a fit, when thinking he might die, the affrighted, but prudent, Russian took this method of getting rid of him, in order to avoid the trouble and expence the police would have imposed upon him, had he been found with the dead body.
iNothing, perhaps, has tended more to check. the nocturnal disorders and licentiousness of large cites, than the modern custom of lighting the streets by night. During summer, how-

ever, this is quite unnecessary in St. Petersburg; at other seasons they are lighted with oil,—gas not having yet been introduced, although its use is in contemplation. An agent of the London Gas Company was treating for a-contract of this kind previous to my departure.

Mendicity prevails in St. Petersburg, as well as in all other great cities; and if the doors of your house happen to be open, beggars do not hesitate to assume it as an invitation to walk in. I was once, during the absence of my servant, while reclining on the sofa, addressed in a supplicating tone, in the German language, by a feeble, pitiful voice; on finding that it proceeded from a female, which I ascer-

. tained by placing my hand on her arm, in order to avoid misconstruction, had any friend happened to have entered, I lost no time in conducting her, in the gentlest manner, from out the apartment; I did not even allow myself time to ascertain whether she was young and handsome, or the reverse.
I was on another occasion intfuded upon in

-much the same way by a man, who presented me with a paper, the nature of which he, in vain, endeavoured to make me comprehend. Imagining, however, that his real object was to beg, or, perhaps, purloin some of my moveables, I placed my hand upon him, and was proceeding to conduct him in the nearest direction to the door, a measure to which he manifested a remarkable degree of reluctance, endeavouring to make for a different part of the room; when at this juncture my servant returned. It then appeared that the paper in question, was an account that he ought to have taken to a friend of mine; and, moreover, that, on entering the room, he had laid down his hat; so that he was not merely anxious to explain the object of his visit, but, also, to “ regain the felt.”
The penal laws are excellently administered in this city, and their code of prison discipline equal, if not superior, to any in Europe.
One great object of the legislature is to find occupation for the prisoners, and, in order to encourage industry, the whole of their earn- | ings are appropriated either for their private

use or public comfort. The reformation which the present regulations have introduced is truly gratifying, for when the system of working was first commenced, the greatest difficulty was found in compelling the prisoners to conformity, whereas now, the only difficulty is to find work adequate to their wishes, so eager have they become for employment. In short, they are not only restricted from idle and depraved habits during theirconfinement, but many of them have acquired principles of industry and honesty, so that after their release, they have commented business, with the assistance of their reserved gaol savings, and become valuable members of society.*

A visit which I made to the principal prison afforded me excessive interest. We were first ushered into a room occupied, gratuitously, by an English bookbinder, for the purpose of employing a number of the prisoners in this occupation, for which, besides instructing them in his trade, he pays some of them twenty-five roubles each per month, as a remu-
* For a translation of the prison regulations, and other interesting documents, see Appendix D,

neration for their services. This person was from home,-but his brother obligingly accompanied us. over the prison. We were next shewn into the committee-room, where some of the prisoners were engaged in the manufacture of pocket-books, and other fancy works, under the instruction of a German; after this we were taken to a cell on the ground floor, where the more depraved prisoners are confined in irons, with a guard of soldiers to controul them. From hence we passed into the receiving-room, where the work of the prisoners is displayed ; whilst we were here, five culprits were brought in, chained, and taken to their cells, without a word escaping from their lips. ._ The persons confined for debt, are kept separate from the,criminals, and as their creditors ere obliged to allow them a rouble per day for their support, with the.addition of donations, they live,extremely well; they are not compelled to work, although most of them do so voluntarily. I afterwards made a second visit to the same prison, and was taken into the female department, where about twenty women, dressed in

the prison uniform, were employed in various kinds of needle-work. I was informed, that they looked extremely clean and neat, and that their apartments were sweet and well regulated. We were, also, conducted through the hospital, which contained only two patients ; and over the school, in which about twenty young vagabonds were occupied in learning their appointed tasks. In short, throughout the whole of this establishment, the best order’ and internal arrangement appear to prevail.
Among other regulations for the management of this city, those ‘intended for its protection from fire, seem particularly deserving of notice.

With a view of affording the most immediate and effectual assistance, the city is divided into twelve quarters, in each of which is a lofty tower, where watchmen are stationed night and day, to detect the first symptom of fire, which is then notified to the whole, by a signal indicative of the quarter in which it has taken place; this signal is made by a flag in the day-time, and by means of lanterns at
night, and is immediately repeated by all the. other quarters.

At every station, engines with excellent horses ready harnessed, are prepared to hasten, at a moment’s notice, to the point of alarm; and, in order to ensure the greatest promptitude, the firemen are punishable if they do not reach the spot within twenty minutes, however distant its situation may be.

In order to render the firemen more exyert in their assistance to the unfortunate inmates of the burning house, they are regularly trained in a very singular exercise. A_ lofty pole, with a platforin near its top, is erected at the height of about the fourth floor of a large house, and ascended by means of ladders: the fireinen are practised in desccnding from this platform with the assistance of plain ropes and rope Jadders. The most ‘singular part of the exercise, is, that they are required to precipitate themselves from the platforin; every precaution, however, being taken to prevent injury, as by placing beneath a sail-cloth suspended by

poles, with feather-beds, hay, straw, and soft substances under it. Even the officers themselves are not exempt from this exercise.

Having casually heard of the existence of the above extraordinary practice, I determined to ascertain the correctness of the information ; and at length, after much inquiry, obtained a full confirmation from the firemen themselves. I did not, however, rest here; for I personally visited the scene of exercise, accompanied by a friend, who obligingly made me a sketch of the apparatus employed, and which accompanies this description.

I dwell the more upon this point, as many of my friends had previously ridiculed the affair, as an imposition on my credulity; and, therefore, I derived no little gratification from triumphing, as it were, over their doubts. Before dismissing the subject, I beg leave to obtrude a hint for the use of my travelling brethren—to hear every thing, but believe nothing, without proof or probability ;—at all events, not to be over fond of detailing as fact, every inconsistent story they may chance to stumble upon, without first examining into

its authenticity: if they meet with obstruction in searching ‘out the truth, this ought only to stimulate them to greater exertions in the pursuit of it. Travellers are, perhaps, more frequently the subjects, than the sources, of imposition, since the great eagerness they evince for novelty, excites the inclination to deceive them. It is said, that when Dr. Clarke was at Petersburg, there were persons who, perceiving his anxiety to obtain information, and his eagerness to note down every thing he heard, used to seek his society, for the express purpose ‘of cramming” him; and I am convinced that, had I allowed myself to have credited all the wonderful stories detailed to me, my book would have teemed with histories not unworthy of Baron Munchausen himself.
Classes of society and mode of living at St. Petersburg.

St. PerERsspurRG, comprising a population drawn from almost every quarter and nation of the world, may be regarded as a city of strangers; so that it will be difficult to derive from it any thing like a correct picture of the manners and customs of the Russian nation at large, as these must be necessarily, more or less, influenced by the national peculiarities of the motley tribes, of foreigners it contains.

It is with a fuil impression of the difficulty of doing justice to the various modifications of character which are from this source produced, that I enter, with much diffidence, on the present chapter, which professes to treat of the manners, customs, and mode of living - of its inhabitants.

As this city is the seat of government, it is natural to suppose that the nobility will, in great measure, take their tone from that of the court; I shall, therefore, first make a few observations relative to the latter, which, it will bé observed, does not materially differ in its usages from those of other capitals of Europe.

His imperial majesty lives in a simple, unaffected manner, breakfasting at an early hour, after which his mornings, from seven till ten o’clock, are occupied with the ministers and other official persons. The business of the court concluded, he proceeds to the parade, or takes exercise, until two or three o’clock, when he dines. About seven, tea is introduced, after which he either attends some private theatri+ cal performance in the palace, or amuses himself with a ball, concert, or select evening party. Between ten and eleven supper is announced, immediately after which he retires for the night..
The nobility live generally in a similar way to the emperor, excepting that they do not all dine at so early an hour.

The Russian merchants are very irregular in their habits, as their families seldom assemble together at the respective meals, unless it happen to be at the supper-table. They have few ideas cf the comforts, which almost every class of society in England enjoy, in daily sitting down to the social meal. The mind of the Russian merchant is too absorbed in business to think of domestic comfort, and he is contented if he satisfies the wants of nature, no matter when or where; and so long as his food has a strong flavour, it scarcely signifies what its composition or qualities may be. One of his more common dinners is sour cabbagesoup, named stchee, and which, with some of the meat it is prepared from, he generally partakes of in his kitchen. In times of. fasting, instead of meat, fish or grain are used in the preparation: of this soup. In short, his mode of living is very little superior to that of a common mechanic, except that he wears better clothes, and possesses some other luxuries, which are out of the latter’s reach.
Occasionally, however, the Russian merchant gives a feast, when he launches. into the most extravagant and luxurious expences, even so as to vie with the richest nobility.

The lower classes of tradesmen, mechanics, and labourers, live in a manner very similar to the merchant. The labourer’s wages are, however, only from five-pence to ten-pence per day; so that he is obliged to live upon black bread, that costs. somewhat less than a halfpenny per pound, and of which he will eat three pounds a day; and although he rarely indulges in more than the additional luxury of an onion, yet he seldom fails to take his glassof brandy before he commences his meal.

The Germans are more numerous than any other class of foreigners in this city, being computed at not less than twenty thousand, comprising merchants, tradesmen, and mechanics. They chiefly follow-the customs of their own country, associating principally among themselves. Some of them, however, mix much with the English, and assimilate more or less with their habits.

The English residents are about three thousand, who carry forward the various occupations of merchants, tradesmen, &c. These, as usual, keep’ prétty closely to the manners and “customs of their native land.

St. Petersburg abounds with all the necessaries, and most of the luxuries, of life. Amongst its greatest delicacies may be named fresh caveare, the: excellence of which cannot be appreciated by those -who have only partaken of the salted article which is met with in England under that name. As soon as winter sets in, large quantities are brought into St. Petersburg and Moscow, principally from Astrachan. The. Russians have, however, various other delicacies, as the nevaga, a small fish, cod, and rein-deer’s tongues, from Archangel; hares, an article of food to which the Russian himself is by no means partial, as well as some others that are prohibited by the Mosaic law; two-kinds of partridges ; woodcocks ; the common and double snipe ; the latter of which, in season, is literally fat as butter, and this of the sweetest kind, combined with the most delicious game flavour. Oysters are considered among the rarest luxu-

ries of the place, being only found native on the coasts of the Black Sea, whence, in consequence of the distance, they cannot be pro-- cured except iri the wintor season; quantities are, however, imported from Germany, Holland, and England, but seldom very fresh; they are, notwithstanding, so precious as to go down here in the most offensive state, even with an Englishman, so keen does the appetite become from previous abstinence; the price fluctuates from one to four pounds sterling per hundred; so that, with porter, you may readily dispose of a sovereign for your luncheon.

There are, perhaps, few cities better supplied with fruits and vegetables than St.,Petersburg and Moscow. The climate, however, docs not admit of many fruits coming to perfection in the open air; the ehief of these are of éxotic origin, and necessarily fostered in the warmth of the hot-house. Many of the choice ones. however, are brought from more genial climes; fur instance, grapes from Astrachan, and apples from the Crimea. Their woods abound with nuts, and various berries of exquisite flavour; and in particular the moroshke, in appearance intermediate to the raspberry and mulberry. Its taste is agreeably subacid; it contains, however, numerous large and hard seeds, which diminish the pleasure of eating it. These berries are either eaten in their natural state, or preserved with sugar, or occasionally in water, like cranberries. J have been informed that they are sometimes met with in the Highlands of Scotland. ‘The berry of the mountain-ash is also made use of in Russia to flavour jellies, wine, brandy, and other articles, to which it imparts a most agreeable bitter flavour.

The fruiterers have a variety of modes of preserving their fruits. The apples, either whole or cut into small pieces, are preserved in casks with qvass, sweetened with honey or sugar, and in such forms are sold in the streets at all seasons. Other fruits are mixed and compounded in a variety of ways. Oranges in abundance are imported from the Mcditerranean, and in the autumn vast quantities of fapples and potatoes are brought in from Germany. j

Early in the spring plentiful supplies of vegetables are brought forward, asparagus and morells taking the lead. These-supplies not only continue throughout the summer, but almost every kind may be had during the winter, a stock being laid up in dry cellars preparatory to the frosts setting in, the temperature of which is then regularly kept a little above freezing point. Some are hung up around the walls of the cellar; others, particularly the various roots, celery, &c. are laid up in dry sand or mould. But the most indispensable article with the Russian is the cucumber, of which immense quantities are preserved in casks of brine.

Among the more common articles of food used by the nobility, particularly during their fasts, may be named the mushroom, or fungi, of which a great number of genera and species are eaten. They have various modes of preserving them, the more common one -being to dry them in a gentle heat; and also
as many ways of preparing them for the table. :
The following are a few only of the fungi used’as articles of food in this country :—
rosaceus. Boletus edulis reticulatus. - edulis non reticulatus autumnalis.

The quantity and variety of vegetable oils made use of would astonish a stranger; the most delicate is that expressed from the seeds of the sun-flower, and prepared by enclosing them in bags and steeping in warm water, after which the oil is expressed; this is actually as sweet as butter. Linseed and nut oils are more commonly used by the lower classes. A very fine oil is also prepared from mustard seed; and large quantities of olive oil are imported for the use of the nobility.
During fast times, the pastry and pdiés given you with the soup, are prepared with oil instead of butter, and I have occasionally found them rancid.

A variety of articles, accommodated to the taste of the lower orders, are, as in other great cities, vended inthe open streets ; the following, however, may be considered as peculiar to St. Petersburg,—a kind of buck-wheat cake, which, when the purchaser receives, his portion, is feathered with common oil, by way of sauce; peas-pudding cut into slices, and vended in the same relishing manner ;
fish pies, with crust round the gdges, and oil poured over the fish;.the offal parts of animal food; hard boiled eggs; boiled potatoes, &c.

A variety of drinks are also carried about with the same intention; as the Zboten, prepared from honey, or treacle and water, with herbs added to give it a flavour; this, when cold, is carried about in glass vessels, and, when hot, in metal ones. Occasionally a better kind of Zboten is prepared from the’ juice of cranberries, pears, prunes, or other fruits, sweetened with honey. Another beverage, is the Kvass, which is brewed with rye-flower, and sometimes flavoured with aromatic herbs, and which is carried in the preparation t,a slight acetous fermentation ; this may. be considered the substitute for English small-beer. There is, however, a superior Kvass, named Buza, prepared from sifted flower and malt; and a third, named Kisloy-stchee, from the finest wheat-flower, and. which is deliciously effervescent. Mead is also much used. Independent of the above beverages, there aré, in this city,
large breweries of superior ale and porter, such as would not be despised in England. The principal brewer is Mr. A. Cazelet.
Tea, ready prepared, is, also, constantly selling in the streets,- particularly in cold ‘weather. :

No country in the world is more tolerant with respect to religious opinions than Russia, for although it adopts the doctrines of the Greek church, which in many points resemble those of Rome, yet it permits the free exercise of every other form and creed.

The Greek differs chiefly from the Roman catholic church in denying the supremacy of the pope, the emperor being at its head, and the ecclesiastical government, under him, vested in a metropolitan, archbishops, and bishops. Its constitution combines in it an immensity of superstition, and, although it disclaims the worship of imageS, admits the mediation of saints, with pictures of whom

188 BAPTISMAL CEREMONY. e the churches abound ; it observes also a great number of fasts, encourages monasteries, and prescribes celibacy amongst the higher orders of its priests, although the parish priests are permitted to marry once.

I believe it maintains. mayiy peculiar views with respect to the sacraments and nature of the Divine essence, which I shall not pretend to discuss, but.confine myself to a description of some of the more common ceremonies which I had opportunities of witnessing.

The baptismal ceremony always takes place in a few days after birth, and consists of a complete immersion in water, accompanied by various rites. The water used, being first consecrated, is placed in a sufficiently capacious vessel in the middle of the room where the ceremony is performed, and then encircled by the company. The priest, now’ receiving the child in his arms, after a preliminary prayer, enquires its sex from the sponsors, and then proceeds to place around its neck a consecrated cross, attached to a gold chain, or riband, according to the circumstances of its parents.

A small portion of hair is then, at three several times, taken by the clerical assistant froin the head of the child, kneaded up with a portion of wax, and given to the godfather or godmother, as the sex may happen to be, who places it upon the surface of the water; if it swims this is regarded as a propitious omen ; on the contrary, its falling to the bottom is an indication of the child’s premature departure from this sublunary scene; either of which results might at pleasure be determined by the peculiar forin given to the wax.

The priest next enquires the name, and as it is announced plunges the infant into the water; after which it is placed “in a wrapper, and according to its sex, given to the male or female sponsor, who then carries it three times axound the vessel, preceded by the priest offering up prayers and followed by the other sponsors. After this the child is committed to the care of the nurse. The priest now directs the sponsors to turn their backs towards hii, and spit three times on the ground, with the view of ejecting the evil spirit. The ceremony,
if performed in private, concludes by presenting refreshments to the company.
One singular circumstance remains to be noticed, which is, that such persons as have officiated together as sponsors are, by the Greek church, afterwards interdicted from intermarrying.

I had the gratification, by particular favour, of being present at the reception into Christianity of the Princess Olga, or Olivia, daughter of the Grand-Duke Nicholas, which was celebrated in the chapel of the beautiful Tauride palace, the dowager empress personally ofliciating as godmother. The ceremony was substantially as above described ; but as all the splendour of the church and court were dis-

‘ played on the occasion, the effect was, ofcourse, most imposing. Her imperial majesty, who was magnificently attired, ] am assured, went through her part of the ceremony with wonderful grace and dignity.
Marriage is, perhaps more in Russia than in any other country, a contract of convenience, rather than an engagement of the

heart. This is, however, an observation more particularly illustrated amongst the lower classes; for instance, if the mother of a family, from age, or any other cause, becomes incapable of attending to, her domestic occapations, an enquiry is set on foot to find out a stout, healthy young woman, able to undertake the charge, to whom one of the sons, although only a child, is immediately married.

A friend of mine once witnessed the ludicrous circumstance of a stout young woman, of twenty-seven, carrying off, in her arms,- her husband, a boy of eight years, who had been amusing himself at babki, a game played with sheep’s bones.
Marriage is often brought about by the intervention of friends, without reference to the inclinations of the parties; nay, occasionally, without their having previously seeneach other.

The peculiarities of the marriage ceremony in Russia have long been notorious. Many, however, of the more singular and barbarous customs, which formerly prevailed, have given way under the light of civilization, although
enough yet remains to interest, and occasionally disgust, the traveller.

I was fortunate enough to have been present at the different ceremonies observed in the families of two wealthy merchants, which I shall take the opportunity of ‘describing ; I shall, however, previously intreduce an account of another, which I have been favoured with by a friend, as illustrating some points, chiefly preliminary, which did not come under my own immediate observation.

My friend, who was particularly intimate with a part of the bride’s family, had accom- * panied them one day to pay a visit of congratulation to a relative of the family of the bridegroom. On their return, she could not avoid ‘ noticing a whisper amongst the party, which she afterwards found to have arisen from a suggestion thrown out by the lady they had been visiting, of the eligibility of a matrimonial connexion between her nephew and a young lady of their family. The proposal was well relished, and nothing remained but to open the affair with the parties themselves, who

were at this time wholly unacquainted with the subject on the tapis. A series of visits were arranged for this purpose, and the bait was readily taken on both sides; and, on the fourth visit, the gentleman. made his declaration in form, and was freely accepted, on the ‘lady being assured that it was a desirable " connexion. In a day or two after, accompa- -nied by his intended bride and his sister, and taking’ an image with them, they presented themselves before his mother, and received her benediction.

From this time all was bustle and confusion. Milliners, dress-makers, and every other kind of work-people, were put into immediate requisition, to prepare the bride’s wardrobe; a matter of no small import, as she was to be
‘ provided with twelve dozen of every article of personal and kousehold linen. The bridegroom is also to be presented with twelve dozen of shirts and handkerchiefs.

This custom of making bridal presents is certainly not peculiar to the Russians; but, perhaps, there is no part of the ‘world where it is carried toa greater extent. Amongst the ltt - BRIDAL PRESENTS.

rich nobility, immense sums are often thus .expended. When the Countess Strogonoff married Prince Galitzin, about two years since, the picture-gallery of her father’s palace is said to have been: crowded with articles furnished on the occasion, so as to have re+ sembled a bazaar. Amongst others, were _ immense numbers of the richest shawls, a silver dressing-table, basin, and ewer, with a* profusion of perfumeries and other materiel for the toilet ; and of shoes alone, there were no less than five hundred pairs—the whole - reputed to have cost half a million of roubles.

I may here take the opportunity of remarking, that marriage in Russia gives the husband no controul over his wife’s property : at her death, she can dispose of it as she pleases. Nor does this merely affect her own’ inheritance ; her husband can thus vest in her any part, or the whole, of his own property, and cheat his creditors with impunity.
To return to my friend’s narrative. On the day before the wedding, the whole of these paraphernalia were submitted to public view, and most minutely inspected by the
visitors, the price.of each article being closely inquired into, A cold collation was laid out on the occasion, for those who chose to partake of it: :

At length the happy day arrived: the bride’s party dined en famille, after which she retired to her chamber. Her hair was first dressed, and then her younger relatives began to attire her in the marriage-garments. When this -was half completed, two of her brothers were separately introduced, to put on her stockings and shoes, each drawing on one, of course only over the ancle, and so far as to admit the shoe upon the foot; and as each article of dress was put on, she made. the sign of the cross. When completed, her dress was simply elegant, consisting of white satin, trimmed with rich blonde lace, every part being new. On her head was a coronet of diamonds, with _a bouquet of pearls, secured with diamond pins; she also wore a diamond necklace and ear-rings.
The whole party, comprising the nearest relatives of the happy couple, now‘proceeded to the private chapel of the bridegroom’s relatives,

where the nuptial ceremony was performed. This concluded, they retired to the residence of the bridegroom, where an elegant supper was provided, to which, however, none but relatives, and no unmarried females, were admitted. -At the conclusion of this repast, the bride was conducted to her chamber by her female friends, who assisted in substituting an elegant robe de chambre for her weddinggarments, ‘her diamond head-dress being replaced by a beautiful cap of -Mecklenburg lace, trimmed with pink satin riband. The . bridegroom and his friends were now per~ mitted to enter, and the health of the new married pair was drank in champaigne. All now retired again, with the exception of the ladies, who remained to put the bride to bed; after which the whole party returned to their respective homes. °

The wedding which I had the opportunity, of personally witnessing, had also been made up between the friends of the parties, the first proposal coming from those of -the bridegroom, and veing deemed too good an offer to be refused, the young lady, as yet only
fourteen years of age, was hurried from school, in order to consummate the union.

of entertainments were, according. to custom after betrothing, given by the friends of the bride, and which, after the marriage, were re turned by those of the bridegroom. "Our first visit was, therefore, to the father of the bride, who was one of the modern, refined. Russian merchants; that is, he did not wear a beard, and knew how to -converse in French. On entering the room, he received us with a. kiss on each cheek, welcoming us in the most polite and cordial manner, and thanking us for the honour we had done him, IIe then conducted us to an inner apartment, and, with his own hand, presented each of us with a glass of champaigne. A crowd of servants now encircled us, offering a variety of refreshments, as chocolate, or tea, succeeded by punch, sweetmeats, fruits, and wines.
After this we mixed with the company, soine joining in the dance, others reconnoitring the various apartments, or participating in whatever amusement was most congenial with their taste,

The various rooms were all most elegantly furnished and decorated ; one, however, deserves particular notice: in its centre, was a large table covered with linen to the floor, but festooned around, and decorated with flowers ; its surface was crowded with the choicest fruits, and ornamented with temples, pyramids, and. festoons of flowers, the whole brilliantly illumi-. nated with lustres. At the further end of this table, was a sofa placed under a canopy, for the occasional retirement of the bride and bridegroom, the former a plump little girl, quite native in her manners, although not very lively; her dress was most splendid, her héad decorated with a diamond tiara ; and she, also; wore a rich necklace of the same precious gem The sofa, however, was so placed as scarcely to leave them visible, unless you approach with the express intention of seeing them, a proceeding by no means deemed an intrusion. -

On this sofa the happy pair freely indulged in avariety of amorous toyings; in short, it is regarded a necessary part of the ceremony to afford the corapany, in this way, repeated indications of happiness ; and although, from their

position behind the table, their persons might not be actually visible, the loud kisses which passed between them were sufficiently audible. After dancing had continued for some time, a man in the attire of a peasant was introduced, who sung a variety of national songs, ina pleasing manner. These songs produced a very ludicrous effect on one of the company, a bearded gentleman, said to be a tutor, and who appeared to be well-lined with punch; this man was so delighted, that he kept stroking and kissing the beard of the singer alternately for some time after he had concluded. The dancing was now resumed, ‘and kept up until four o’clock, when it terminated with a polonaise; after which the company sat down to a most sumptuous supper, comprising every delicacy of the season, and a variety of excellent wines.‘ During the supper, a long series of toasts were given, at the announcement of each of which a herald exclaimed, “ touche,” when a flourish of trumpets took place, and the band struck up a lively air; each toast was accompanied by three cheers, and

on the occasion of our host’s health being drank, we threw our glasses over our heads upon the ground, which was regarded as a most distinguished honour paid to him; after this, the foreign visitors chaired both him and the bridegroom, and carried them around the table.

Toward seven inthe morning, the entertainment concluded by the English part of the company dancing a Scotch reel, to the no small delight of the natives. We then saluted the bride again and again, and took leave of our spirited host, who gave us many embraces, and a pressing invitation to his next party.

From the above specimens of a Russian merchant’s festival, an inference will necessarily be drawn of his great wealth, in which respect some of these people, in their entertainments, vie with the richest of the nobility. They are, however, notwithstanding, looked upon by the latter as an inferior race of beings, with whom it would be a degradation to associate. It is their wealth only which gives them consequence; and as most of them have originally been slaves, and brought up in the grossest

ignorance, it is not surprising that few motives of honour or morality should interfere with their means of acquiring money. In cunning and the art of over-reaching, they yield not to the Chinese themselves, but such is the deficiency of their education, that few of them are able to transact business by the most common rules of arithmetic ; for this purpose they make use of an instrument named the stchot, very analogous in its principle with the Chinese swan-pan, from which it has probably been derived.* These deficiencies are, however, the results of a neglected education, not of a want of natural genius; for some have succeeded in breaking through the trammels of opposing circumstances, and attained eminence in the arts and sciences of their country. The celebrated architect of the Cazan church was of this class, and originally a slave to Count Strogonoff.
What tends much to prevent the advancement of this important.class of the Russian nation is, that whatever riches they may ac-
* For an account of the stchot, see Appendix E.

quire, the law precludes them from becoming landed proprietors ; they are allowed, however, to purchase and build houses, the consequence of which is that a large part of St. Petersburg belongs to them. More pains, is also taking of their education, and it is to be expected that the prejudices and restrictions with regard to them will eventually be removed. In short, they may already be occasionally seen in the society of people of rank. Such is the allpowerful influence of gold, ‘
