« —_____. This yellow slave ‘Will make black, white; foul, fair; base, noble; And give them title, knee, and approbation With senators on the bench.”

The marriages of the Russians are generally celebrated on a Sunday, and always in the evening. This was the case in the present instance. At the end of a fortnight after the above entertainment, the marriage was solemnized in the Cazan church; on which occasion, I had the satisfaction of being present. Previous to setting out to church, the bride and bridegroom presented themselves on their knees before their respective parents, en-

treating their forgiveness of past offences and imploring blessings on their future prospects. In token of acquiescence, the parents gave _ them an image, accompanying it with many tears and embraces. Immediately after this ceremony, the party set out for the church, but, what is strange, the parents themselves are forbidden to be present, although among: the higher ranks the priests occasionally concede this point.

On entering the church, which.on the ‘present occasion was crowded by numbers whom curiosity had attracted to witness the ceremony, the parties being in high consideration, the bride and bridegroom were conducted to a temporary altar erected in the middle of it; opposite to them were ranged the priest and the friends of the parties. The bridegroom, with the bride, stéod upon a rich carpet, their attendants, or the groomsmen, as they are called in England, being placed behind them.
The priest, having presented them with a lighted wax-taper, which they received with all possible respect, at the same time kissing his hand, now commenced the prayers

appropriated for the occasion, in whith they concurred, by occasionally making the sign of the cross. Twocrowns,a larger andsmaller one, ’ were now brought forward, which, after being “consecrated, were presented by the priest, the larger one to the bridegroom, the lesser-one to the bride, who kissed them, crossing themselves at the same time. The priest now gave these crowns to the attendants, who held them over the heads of the respectiveparties. The whole then made, three times, a circuit of the altar, preceded by the priest, the groomsmen still holding the crowns over the heads of the bride and bridegroom. The priest now consecrated two rings, after which he presented one to the bride, and the other to the bridegroom, who respectively kissed, and returned them to him, when he placed one on the finger of the bridegroom, and united their hands. The husband then placed the other ring on the finger of his wife, and embraced her. Another circuit was made round the temporary altar, from which the wedded pair now retired, approaching the larger altar, which, as in all Greek churches,
was surrounded by the pictures of saints ; here they made devotional obeisances to their patron ones; after which, on retiring therefrom, the whole company began to offer their congratulations.

The ceremony being thus concluded, the party returned tothe house of the bride’s father, where a splendid entertainment was given to a select party, previous to the wedded pair retiring to the nuptial bed.

On the following evening, I attended the wedding ball, at the residence of the bridegroom’s father; the amusements of which were very similar to what I had previously participated in at the bride’s father's, only, as the house was larger, it admitted of things being effected on a more extensive scale. In addition, the bride’s chamber was to be seen, in Which the various presents of plate, china, &c. were ranged in order around the room.
The dance was kept up with great spirit until nearly five o’clock, when to the disappointment of many, instead of sitting down to a splendid supper, the party broke up; in fact,
dinner had not concluded before twelve o’clock, and therefore a supper was thought superfluous ; there was, however, an abundance of every kind of refreshment, wines, &c. &c.

Among the higher classes in this country, no ceremony is more imposing than that solemn one which drops the curtain upon all sublunary scenes, when the mute subject -lies unconscious of the tokens of respect paid him by his surviving relatives. For some days after death, the body is exposed in state in the chief apartment of the house, surrounded by all the paraphernalia adapted for the occasion. A train of servants, in deep mourning, usher you through suites of apartments hung with funeral livery, and lighted by wax candles. At length you reach the apartment where the body lies, extended on the state bed, in a splendid coffin, covered with: crimson velvet ; the escutcheon placed at the foot, and a su- .perbly decorated canopy at the head of the bed; the whole bed, as well as various parts of the walls of the room, which are hung with black drapery, are illuminated with immense
wax flambeaux, while a number of priests are in attendance who offer up constant prayers for the soul of the deceased. —

The corpse itself is attired in its best clothing; or in an expensive substitute for it; or if the individual held any situation under government, in his appropriate uniform. This custom led to a singular occurrence on the decease of the late General Alabief, After his interment, a bill of thirty thousand roubles was missing; suspicion fell upon his secretary, who was threatened with a prosecution, unless it was reproduced. Unable to account for the deficiency, the idea at length occurred to him, that the paper might have been buried with ‘ his master; the coffin was opened and the bill found safe in the general’s pocket !

On the day of the funeral, the streets through which it passes are strewed with cypress leaves. The coffin with its lid on, but as yet unsecured, is placed on a rich car, with the canopy before mentioned over it, supported by six wooden pillars, and carried by men in deep mourning. The procession now marches slowly towards the

church, preceded by numerous choristers, who chant, as it advances, the most affecting and solemn dirges. Succeeding to these come an immense number of priests, attired in their clerical robes. Behind the car, the relatives of the deceased follow, with their heads uncovered; such as are military men, in full uniform; or if they hold situations at court, in their richest court-dresses. Ladies frequently join in the procession, some on foot, others in carriages; and the carriages of the relatives bring up the rear.

Having entered the church, the coffin is placed on a bier, with the canopy over it; the lid is removed, and the relatives and attendants take their stations on each side. The prayers now commence, accompanied by the most solemn vocal and instrumental music; this part of the ceremony continuing for not less than two hours. At its conclusion, the father confessor of the deceased reads aloud the contents of a scroll of paper, consisting of a pardon for his sins, and which is then, together with a piece of money, placed in the
-hand of the departed Christian. These may
be considered as his passports into the other ~ world.*

The mourners and other attendants now, one by one, take their final leave of their departed relative and friend, by embracing his corpse; the lid is then secured, and the coffin once more placed on the car, for the purpose of being conveyed to its last earthly habitation—the family vault. The company now enter their carriages, and return to the house of the deceased, where a splendid entertainment is provided for them.

It will readily be conceived that the expences attending such a funeral must be very considerable.. In the instance of Prince Plata- ‘Zauboff, who was lately buried at the Strelna Monastery, they are said to have amounted to nearly a hundred thousand roubles; and the canopy used at the death of Madame Narishkin alone cost six thousand roubles.
It is customary in Russia, on the annivergaries of the death of any respected relative,
160 VISIT TO THE TOMB OF PAUL.
to make a solemn visit to his tomb. ~ The following account of the honours paid in this
way by his present imperial majesty, to the.
manes of his father, Paul, at the church of the fortress, was communicated to me by a friend.

As the imperial family approached the place of sepulture, its was met by the metropolitan and heads of the clergy, accompanied by the governor of the city. The procession then entered the church in the following order :—.

First came the clergy, in their respective orders and full canonicals; after them followed the emperor, in military uniform, with the two empresses, one on each side of him, both being in deep mourning and covered by black veils; next came the Grand Duke Nicholas, leading his duchess, and then the Grand Duke Michael, accompanied by the governor. The whole stationed themselves near the tomb, without the railing. The dowager empress was now conducted by the emperor within the enclosure of the tomb, where she continued for a considerable time, in the act
of prayer, and in frequent apparent agitation, his majesty having, during this time, returned to his former station.

Iler majesty’s devotions having concluded, the emperor, with all the other members of the imperial family, one by one in succession, according to their rank, approached, and, on their knees, impressed three distinct kisses, first on the tomb, and then on the pavement, crossing themselves at the commencement and termination of this their participation in the ceremony. The emperor now conducted his mother from out of the chapel; after which the party returned to the winter palace. It ought to be added, that the whole of this impressive ceremony was accompanied by the most affecting vocal music.

There is, however, one day of the year more particularly held sacred to the memory of the dead, the 22d of October, (O. S.) when most of the lower orders repair to the churches and burial grounds, taking with them a quantity of rice, baked with honey, for the purpose of having it blessed by the priests, after which they return home to eat it, pro-
nouncing at the time the names of their departed friends, and taking care to comfort themselves with no small quantity of brandy.

When the death of any rich ‘person is expected, it is by no means uncommon for an undertaker to bribe the servants to admit him to some private room of the house, in order that he may be the first to measure the corpse for the coffin, and thus secure the funcral arrangements. Whatever property falls in the way of the servants, is regarded by them as fair plunder, provided they have the address to steal it undetected.

As soon as a person dies, his effects are placed under the seal of proper authorities, the dilatoriness of whose proceedings in its distribution is such, that the relatives make it a rule to possess themselves of all the moveables they can, before announcing the event.
I shall describe one more religiousceremony, named the “ Blessing of the Waters,” and which is observed annually on the morning of the 6th of January, O. S.
On this occasion, after divine service in the chapel of the winter palace, the emperor,

accompanied by thé various members of the imperial family, the clergy, and different public functionaries, repairs in grand procession to the Neva, where a large and splendid pavilion, decorated with paintings from subjects in holy writ, is erected over an opening cut through the ice. ;

The order of procession is as follows :— First come the choir, singing appropriate hymns, and followed by the archbishops, bishops, and inferior clergy, the former habited' in richly embroidered robes, with their episcopal mitres on their heads, beset with pearls and brilliants, and wearing also the splendid crosses of the orders of St. Alexander Nefsky and St. Vladimir. This whole body of priests, with their long white beards, makes a remarkably venerable appearance. Next in the procession is the emperor, attended by his officers of state, and followed by the grand dukes end a numerous train of the nobility.
On entering the pavilion, the emperor and his court uncover their heads, and, notwithstanding the intense severity of the wea.

ther, remain in this state throughout the ceremony. The whole now arrange themselves in their respective situations, and the archbishop proceeds to bestow his benediction on the waters of the river. A cup full is taken from it, with which he in succession sprinkles the emperor, his brothers, and, the whole party, each respectfully kissing his hand on receiving the holy fluid.
The procession now returns to the palace, in the same order as before, amidst salutes of cannon from the fortress; after whigh a splendid breakfast is partaken of.

In Catharine the Second’s time the ladics of the court used to join in the ceremony; they now, however, in consequence of the severe cold, merely witness the procession from the windows of the palace.

The crowds which assemble on the occasion are immense; and such is the opinion entertained.by all classes, from the palace to the cottage, of the virtues of the blessed water, that thousands of vessels full are taken from the river, to be reserved as a panacea against every disorder to which the human body is

‘incidental.* ‘Nay, notwithstanding the rigour of the season, numberless mothers take their infants to be baptized in the river; and I have been informed that, on such occasions, the hands of the officiating priest have sometimes been so benumbed by cold, that the child has been known to slip through his fingers, when the current has immediately, - and irretrievably, carried it under the ice. Inthis casé, the mother readily consoles herself in the firm belief, that an infant, thus drowned in holy water, goes the shortest way to heaven.

* A foreign gentleman being seized one day with a fit of the cholic, the lady of the house administered to him a glass of this blessed water, under the full impression that it would immediately cure him: unfortunately, however, it aggravated the complaint, which was attributed to his want of faith. The husband now prescribed a glass of Cogniac, which proved more efficacious on the stomach of the unbeliever.

THE extensive intercourse I had the opportunity of enjoying during my residence in St. Petersburg, with many of its more eminent merchants, induces me to offer a few remarks respecting the commercial relations of Russia with other countries, but more particularly Great Britain. | In the first place, I beg to observe, that, by the prohibitory system, a considerable alteration appears to have lately taken place with regard to those relations. Other causes, have also combined to deteriorate them; even so far back as the time of Catharine the Second, a con- * siderable jealousy began to be evidenced on the part of Russia; the temporary influence which the French attained trom the year 1807 to 1812, tended materially to aggravate this unfriendly disposition ; and the professed object of the government is, at the present time, to render themselves entirely independent of other countries, by encouraging native manufactories of every description ; a line of policy, however, which has been carried into effect with so little judgment, as to have almost universally failed in its execution, notwithstanding many of the measures adopted to promote it have beén most decided and energetic; such as assisting individuals with Toons of money for stated. periods, the absolute prohibition of many foreign manufactures, and the imposition of high duties on others, besides affording many other important advantages intended to encourage the object in view. |

The actual result of these measures has been, that the Russian manufacturer, unable to produce the finer articles so cheap as they can be supplied from other countries, and availing himself of the extensive contraband trade, which the government, from their great line of frontier, has not the power to suppress, has attached his mark to foreign goods and vended them as his own. In short, this system of the Russian government has generally terminated in the ruin of the manufacturer, so that eventually the former has been glad to seize upon the remainizig property of the latter, in order to reimburse itself for the money that has been advanced. ‘

The above pernicious system is, however, further subversive of the morality of the people, since it holds out to them the strongest inducement to engage in Ulicit traffic, and which, I am assured, is carried on to an almost incredible extent, principally through the intervention of the Jews. It is also, at the same time, injurious to the revenue, which would, without doubt, be better promoted by a repeal ° of the prohibitory laws, and the imposition of moderate duties on the various articles of foreign produce.

It can scarcely he imagined, that the governmment is unaware of the injurious tendency of their measures ;—to what then can their persistence in them be attributed? without doubt they are considerably influenced by a spirit of retaliation for the restrictions imposed by the British government on the importation of their linen and sailcloths. They alledge, however, that the diminution of the duties would occasion an excess of the imports over the exports, and thus lead to the ruin of .their manufacturers. Specious as this may appear in reason, it is futile in fact, since every one acquainted with Russian commerce knows that, as the affair now stands, the imports, in consequence of the illicit trade, have actually and virtually much exceeded the exports, although the tustom-house documents do not make it appear; and this, of course, without the due advantage being derived by the revenue itself.

Would it not be better for Russia, until her population has materially increased to discontinue all manufactures excepting those of her native raw material, the barter of which would, in all probability, be equivalent to the introduction of her necessary foreign commodities and luxuries? since it is by no means probable that the demand for the latter would be greater than the former would be capable of covering. It is an acknowledged axiom, that increased imports will be productive of increased exports, and vice versa ; for the stream of commerce, like that of water, has a tendency to keep its level; so that you cannot detract from one extremity without producing a determination to it from the other.

As matters now stand, the English merchant is no great gainer by his connexion with Russia; for the obstructions he meets with are innumerable, and certain to do away with any competent profit; he has not merely to contend with prohibitions, excessive duties, and obscure tariffs, but with the necessity of an immense floating capital ; a variety of competition; and the bad faith of the Russian merchants.

The liberty of the British merchant has also of late been materially infringed upon. Previous to 1806, he was only amenable to the representative of his nation, whose pass was his protection; this privilege he has been deprived of, and he is now placed on the same footing as the common mechanics of the country, and liable to be dragged before the lowest courts of justice on every trivial occasion. How dif:
ferent is this treatment from what our countrymen experienced during the reign of Catharine, and which shed a lustre upon them and their nation.

The Russians, notwithstanding, are under the greatest obligations to the English merchants, by whose capital they may be said to be supported ; since if ‘the latter enters into a contract with the former for the sale and delivery: of goods at the expiration of six months, he is obliged to pay down half, and sometimes the whole money at the time ; whereas; in the reverse case, of a Russian purchasing from an Englishman, although the delivery be immediate, the payment must be long deferred ; and yet, at the same time, they will deal with the Americans, for barter or money, or only short credits.

In the reign of Catharine the Second, which may be regarded as the Augustan age of the country, the exchange, between St. Petersburg and London, was as high as forty-eight pence for the rouble, while bank-notes and agio were six per cent on silver, in favour of the bank-note; now, the exchange is under ten pence per rouble, and the agio two hundred and seventy-five per cent. (it has been at three hundred) in favour of silver, or rather against the bank-note. This is attributable to the excess of paper-money arbitrarily issued, and to the impolitic measures of the government.

Russia, undoubtedly, from the vast extent of her territory, and the immense variety of her climate, soil, and productions, possesses within herself all the elements of extensive commerce. When she knows‘how to avail herself properly of the local advantages nature has so abundantly lavished upon her, she will undoubtedly become a great commercial nation. At present, however, her power, notwithstanding she has the vanity to think otherwise, is more ideal than real; she may, not unaptly, be resembled to a gigantic child, too little advanced from infancy to throw aside external support, without the risk of injuring those principles which are calculated eventually to carry it to manhood.

As to her trade, it is scarcely, at this time, worth the attention of a man of capital; unless he be a Jew, or a smuggler, and well acquainted with every species of chicanery and meanness; even such an one; must be possessed of consummate cunning, and may esteem himself fortunate if he succeeds in carrying his point with- . out the Ryssian outwitting him.

To conclude—it appears impossible that the emperor can long remain unacquainted with the injurious consequences of this system of high duties and prohibitions, and from his known character, it may be hoped, that he will direct it to be altered; particularly when he secs the effects of our new and liberal system of commerce in producing the extension of our national power, and the welfare of all mankind.

To an English reader, whose situation and habits have led him to experience only a slight difference between the various seasons of the changing year, and particularly to the inhabitants of the more genial and less variable climate of the south, a short description of a winter at St. Petersburg may, possibly, prove interesting: I shall, therefore, endeavour to pourtray the leading features of the one I passed in that city.

The previous summer had proved peculiarly warm, and comparatively finer than usual, so that it was not until the middle of September, that the variability of the weather gave the first intimations of the approach of winter, a season so highly desirable and important to the Russian. We now, indeed, experienced so much variability, that I have one hour basked in the warmest sunshine, and the next been deluged by torrents of rain. Such changes certainly, are not exclusively peculiar to this country; St. Petersburg, however, appears, by nature, more adapted to these transitions than any other city in Europe, in consequence of its situation in the midst of marshes, which afford an abundance of exhalations. The atmosphere, being further surcharged with moisture from the Gulf of Finland on one side, and Lake Ladoga on the other, contributes to make it a repository for the watery elements; it is fortunate, however, that a frequency of high winds assist in carrying away this excessive humidity, by the great evaporation they occasion. Krafft states the average result of several years calculation of the state of the weather here, as follows :—Rain, one hundred and three days; snow, seventy-two; unsettled, ninety-three; clear and serene weather, ninety-seven.
At length, November was ushered in, and with it came all the harbingers of approaching

winter. Most of the families who had been enjoying: their summer ‘residences had now returned to the city. On the first day of this month, the morning broke forth with a gloomy appearance ; the thermometer indicated frost, and at two-o’clock it commenced snowing, which continued until midnight. The wirid, however, now veered round to S. W. and for some days it became milder again. Many of the vessels in the harbour of Cronstadt prepared to sai] with the first fait wind.
On the 6th the wind changed to the north, the weather becoming sensibly colder. We now began to experience a regular clear frost, with occasional interruptions of snow.

On the 13th most of the vessels that remained at Cronstadt sailed; and it was reported that a quantity of ice from Ladoga Lake had entered the Neva; the communication with Cronstadt by steam-boats was, consequently, interrupted; and those who reside on the Island, as it is termed, hesitated to visit the court side of the Neva.

When the river closes, the first symptom is an appearance of sheets of ice floating down it, so thin as scarcely to be discernible; this is termed*by the Russians, salo, or tallow. Quantities of ice are now every instant expected down the river, and the proper authorities are on the alert to remove the bridges, on the instant that it becomes necessary. After this, the ice which forms on the border of Lake Ladoga separates, and is driven by the wind into the current of the Neva; the masses -here gradually accumulate, and at length combine into one solid body.
On the 15th the thermometer was at seven degrees (Reaumur) below freezing; and before midnight three of the bridges were removed.

On the I7th the weather became milder again, the thermometer rising to two and a half of heat. On the following day, a heavy westerly gale came on, and the water in the river rose to an unusual height. The bridges were now replaced: the season, in short, is so variable at this time, that it is not unusual to remove and replace the bridges three or four times, before the river is permanently closed for the winter, The river now

became free from ice, so that the communication with Cronstadt was renewed, and the weather was once more so mild, that the Rus- | sians began to apprehend an open winter; to them a most serious occurrence, as it interferes with their supplies of provisions by sledges from the interior, and renders the necessaries of life unusually dear. The expence of transferring all articles of commerce in Russia, is much less in winter than in summer.

On the evening of the 25th a sensible change again took place: snow fell, and the thermometer indicated two degrees- of frost. On the 28th we had seven degrees of frost; and, on the following day, large masses of ice floating down the Neva, the bridges were again taken away. ’

Notwithstanding this stzong indication, December came in with a mild aspect, so that, on the 2d, the Isaac Bridge was again replaced. This open weather continued, with little interruption, until the 16th, when the thermometer sunk to three degrees of frost ; and, on the following day, one of the bridges was, for the last time, removed. It was remarked, that precisely nine months had now elapsed since the breaking up of the ice of last winter; the longest period in which the river had ever been known to be free. On the 23d of September, (O. 8.) 1715, the river was. completely frozen over in twenty-four hours, and continued so until the May following; such were the great distinctions of the two seasons.. There appears little doubt but that the climate has experienced a material change here, so that the winters are neither of the same intensity, or duration, as formerly; and probably this is the result of the land being better drained, so that the evaporation from its surface is diminished ; while the great quantity ef wood cleared from the face of the country has contributed to diminish the quantity of humidity.

On the 21st the current of the river was again arrested; the Neva was finally closed for the season, and its surface destined to become the scene of many a joyous sport, ere the genial warmth of spring should restore its fluidity. The thermometer stood this day at

nine degrees of frost. In six hours after the river had closed, a few Russians had the hardihood to cross over it. Notwithstanding the precautions of the police, some lives are generally lost,,in this way, every season.

As soon as the river was deemed sufficiently solid, the police began forming roads across it, at the usual ferries, by levelling the ice, in which operation they were materially assisted by a fall of snow. The line of road was then more clearly indicated by fir-trees planted on each side, with slips laid in inclined planes on the banks of the river, to facilitate the passage of carriages. The scene now became truly animating, the people beginning to cross the river in all directions, every one apparently gratified at the earnest thus received of a permanent winter.

Soon afterward, the Isaac Bridge was replaced, which was effected by cutting out the ice piecemeal, and forcing it under the surface of the main mass, when it is carried away by the current of the river. Inthis manner a channel is formed, into which the pontoons are replaced, one by one, until the whole are restored; a { ; more pleasant road is thus made by the bridges, than what is afforded by the slips and inclined planes of boards before described.

During the remainder of the month, the whole of January, and the commencement of February, the frost continued without interruption, the greatest intensity of cold being on the 5th of February, when the thermometer was down at twenty-four degrees of frost, equal to twenty-two degrees below zero, of Fahrenheit.*

Whenever the cold exceeds seventeen degrecs of frost, the various public amusements, as_ well as private parties, are suspended ; that is, either do not take place, or break up earlier than usual. This regulation was adopted in consequence of some coachmen having been frozen to death, while waiting in the streets with their carriages.
On the 13th of February a great change was experienced, the weather becoming sensibly warmer, and the thermometer rising to the freezing point, after which it continued
* See Appendix G for a register of the thermometer during the present winter.

mild for the remainder of the month. On the - Ath of March the snow began to disappear from the streets, and, in a few days after, wheel carriages to resume the places of sledges. On the 10th the snow was so far melted on the surface of the river, that in crossing with my droshka, the water in some places reached to the horses’ middles. Of course the ice underneath must now become more tender; however, the roads are always the last parts to give way, owing to the repeated pressure | having rendered them' so compact, that it is not unusual, after other parts of the river have become clear, to see them go off separately.in solid bodies. In order to prevent accidents, the police, for some days before the ice is expected to break up, try its strength from time to time ; and when it is no longer deemed safe, its passage is interdicted, at first to carriages, and afterwards to foot passengers. Previous to the river breaking up, the inhabitants fill their cellars with ice, for summer use. This is generally done by contract, at the expence of from one to three guineas, according to the size of the cellar. For this purpose a portion of the river is railed in, and the ice cut out into cubes of about-a yard square.

At length, on the 8th of April, the chains of the Neva were once more loosened ; the bridges were consequently taken away to allow the masses of ice to pass, and the communications with the opposite sides of the river again interrupted.

When the river becomes sufficiently free from ice, a particular ceremony is observed, previous to any boats being allowed to cross. The governor passes over in his boat from the fortress to the palace, where he presents the emperor with a goblet of the water of the river; the emperor then returns a silver goblet filled with wine, which, with the salver on which it is presented, becomes the perquisite of the gavernor.* As soon as the governor places his foot ‘on shore, a signal-gun fires, the free passage of the river is then restored.
I shall conclude this chapter with a few
* This vessel formerly, instead of wine, used to be filled with ducats.
szemarks on the capability of the Russians to bear the variations of temperature, to which their climate is subject.

Although the Russian is generally supposed to be adapted by constitution to support in- _ tensity of cold, and certainly is enabled to do so by the precautions he, takes against it, being almost literally imbedded in furs or woollen clothing, yet heat appears to be his favourite element; at least, he puts on his winter clothing sooner than the foreign resident, and continues to wear it longer in the spring. If you inquire why he does so, you receive a proverb in reply, the literal sense of which is, that “ Heat breaks no bones.”

The apartments of the higher classes of Russians, in winter, are carefully guarded from the external cold by double windows and other precautions, and kept at a temperature of from sixty to seventy degrees, Fahrenheit, by means of. stoves. Those of the lower classes, termed isbas, are heated to such a degree, that a person unaccustomed to them would find a difficulty in supporting the temperature ;: the heat, however, is not more annoying than the smell, as they not only make use of the same apartment for every domestic purpose, but also as a sleeping room; in short, the smell of a stable is comparatively odoriferous. If a Russian is sent to prison, and finds it warm and close, he enters it with apparent satisfaction, exclaiming, “ Oh, it is warm!” I am satisfied, therefore, that the general opinion of his preferring cold is erroneous;—he accommodates himself to it, because it is his interest to do so; and supports it better, because he is better provided, since, during the winter season, his house-keeping expences are diminished, by the great facility afforded to the conveyance of provisions from the inland districts, or distant provinces, without which advantage the Russian capital could ill sustain the rigour of a severe winter. It may be added, as a farther reason why the Russian is not better adapted to bear’a rigorous winter than his more southern neighbours, that the frequent indulgence in warm, re-

laxing baths, as well as the excessive heat of his apartment, where he always crowds to the warmest place, sleeping even on the stove itself, must necessarily increase his susceptibility of the influence of cold.

Tus 13th of March, 1823, was the day I determined upon for my departure from St. Petersburg, having taken my place in the diligence of that day, from thence to Moscow. The hour fixed was nine o'clock. I was, however, in considerable darger of being left behind, owing to the delay experienced in packing my baggage; an arrangement which requires very deliberate attention on my part, and which I had been prevented effecting, according to my ordinary custom, on the preceding evening, in consequence. of having been detained at a party, where I had been taking leave of many of my kind friends. It is true, I had plenty of offers of assistance, elicited by the opinion entertained of my own helplessness; an opinion, by the bye, which is very erroneous. I find, by experience, that the best way is to lock myselfup in my room, like a schoolboy, who has a difficult task to perform; for were I once to get confused, the presence and assistance of a second person would only serve to distract me further, and to make confusion more confused. By observing this principle, I have acquired such methods of arrangement, that I not only know precisely where every thing lies that is contained in my personal baggage, but even to direct my friends at home how to find any article that I may have left behind me.

Before I had completed this indispensable business, several successive messengers came to apprise me that the coach was in readiness; and, I believe, I am indebted for ‘its detention to a party of my friends, who had assembled at the office to take their last leave of me. The chief amongst these was my old and particular friend C——, to whose kindness I feel myself indebted for the greater part of the happiness I had so long been enjoying, and who appeared to make it his study to throw me into the way of every thing that could contribute to my gratification, by introducing me amongst the respectable and extensive circle of his acquaint-, ance, by whom he is universally beloved and
“esteemed. I shall leave it to the reader to imagine the emotions of mind with which I bade adicu to such a friend.
“ Ah never shall my soul forget
The friend I found so cordial hearted ; Dear shall be the hour we met,
And dear shall be the time we parted.”

But in thus eulogising my estimable friend, let me not appear forgetfulof the many others, whose constant kindness and hospitality have left upon my heart, an impression never to be erased. To these kind souls, I again repeat the truest farewell of as sincere a heart as ever throbbed with the warm pulse of gratitude.
I had now the pleasure of finding a couns

tryman in one of my fellow travellers, a Mr. M--, to whom I received an introduction, from a mutual friend, on entering the coach. As soon as my first emotions had subsided, I began to reconnoitre our vehicle, and found it a comfortable well-stuffed carriage mounted on easy springs; intended to convey four -inside and as many outside: passengers, two of the latter of whom were seated in a kind of cabriolet in front, and the other two in’ a similar structure at the back of the carriage. The coachman and guard sat together on a box in front, and the whole were drawn by six horses, four of which ran abreast near the carriage, with two leaders, mounted by a postillion on the right, in front of them. Besides Mr. M. and myself, the inside was occupied by an officer of engineers and his servant, the former of whom proved a very gentlemanly, intelligent man, well acquainted with the French and German languages. On the outside were, an old German, who superintended some manufactory near Moscow, a Russian money-changer, a fishmonger, and another person, of whose calling I am ignorant,

We travelled the first fourteen versts from the city gate on a straight and level road; after which, we ascended a hill, about half way up which is a beautiful fountain that was erected in 1807: The top of this hill commands a fine -prospect, with St. Petersburg in the distance. Two versts farther is a village, called the Emperor’s Colony, consisting of arow of twenty-four handsome wooden houses, with @ watch-tower in the centre. At the distance of twenty-two versts we passed through the town of Sarskoe-Selo, close to which there is a village built in the Chinese style, which has a very pleasing effect. The imperial palace at this place I have already described.

Our first stage, which consisted of thirtythree versts, terminated at the village of Ijora. After this we travelled twenty-four versts to Tosna, a neat and extensive village of nearly two versts and a half in length. Soon after leaving the latter place, our progress was arrested by a direful quarrel between our guard and coachman ; the former of whom had given the latter a good thrashing, because he did not drive fast enough to please him.

Mr. Coachee in consequence dismounted from his box and announced his determination to drive no farther, appealing at the same time to . the passengers to justify the propriety of his conduct. At length, by dint of reasoning, and the still more powerful influence of a bribe, a mode of argument very persuasive to a Russian, he was prevailed upon to resume his seat; after which he drove -the remainder of. his stage at a much greater rate, concealing his chagrin, if he felt any, by singing all the way. I believe it is not unusual for the lower classes in Russia to settle all disputes by the above kind of reference or arbitration; perhaps it would be better if the custom extended itself to the higher classes. We had strong reason, afterward, to imagine that the above altercation was concerted between the parties, in order to get a feeling into the pockets of their passengers. Many of these people, I am assured, will readily submit to a good beating, provided they can be remunerated for it with drink-money. Our route now lay through an uninteresting country, with immense forests of fir timber,

extending on each side of the road; and where with the exception of occasional villages, little evidence of population could be traced. On entering each of these villages you are struck by a notification, attached toa pole, of the number of souls it contains —that is, of male inhabitants; were it not too gross a libel on the sex—a libel decidedly contradicted in their history, by the names of Catharine and other heroines, one would imagine that this was intended to intimate that their women had no souls.

At seven in the evening we arrived at a decent post-house, about sixty miles distant from St. Petersburg, where we made a comfortable dinner. Here we were joined by a gentleman and lady, who had travelled from St. Petersburg in their own sledge, and who were proceeding to the most eastern parts of Siberia, where the former had an appointment as agent to the American Fur Company at Okotsk. They were impatient to get without delay to the end of their journey, which did not accord with my arrangements for making | more or less protracted stays iu the principal

we met the sledge diligence from Moscow, which we exchanged for our wheel carriage ; to effect this, however, we were obliged to return four miles to the last station. The party we took the places of were a company of French comedians ; and we found the exchange far from being in our favour, and were convinced that these actors would have an easier part to perform on the stage they had now entered upon, than on the rough boards they had so lately quitted.

About a mile from this place, our party noticed a large wolf, who was marching very leisurely along the side of a wood, and who would not deign to hasten his pace, although considerable noise was made with the view of alarming him. Svon after this, we crossed the river Volzhof, over a long wooden bridge, and entered the ancient city and republic of Novogorod. My companions noticed that the country had, for some time, become more hilly, diversified and picturesque, as well as more thickly inhabited. Among the edifices observed in the vicinity of this city, were sevcral monasteries, a class of building in general

most advantageously situated, the monks, in all ages, having, in the midst of their heavenly aspirations, sufficient eye to the good things of this world, as well as sufficient taste, to select the most favoured spots for their earthly tabernacles.

Among the more. interesting places in this neighbourhood, is a military colony, lately established according to the plan‘ of Count Araktcheef, consisting of an extensive line of buildings, with a steepled church in the centre, and ornamented in front, with a row of lime | trees.* °

We arranged with the guard not to hurry us away, that we might have the opportunity of visiting some of the more interesting points of Novogorod. Accordingly we went to the residence of the celebrated Marpha, widow of the last president of this republic, who made so noble an effort, after the death of her husband, to maintain its independence. A small portion only of this house is standing. We also went to the cathedral, dedicated to St. Sophia,
* Sce Dr. Lyall’s pamphlet on the Military Colonies of Russia.

and which has been erected more than six hundred years. Here we were shewn the incorruptible remains of several saints, parti- . cularly of Saint Nikita, which are said to have lain five hundred and fifty years; also of Vladimer, the son of Yarosloff; of St. Anne, his wife, and of his uncle, Prince Theodore. One of the doors, which is of brass,and covered with scriptural characters in basso relievo, is said to have been sent by Yladimer; from Kerson, in the Crimea, after the capture of that city from the Greeks. In the dome is a picture of ourSaviour, which tradition says, was originally painted with the hand held up and expanded, in the act of blessing the people, but which, on the following day, was discovered to be closed, a state in which it has ever since remained.

On leaving Novogorod, we crossed the Volghof again, on a raft, and proceeded by a byeroad, which saved us one-third of the distance, to the next stage. This road, however, was very bad, partly in consequence of the deficiency of snow, and partly from its being made of trees, We drank “tea, at the distance of
about forty miles from Novogérod, at a point where the Valdai Hills are said to. commence.

About two o’clock on the following morning, we arrived at the small town of Crestzi, containing about four hundred male inhabitants ; and in two hours afterwards at a station where we took our tea, in company with two Germans, who were on their way to St. Petersburg; from Salataouste, or Soningham, in the Ural Mountains, where there is an extensive manufacture of swords, thirty-thousand of which are annually sent to the capital.

At eight o'clock we breakfasted at Yajelbitza, distant three hundred and eleven versts from St. Petersburg, and four hundred and seventeen from Moscow. The peasants of this place not unfrequently offer pearls for sale to the traveller, and which are the produce of a shell-fish (the Unio Margaritifera) that inhabits the River Polimite, as well as a lake that is situated in this neighbourhood. They are also found in a variety of rivers belonging to the governments of Novogorod, Tver, and some others.
The following account of the pear] fisheries of this country, taken froma pamphlet written on the subject by Dr. Fischer, president of the Medical Academy at Moscow, may not be uninteresting. )

“ In 1721, the search and fishing for pearls was, by order of the College of Mines, settled on the crown, and in the above mentioned provinces, several noblemen received private instructions to superintend the fishing. As the result, however, did not answer their expectations, in the year 1731 the fishing was declared, by order of the sehate, free to all, upon condition only, that the largest and clearest pearls should be brought to the Cullege of Commerce, by the chief fishermen, who were to receive a reward in proportion to their quality; the smallest pearls were to be ‘the property of the fishermen.”
Subsequent licenses have confirmed this freedom of fishery, reserving in full force, the claim to the clearest and largest pearls, particularly such as are of the size of a sparrow’s ege.
There is a pearl, which Dr. F. describes in

the above work, to be seen at Moscow, the property of a Greek merchant, named Zosima, which, perhaps, has not its equal in the world. It is, however, not the produce of this country, but said to have been brought from the East Indies.

This inestimable pearl, which is preserved in a triple box, inlaid with precious stones, faced with a convex lens, intended to increase still farther its apparent magnitude, and under which it lies embedded in cotton wool, like a pheenix amidst its ashes, weighs no less than twenty-seven cdrats and seven-eights; it is perfectly spherical; its colour exceeds the metallic splendour of highly polished silver ; but at the same time posseses the most transparent brightness. When separated from its coverings, and placed on a sheet of white paper, it rolls upon the surface like a ball of quicksilver, and, somewhat like the latter, is only secured by the finger with the greatest nicety. Dr. Fischer bears personal testimony to the admiration—nay, astonishment! with which it is viewed by all strangers.

" bad, as frequently to- compel us to quit them, and take to the fields, or where most snow was to be found.. At one o’clock we came within sight of the town of Valdai, with Lake Itmen on its left; in the centre of which is a small island, with a monastery upon it, which makes a very picturesque appearance. In this convent the unfortunate Ivan was confined, previous to his being removed to his last place of imprisonment, at the-fortress of Schlusselberg, where he met his untimely fate, in consequence of the misdirected zeal of an enthusiast. si We were here informed that there was so great a scarcity of corn in this neighbourhood, during the last summer, that the peasants were compelled to use dried moss as a substitute; and yet the neighbouring monks would not allow the half starving people to take any of the fish with which the lake abounds. This water contains a fish which so much resembles the herring, that it might be called the freshwater herring. Linnzus terms it the clapea harengus. Immense quantities of a small fish are taken here, called snitke; it is the eperda-

nus of Linneeus, and said to be the same as our smelt; these fish are about two inches and a half in length, and, when fresh, of a beautiful silvery hue. The peasants have a mode of curing them, by putting them, as soon as caught, into ovens of a moderate temperature, and gradually, but thoroughly, drying them; they are then packed in baskets, and sent off to St. Petersburg, Moscow, and other parts of Russia, where they are retailed at from threepence to four-pence per pouud. They are also forwarded in their fresh state during the winter. :

Our neat stage was Edrova, which we found ’ all animation, in consequence of its being the maslanitza, or butter week, so named, from its being permitted to eat butter, milk, and cheese during its continuance. These holidays precede the long and rigid fast of Lent. This period is joyously celebrated, particularly among the lower classes, who partake of the various amusements of ice-hills, &c. &c. We met several carts filled with young damsels, in their holiday attire, and who appeared very happy in singing their national airs.
We even got into the midst of some groups of them in the streets, when my companions de- - lighted them much with presents of gingerbread.

In our next stage, we found the road con-, siderably improved. We were not a little amused with the eccentricity of our driver, who appeared to have been making too free with the good cheer at Edrova. He had, however, his horses under such excellent command, that he could, at any time, set them off at full speed, by merely holding his hand up. The horses in Russia, it must be observed, are rarely driven, even in gentlemen’s carriages, without blinkers over their eyes. Nor does this appear productive of accidents; on the contrary, I am told, that it is unusual for a horse even to start in this country. The peasantry are uniformly expert in their Management: they often talk to them as if they were children, telling them that they shall receive an additional quantity of oats, if they behave well; or that the gentle; men they are conveying will treat them with a glass c{ brandy—an ingenious mode ot

giving their passengers a hint. At ail events, the poor animals themselves profit but little by this professed kindness; for, with the exception of having enough to eat, they have little attention paid them, but are turned, after the severest journeys, into unstalled stables, without cleaning, or any other care. These horses are small, ugly creatures, possessing, it is true, great hardihood, but which, in the posting service, seldom holds out for more than two or three years.

As the posting between St. Petersburg and Moscow forms a peculiar establishment, I shall avail myself of this opportunity of detailing its leading features. In order to facilitate the communication between his old and new capitals, and diminish the expences of travellingy Peter the Great caused villages, with a popu. lation of five or six hundred boors, to be attached to each post station, at the distance of every twenty or thirty versts, and who were obliged to convey the traveller at a fixed and reasonable rate. These people were freed from other duties, and had peculiar privileges
‘granted to them, which they still enjoy.

A certain number of these boors are obliged to be on constant duty at the post-house, and in which they relieve each other, according to such arrangement as may be agreed on between themselves, those who are disengaged being then at liberty to occupy themselves in such other pursuits as their interests or inclinations may suggest. Some of them become carriers of goods to distant places; as Dresden, Leipsic, &c. ; and others engage in various trades. It often happens that the latter have no horses fit for the duties of the post; in which case they are allowed to engage , With their brethren to act as their substitutes. In consequence of this arrangement, the traveller generally finds plenty of horses on the road ;~-there is, however, one result from it which occasionally appears incomprehensible tohim. Itis this: that when he arrives at a station where the driver, whose turn it is to take him forward, happens to have no horses, he observes a number of these people form a circle, and commence a warm and earnest conyersation, which terminates, at length, in

an appeal to luck, by a casting of lots. * This ‘arises from the necessity the driver for the occasion is under to hire a substitute, and his matural anxiety to incur as little expence, in so doing, as possible. At length, having brought some one individual ‘down to his lowest point, it generally happens that several others immediately offer to serve him for the same price. In this case, the future driver is determined by each marking a piece of money, for instance, a copeck, which is put-into & hat, when, the whole being shaken together, one is drawn out, and its owner declared the successful candidate.
These regulations apply to all the post stations intermediate to the two cities, excepting the three nearest to Moscow, which are regularly contracted for by government, as on other post roads.,

The price of posting, on two or three occasions, has been raised since the time of Peter the Great. It is now eight copecks, or eighttenths of a penny, per verst, for each horse ; which, with two copecks for the government
licence, or padarogeney as it is called, to take post-horses, makes one penny per verst, or three halfpence per mile..

On Sunday, the 16th, we arrived, soon after midnight, at Vychni-Volotchok, a town of some magnitude, chiefly remarkable for a fine canal, which unites the rivers Tsna and Tvertza, and establishes the communication between St. Petersburg and the Volga. A friend of mine observed last summer, in passing through this place, many of the Women walking about the town with their teeth blackened, and which is effected by applying a wash formed with corrosive sublimate and nitrous acid. This custom, I believe, was formerly very general throughout Russia. I am told that their teeth not unfrequently acquire this engaging colour through mere neglect, without the trouble of staining them artificially.

At eight o’clock we arrived at the town of Torjak, where we refreshed ourselves with ablution, clean linen, and a good breakfast, the comforts of the whole of -which, those who, like ourselves, had been travelling three

days and nights, over bad roads, and without ” sleep, will readily appreciate. This is a neat town; with fourteen principal churches, and the river Tvertza running through the middle of it. -It has an extensive manufactory of fine leather, embroidered with gold and silver.

I took some pains to ascertain: the mode in which the well-known Russian leather is prepared. Its peculiar smell is given in the first stage of dressing, by using, instead of oil, or in combination with it, a bituminous matter, called dyoggett, which is extracted from the young birch trees in the following manner: ~The roots and branches being first cut

"-off, the trunk of the tree is laid on an inclined plane, upon a wire grating, under which ‘a fire is lighted; this causes the sap contained in the bark, and particularly the outer coat, to ferment and ooze out froin the lower extremity, where it is received in a vessel placed for that purpose,,The liquor thus obtained, after being cleaned from dirt and woody particles, is boiled down to a proper consistency, or until it much resembles tar. The best dyoggett is, however, said to be
procured from the bark alone, when stripped from the tree.

Our next station was Medoe, which we quitted at three o’clock. The road was-now so bad, that our outside passengers, who were in a smaller sledge behind us, were three different times turned over, and left cooling — themselves in the snow. We now arrived within sight of the town of Tver, still distant twelve miles from us; and soon after passed two monasteries, one on each side of the road. About six miles from Tver, we entered.an avenue of trees, which apparently extended.to the town, but terminated at the end of two miles. After this, the country became more picturesque, possessing many fine extensive prospects, in which the city, with its glittering cupolas, illuminated by the setting sun, as my companions informed me, shone beautifully conspicuous.

On entering Tver, we crossed the celebrated Volga on the ice. My companions here observed several groups of females, dressed in a novel and beautiful costume, and who were enjoying the last holiday previous to Lent.

Their dress consisted of a white or coloured muslin or silken gown, embroidered with various colours, or with gold or silver, over which was worn a mantle of an elegant figured. silk, bordered with fur, which reached to the lower part of the back; the head-dress was a small pointed bonnet, embroidered with gold. We were driven to a decent inn, kept by an Italian, where we were much refreshed by a tolerably fair dinner; any kind of stimulus naturally would have this effect, after the great. exertion and fatigue we had undergone.

We at length recommenced our journey, and experienced a very cold night, the thermometer indicating ten degrees of frost, equal to about twenty-two degrees below the freezing point of Fahrenheit. The worst of it was, that it was impossible to sleep, such was the jolting of our carriage, except, indeed, during the periods of changing horses, and then we were soon started from out of it again. At seven o’clock we breakfasted at Klin, and were comforted with the information that our road to Moscow was still worse than any we had yet experienced. We had, however, the
satisfaction of knowing that we should certainly arrive at the great city before the close of day.

The country now became more hilly and picturesque, and, as we approached nearer to Moscow, was ornamented with monasteries and gentlemen’s seats. About four versts from the city we passed the Petrovsky Palace, which was occupied by Napoleon, previous to his taking up his residence at the Kremlin.

During this last stage, the motion of our sledge could only be compared to the pitching of a small vessel in a short sea, and, I believe, had a similar effect on some’of my companions. It occasioned one of our shafts’ to break ; but the deficiency was soon replaced.

At six o’clock we entered the gates of Moscow, and soon reached the diligence-oflice, from whence I lost no time in finding out, with the kind assistance of Mr. M——, my bankers, Messrs. G and H-——, to whom I had previously written, to request they would do me the favour of causing lodgings to be secured ‘for me. They received me with every kindness and attention, and placed me in the same hotel where Mr. M—— also purposed to take up his quarters. I was fortunate, however, in another respect: Messrs. G—— and H—— were that evening parting with a servant, whom they thought might suit my purpose. There were two objections to him: the one, that he was guilty of impertinence; the other, that he only spoke the - Russian language. However, after well revolving the point, [ determined to engage him, as my ignorance of this language would, in great measure, do away with the sense of his impertinence; at the same time I hoped to glean’ some words, at least, of the - Russian tongue, in consequence of the intercourse which would necessarily subsist between us, ‘

Some of my readers will be inclined to inquire what pleasure or information I could have derived, under my igngrance of the language, from the journey I have just been describing, had I not met with two companions who were able to converse with me, and consequently to explain ‘every thing of interest which occurred on the road? and also how I would have acted, under such circumstances, on my arrival at Moscow, without such assistance ?

To the first of these questions I reply, that I should, as I am prepared to do on all occasions when left to myself, have depended on the resources of my own mind, if nothing of* sufficient interest to elicit my attention occurred. But although I have eyes, and do not see, and ears, without being able to understand the language in which they are addressed, yet I still find ways of comprehending the more ordinary occurrences of life. For instance: when ‘the horses, are changed, I hear the foriner ones removed and - others substituted, as well as the remarks of their attendants; and it requires no great ~ stretch of imagination to divine the conversation of ostlers and drivers;—nor should I have been at a’loss to recognize the pitiful solicitations of the beggars on the road side. The same principl> applies, more or less, to the higher incidents of a journey. In travelling, however, through Russia, there is no great use for eyes, for the general features are ordinary and little varied, its towns and Villages very similar in appearance; there are few spots where contending armies have fought their battles, and no indications of former heroes, with the exception of a few tumuli, ‘which the Tartar hordes have reared as the memorials of their dead; besides, the movements of the post neither allow time for the. artist or antiquary to indulge in their favourite pursuits. Perhaps the best way is to get forward, as fast ds possible, from one large town to another, where better chances of collecting matter of interest will be likely to present themselves. Italy! fair Italy! is the country which offers the highest allurements to the traveller, and where every step he takes is classic ground !

With regard to the second question, I beg to remark, that I never attémpt a journey to a strange place, without being provided with the address of some house or other, to which I can appeal. On arriving at the coach-office, I should have waited patiently until the guard had settled his office business ;

after which, the hope of reward would have induced him to conduct me to the place I desired. In this way I have often proceeded, under similar circumstances, and never met’ with any difficulty which I was unable to ‘surmount.

My kind bankers had not placed me in the most fashionable hotel in, Moscow, but in one where they knew my comforts would be attended to, and which from its central situation would facilitate my pursuits of information and amusement.

My first object was to hire a sledge, for, although the snow was rapidly disappearing, there was still sufficient in the streets of Moscow to make this the preferable mode of conveyance. The expence of this carriage, including the coachman, was from four to five roubles per day; however, after using it for a week, I was induced to exchange it for a droshka, at an additional charge of one rouble.

The regular wages of my servant were about one guinea per month, but on enquiring how much J should pay him in addition to board himself, to my great surpfise, he only demanded five roubles per month ; I discovered, however, that he calculated upon a variety of perquisites, and fees from the different tradesmen he might be the means of intro-* ducing me to; nay, he even had the impudence one day to complain, that a coachman whom I had engaged, had failed to give him the promised silver rouble, adding, that it was impossible a servant could live without perquisites. I know not, but was informed that he com-
plained of my frequently suspecting him of

cheating, or robbing me, particularly if I happened to enquire for any article that might have been mislaid, or removed, by the servants of the house. This ts a general feature, in Russian servants, who on such occasions commonly reply, “ Do you think that I have done it?” or “ Do you suppose I have stolen it?”

On the day after my arrival, hearing that my friends, the Captains J——, were still” at Moscow, I succeeded in making out their residence, but was sorry to learn that they’ were both on the point of leaving Moscow; the one for the Crimea, the other for Germany and England. This I regretted exceedingly, as, independent of their uniform friendly attentions to myself, they were men of intelligence ; their pursuits similar to my own, as they were inordinately intent on acquiring. information respecting the institutions, cus+ toms, and manners of the people we were travelling amongst.
I dined with them, and in the evening had the pleasure of meeting them at Dr. K’s where many of the English residents were assembled; I

was compelled; however, to retire early, in consequence of the excessive soreness of various muscles of my neck and shoulders, occasioned by the constant jolting to which I had been exposed during my late journey, my head having had, for the greater part of the time, to perform the office of an inverted pendulum, the effects of which did not cease for nearly a fortnight,

On. the 20th I paid a visit to the Countess Orloff, whom I had the honour of knowing at St. Petersburg. This lady, who is extremely amiable and rich, continues, it is said, in the single state, from an apprehension that a favoured gentleman would be more influenced by affection fur her property than her person; an apprehension, however, which, in my hum- * ble opinion, ought to be negatived by her many virtues, as well as personal attractions. I believe there is no lady in Russia better known, or more deservedly estimated, than this princess.
On Sunday I attended divine service, at the church of Galitzin’s Hospital, where there is an excellent choir; after which, I had the
honour of dining with Major-General Verofkin, the commandant of Moscow.

On the succeeding day, I] accompanied a a friend to hear the service at the Convent of Devichi-poley, where the principal part of the vocal performers are young nuns. There was a gentleman present on this occasion, whose attention to these young devotees, expressed by keeping his eyes fixed upon them, making signs, &c. were so marked as to attract the notice of the older sisters, many of whom were mixed with the congregation. This gave rise to a ludicrous occurrence ; after the service was concluded, these good ladies actually followed him out of the church, and made a violent attack upon him; which he, by a foolish attempt to defend himself, only served to aggiravate. When their warmth had somewhat abated, my friend ventured to enter into conversation with them; and at length obtained permission to visit: their cells; when we were ushered into a small room of about ten feet square, with a smaller one adjoining toitasa dormitory. On the table were lying needlework representations, on velvet, of their saints,

The working of these seemed to be their chief employment, and certainly it is preferable to complete idleness ; but it appears to me, that if these good christians were anxious to benefit the community, they might occupy their time more consistently in imparting instruction to the children of the poor; since it is notorious, that in this country the females of the lower order are not only unable to read or write, but incapable af using the needle; the consequences of which are, that having no resources within themselves, when the domestic occupations of the day are over, they generally dispose of the remainder of ‘their time in sleep, or idleness. It was in this convent that Murat, after the destruction of the city, took up his residence; a circumstance that contributed essentially to its protection. On the 25th visited the Military School, originally an old palace, situated near the Summer Gardens, and conducted upon the Lancasterian plan. It is applied to the education of the soldiers’ sons, generally with a view of qualifying them to act as non-commissioned officers. Some of these boys are instructed in

music, under a German master, for the service of the military bands, and are by no means des« picable performers ; others are taught drawing, particularly as applicable to the planning of military manoeuvres, fortifications, &e. Every thing is conducted in military order ; they are marched to their desks, and sit down by word of command; and when-the master calls up a class, they are formed and marched up to him by the head boy. The dinner is conducted upon the same’principle, which, I believe, applies to every institution of the kind throughout " the empire, there being one in the chief town of each government. We can scarcely wonder that, under such a system, the Russian army should prove superior soldiers. On the 26th I accompanied a party of friends to the Treasury, where the thrones, crowns, jewels, &c. &c. of the czars,* and emperors of * «This word is not a corruption of Ceesar, as many have suppoeed. It is an ancient oriental title found in the Sclavonian translation of the Bible, given originally to the emperor’s of the East, and afterwards to the khans of the Tartars. It. signifies, in Persian, supreme authority; and is to be observed in the terminations of the names of the kings of Assyria and
Babylon, as Phalassar, Nabonassar, &c.” Vide Caramzin’s History of Russia.

Russia are preserved, and had the honour of seating myself in one of the former, which was that of Bores Godenoff; I was informed, however, that one of the attendants appeared very indignant at this presumption.

After leaving this place, we visited the beautiful bronze statues of Minin and Pajorsky ; the former of whom was a butcher of Novogorod, said to have been chiefly instrumental, by his wealth, and energetic exertions, in promoting the successes of the latter against the Poles, when they were masters of this city, and whom they eventually succeeded in expelling. ~ On the following day I went over the Military Hospital, a noble building, situated near the Summer Gardens, at the opposite end to where the Military School stands; two of its wards are so large, that on throwing open the folding doors between them, you have a range of not less than two hundred and ten paces; the patients are placed on each side of these wards, and every care appears to be taken of their comforts as well as of their health.
The soldiers’ wives are received into an adjoining building.

On Saturday I walked to the Kremlin, and examined the wonderful bell that is to be seen there, to the top of which I mounted with the assistance of a ladder. It lies on the ground, into which its lower part has sunk considerably. The reason assigned for. this situation is, that having been cast and hung on this spot, the beam to which it was suspended was accidentally burnt; the bell, in consequence, fell to the ground, and broke a piece from out of its side. I am _ inclined, however, to imagine that it had been flawed in casting, as the edge of the fractured part has a smooth surface.

This enormous bell was recast from a former one of immense size, with the addition of two thousand poods more of metal] in the year 1734, during the reign of the Empress Anna, It weighs three hurdred and sixty thousand pounds English, equal to more than a hundred and sixty tons; whereas the heaviest bell in England, which is in Exeter Cathedral, scarcely weighs five tons and a half. Its height is nearly twenty-one feet, its diameter twenty-two feet eight inches, and

the height of the opening made by the piece falling out, five feet nine inches. - On Sunday I attended the service of the Protestant Church, which was performed by a Swiss clergyman, at the house of Prince Galitzin. Very active measures were taken sometime since by the English residents, to build themselves a church in Moscow; but, unfortunately, misunderstandings arose between the members of the committee, in consequence of which the proceedings have been suspended ; and, at present, IT am informed there is litde prospect of an adjustment of the dispute.* °

I dined this day with the commandant, whose lady had the day before been delivered of a son. This happy event leads me to notice a singular custom amongst the Russian ladies on such occasians, that when their female friends pay the lying-in visit, each places a ducat under the pillow previous to taking leave.

“ Thave lately learnt that the Russian Company has contributed a considerable sum towards the erection of a church in this city, and endowed it with a hundred pounds sterling per annum, for the support of a clergyman.

Gn Monday I repeated my visit to the Kremlin, for the purpose of examining the artillery and other‘arms taken from the enemy during the late war, comprising no less than eight hundred and seventy-five pieces of cannon. We examined also a number of curious brass pieces, some of Russian manufacture, others the spoils of war. Amongst these was a mortar, cast in 1694, by order of Peter the Great, and which, from its immense size, was probably intended for ornament rather than utility, as it appeared too bulky to be manageable; it is five- yards long, and its mouth a yard in diameter in the bore. I much astonished the serjeant who accompanied us, by coolly taking off my coat, and creeping to the bottom of it. There is one gun, a sixty-six pounder, not less than eight yards in length, and also some very large and rich brass Turkish pieces, of peculiar workmanship, as well as various others, that are considered great curiosities.
On Tuesday, the Ist of April, I had the gratification of accompanying Professor Fischer to the Museum of Natural History; after

whch he took me to the University, where he shewed me the museum attached to that institution. I shall not, however, trouble my veaders with a description of the contents of either of them, as there was nothing which excited particular interest. The more uncommon animals I examined were the sloth, and another animal found in great numbers on the steppes in the south of Russia, somewhat resembling the kangaroo, and which burrows in the earth after the manner of a rabbit. Dr. Clarke speaks of them, and, indeed, made a pet of one, which became his travelling companion. ‘ ‘

On the following day I again visited the Kremlin, and ascended the Tower of Ivan- Veleki, which rises three hundred and eight English feet from the ground. The interior comprises three stories, and contains thirtyone bells; one, which has been cast since the French invasion, weighing more than seveny tons. It is only made use of on grand occasions, when its deep tones are heard in every part of the city.
About this time I was induced to change

my residence, and engaged a very commodious and well-furnished apartment in a private house, at the rate of only two guineas per month. I was also to be provided with breakfast, at the expence of about two shillings per week; and, in the event of my choosing to dine at home, I was to pay two roubles and a half for each dinner. These lodgings proved very agreeable, as the other occupants of the house were exquisite professional musicians, and I was frequently delighted with their performances; one lady, in particular, played the harp with unusual taste and science.

Sunday, the 6th of April,was the feast of the annunciation of the Virgin Mary, which is held in great respect among the Russians. On this day it is customary to purchase birds, and give them their liberty. have to remark, however, that the magpie genus do not appear to profit by this act of benevolence, since it is asserted that none of this tribe are ever to be seen within the precincts of the city, the reason assigned for which is as follows:—A holy monk was one day so much annoyed by

the prattling of these birds, that, in his anger, he cursed them; the consequence was, that the unhappy wretches found it prudent to remove to the respectful distance of forty versts, and have never since presumed to venture within that circle.

The most noble purpose, however, to which the above principle of benevolence extends itself on this day, is the release of the various prisoners confined for debt in the city gaols; those whose debts are small, by individual acts of charity ; and those of a larger amount, by general subscription. Provisions are also sent to such as are imprisoned on criminal accounts,

On this day I again visited the Kremlin, where the various parts of that immense assemblage of buildings were explained to me. We afterwards proceeded to the Alexandrofski, or Kremlin Gardens, that have lately been laid out as a public promenade. They are very beautiful, inclosed in handsome iron railings, and a truly great accommodation to the city. The site of them, two years since, was but a compound of mud and rubbish; so
rapid is the progress of improvement in this country !

On Wednesday I took an opportunity of going to the College of Foreign Affairs, where — the archives of the empire are kept, and had the pleasure of examining many interesting © documents of antiquity, the most ancient of which was a treaty between Yaroslaff Yaros- Jovitch, Grand Duke of Tver, and the inhabitants of Novogorod, bearing date 1265. There are also preserved here a variety of letters and treaties- between Elizabeth of England and the czar Ivan Vasilo-vitch, relative to the

.commercial relations of the two countries, as well as on other subjects; and amongst the more interesting, was one in which Elizabeth, in reply to a request to that effect, promises the Russian monarch an asylum in her kingdom, with every due honour, in the event of a revolution in his empire; and another in which he begs of her to send him a doctor; the result of which was, that Dr. Robert Jacobs was appointed to that office.

I dined on Friday with a party where I partock, for the first time in my life, cf nettle soup, which is, in Russia, the first green soup of the spring. As to the peculiar flavour, I know not how to describe it. I should rather have denominated the mixture, egg soup, from the great quantity it contained of that ingredient.

* On the 12th had the gratification of dining with the English club of this place, but which ought rather to be denominated the Russian club, as nineteen out of twenty of its members are of the latter nation. It is even a more splendid establishment than the club of the same name at St. Petersburg, which I have before described. The service of plate, in particular, is of immense value. Public dinners, are given twice in the week, and are served up in superior style. The readingroom is supplied with a great variety of periodical works, including the English, French, and German newspapers. The principal attractions, however, are the card and billiard tables. There is an excellent regulation here to prevent the members continuing play at unseasonable hours, which is a fine of three roubles for each person who remains after midnight, and which is doubled in a geometrical ratio for every subsequent half hour. This regulation once led to an amusing result with respect to a Russian gentleman, who, having accidentally laid himself upon a sofa, slept there soundly until five o’clock. His fine for this, accordingly, amounted to not less than fifteen hundred and thirty-six roubles,. or sixty-four pounds sterling.
