It was debated amongst the members: whether, as the circumstance was accidental, and not the result of any occupation at cards, &c. he had been guilty of any infringement of the law, so as to be amenable to its penalties. The question was at length, however, decided against him, upon the principle, that the object of the regulation was to prevent the servants from being kept up beyond a reasonable hour. I am informed ‘that the produce of this laudable regulation averages fifty pounds per week, the whole of which is distributed among the poor.
« Sunday was the first of April, (O. S.) when the custom prevalent in England, as well as in other parts of Europe, of making, April-

fools, was observed here. I attended divine: service this day, at the Greek church of the noble Hospital of Count Scharametief, in company with a friend. We-stood for some time among the mass of the congregation, which General Malanoffsky observing, he politely sent to invite us to join his family party. During the service, I heard the general and his lady eating, which I thought rather indecorous, notwithstanding I had often remarked that the Russians did not refrain from talking on such occasions. I afterwards named this to a friend, who informed me that they were partaking of a kind of roll made expressly for the occasion, and which had previously been blessed by the priest, and which is the first morsel their reli- ° gion allows them to take when they go to mass. ‘ ;

On the following day I dined with the Princess Bores Galitzin, who took me with her to visit a Scotch lady who was ill, and who, I afterwards learnt, was subsisting on her bounty. This lady had formerly been go-

verness ip the Galitzin and other families, an occupation which illness had compelled her to relinquish. She had lately suffered the loss of all her savings, by the bankruptcy of her agent, and was thus reduced to the extreme of indigence. This amiable and benevolent princess was not only providing the above unfortunate lady with the necessaries and comforts of life, as well as medical attendance, but either personally, or at least in the person of some part of her family, carried her attentions so far as to visit her daily; nay, I was assured, that the young ladies frequently spent great part of the day in reading to her. The above is one instance of the charitable principles of the Russians, the action of which, I am assured, is too extensive to be generally known. I have heard many Russian and German tutors complain of being weated by their employers as mere serviles, but am satisfied this‘ is chiefly attributable to their ownconduct; at least, I have visited in various families where the English and Swiss instructors have met with the most uniform kindness and respectful treat-
ASSEMBLY ROOM. 235ment, and deservedly so, since none have more claim to attention than those who are worthily employed in forming and ennobling the human mind.
On the 15th I went to a concert at the nobility’s assembly room, the only mode of public amusement permitted during Lent, when the theatres, opera, and dancing assemblies are all closed.

This assembly room is fifty-six paces in length and thirty-five in breadth, and commodiously fitted up; it is surrounded by an arcade, within its walls, the pillars of which support a gallery; and adjoining, is a suite of apartments intended for card and supper rooms. The principal performers, on the present occasion, were Italians belonging to the opera.

The society to which the rooms belong is very select, as none can be admitted members unless they bear the rank of nobility. The annual subscription is fifty roubles for a gentleman; twenty-five for a married, and ten for an unmarried lady. This subscription prov ides a concert every Tuesday during Lent anda
ball once a week, throughout the winter; supper and other refreshments are of course considered extras.

On Wednesday the 16th I accompanied two friends to partake of a fish dinner at a Russian traiteur’s, no other kind of meat being provided in this house during Lent. Of this, however, there was great abundance dressed in every way that could be imagined. Not even eggs, butter, or milk are allowed at this time, although they use a substitute for the latter, prepared from almonds, and which they term almond cream.

We began our dinner, a la Kusse, with a glass of' bitter brandy, and caviare; then fish soup was placed before us, followed by fish cutlets, minced up, enclosed in paper and fried. As beverage, we had beer, mead, ‘and English porter, our repast concludéd, as usual, with coffee.

I was much interested with the arrangements of this house, named the New Trinity, and situated near the Exchange. It contains twelve rooms, and occupies no less than fifty waiters, all dressed in a kind of uniform —that

is, in a shirt and trowsers, both of them either red or blue, or checquered with both; or else the trowsers are blue, and the shirt red, or vice cersa. This shirt, which has no collar, but is buttoned like a frock, close round the neck, descends over the trowsers as low as the knee, and is secured with a girdle round the waist.

The first room you pass through, on entering the house, is the bar, where you are struck with surprise at the immense number of teaurns, cups, and saucers, piled around it; the wonder, however, ceases on passing through the different apartments, which are crowded with persons enjoying that beverage. “One man, who was there at the same time with ourselves, appeared to have a peculiar taste, as he was eating salted cucumbers with his coffee. This house is chiefly frequented by the Russian shopkeepers, whe after making a bargain at the exchange, come into conclude it by paying their money, and drinking it off, as they term it.
In the evening I went to General Balk- Polief’s, where a splendid party was assembled. Soon after eleven o’clock we were conducted through a suite of apartments to a

small theatre, to witness a tableau vivant, re~ presenting the inspiration of St. Cecilia, and. taken from Reuben’scelebrated painting on that subject. In this animated picture the general’s eldest daughter personated St. Cecilia. “The exhibition lasted about five minutes, being as long a time as the different figures could reasonably be expected to retain their proper positions.

We were now conducted into another apartment, where I was enraptured by a concert of most delightful music. One German master displayed more execution on the piano-forte than I ever remember to have heard elsewhere. He was a pupil of the celebrated Field, an Englishman, who is well known to every lover of music in St. Petersburg and Moscow, as a performer and composer, and who might soon - realize a large fortune, as he-could occupy his whole mornings at «a guinea a lesson, and I am assured, be engaged every evening at five guineas a night; but, alas! like many men of genius, he is accused of indolence and gross . negligence of his own interests.
From the music room we returned to the

theatre, where a clever Italian exhibited many surprising tricks of legerdemain. His last trick, and chef d’@uvre, was the killing, depluming, and cutting into pieces several small birds, which were then put into a stew-pan, with butter and water poured over them; they were now apparently stewed for a minute or two, over a spirit of wine lamp; after which, the cover being removed, out started these little birds, and flew about the room.

The company now, full of wonder and astonishment, left the conjuror to himself, and returned to the music room, Where the merry dance commenced with waltzing, followed by a variety of other dances; these were continued ‘until supper was nearly ready; previous to which the fullowing game, named cat and mouse, was started by the younger part of the company. The party first formed a ring; there being a lady and gentloman placed alternately ; one person remains within, and another on -the outside of the circle; the former representing the cat, the latter the mouse. The object of the cat is to dart out, under the hands of any two of the circle, and

seize the mouse, who keeps running round on the outside. The persons forming the ring ‘are to prevent, if possible, the cat’s escape from their inclosure, for whenever she gets, out, the two who allow the breach are obliged to take the places of cat’and mouse. This amusement is not unfrequently carried on at the expence of the flap of a gentleman’s coat, or the ornamental parts of a lady’s dress. About four o’clock more than one hundred persons sat down to a most elegant’ supper ; after which, the company returned to the dancing room, and kept up the spirit of the entertainment until seven or eight in the morning.. General Balk-Polief and his family, consisting of his: lady and two daughters, without doubt, may be considered among the most polished and accomplished of the Russian nobility; They all speak the English, French, and Italian languages, with great fluency, be- ° sides which, the young ladies are conversant with Greek, Latin, and German. As to the *General himself, I have heard him at his own table, where he is fond of collecting foreigners

of all nations, speak French to one, Italian to another, Portuguese to a third, English toa fourth, German to a fifth, Polish to a sixth; and God knows how many more languages he was not familiar with. He has travelled much in different parts of the continent ; was ambassador at the Brazils; and has been twice in England, to the customs of which country he appears particularly partial, as is evidenced by his dinners being occasionally served up in that style; besides his house is fitted up with © such taste, elegance, and comfort, that you would almost suppose yourself in a splendid English mansion ; he is also a great amateur, and possesses many fine specimens of the arts.

The variability of the weather is such at this time, that it is impossible to foresee, or provide against, the changes of the day ; the streets are also, in consequence of the breaking up of the winter, so bad as to make travelling dangerous. My droshka has frequently been on the point of overturning, and once actually was upset. This danger is partly to be attributed to the bad principles on which the pavé is constructed ; and partly to the effect of the
severe frost and subsequent thaws upon the ground itself.

“On the evening of the 17th I. accompanied the French consul to a concert at the nobility’s assembly rooms, which was for the. benefit of Madame Anti, prima donna of the opera. Her voice was powerful, but not sufficiently flexible to make her singing entirely agreeable. I remember when I first heard Catalani, that I was more astonished at the power of her voice, than pleased with her execution.
A few days after I made an interesting visit to the Foundling Hospital.

There is, perhaps, no country in which institutions of this nature are more beneficial than in Russia. In the first place, the individuals thus protected, become exclusively the property of the crown, and which, as population is defective, is politically an essential advantage to the community. Secondly, the want of morality in the people. is favourable to the increase of illegitimacy; and although there may not be so high a degree of turpitude, or sense of shame, attached to offences of this natur2, yet when to this feeling we add the interruption which is experienced to the personal exertions and future prospects of the unfortunate mother, there would, otherwise, be sufficient temptations to lead her to unwarrantable means of getting rid of her unfortunate offspring; even when, as was once the case, a small sum of money was required to be paid on the admission of a child, it was found that this measure led to several acts of infanticide, and the regulation was consequently abolished. Within the first twenty years after the foundation of this institution, thirty-seven thousand six hundred and nine children were ‘admitted; and the present annual average is between four and five thousand, being a tenth part of the number of births in the whole district of Moscow. The majority of the children are brought up in the country, where at the period of my visit, there were eleven thousand and ninety-seven at nurse, while within the walls of the institution were | contained only three hundred and forty-seven boys, and three hundred and seventy-three girls,.

The system of bringing up these foundlings is, if we may judge from its results, superior to what has been adopted in similar institutions ) of other countries. The following facts would appear to confirm this position.

The Foundling Hospital of London, from its establishment in 1739 to December 1757, only put out one hundred and seven children, after incurring the enormous expence of one hundred and sixty-six thousand pounds.

In 1791, Sir John Blaquire stated in the Irish House of Commons, that of nineteen thousand four hundred and twenty infants received,during the preceding ten years, into the Foundling Hospital of Dublin, seventeen thousand four hundred and twenty had died; and that of two thousand one hundred and eighty, which had been admitted during 1790, only one hundred and eighty-seven were then living.

, experience, under an expence of twenty thousand dollars, not one individual arrived at menhood. At Cassel, only ten ovt of one hundred and seventy-one lived to seventeen years of age. At Rome, one in twenty-seven reached manhood; and at Vienna, one in nineteen.
Liancourt, in his report to the National Assembly of France, states, that two-thirds of the children admitted into the Foundling Hospitals of Paris, die within the first twelvemonths.

In consequence of these facts, many have disputed the utility of institutions of this nature. Lord Kaimes says, that “of all the mischiefs that have been éngendered by over anxiety for the poor, none have proved more fatal than foundling hospitals.” And Malthus contends, that if the children received into foundling hospitals had been left to the management of their parents, taking the chance of all the difficulties in which they might have been involved, ¢ much greater portion of them would have reached manhood and become useful members of society.
After leaving the Foundling Hospital, I dined at the residence of Mr. K: brate the first anniversary of the birth of his , to celechild; when out of compliment to the parents,
I drank its health. Here I was taxed with irregularity; as it is contrary to the custom of the country to drink a child’s health on its first anniversary.

On Friday, the 25th of April, the people of Moscow were busily occupied in preparations for the ensuing Sunday, or Palm Sunday; that is, in providing themselves with palm branches to be used in the ceremonial of the day, as commemorative of our Saviour’s entry into Jerusalem. For the want of real palm, they substitute branches of willow, or artificial ones, of paper or other materials, which are made by the nuns of: the Voskrosenski Convent, in the Kremlin.

At the church in Galitzin’s Hospital, the service’ for Palm Sunday commenced on the preceding evening, and I was induced, with a friend, to attend it. On our way we had to pass a most extensive procession of carriages, of all descriptions, amounting to not less thah three thousand equipages, together with an immense number of people on horseback, this being one of the gayest ceremonies of the season. The whole of these collected abcut four

PROCESSION, &c. 247 in the afternoon, in-a spacious place called the Krasnoi Plosched, where the statues of Minin and Pojarsky stand ; from hence they proceeded ‘through the Voskrosenski Gate, in direction of the Devitchey-poley, the whole forming a double line of nearly four miles in extent. This procession originated in an ancient custom of the people going to this part of the city to purchase their palm branches.

On arriving at Galitzin’s Hospital, we were entertained with tea, at the apartments of Dr. A——, the physician to the institution, having the pleasure at the same time of being introduced to the ladies of his family, who I found particularly interesting and beautiful.

My power of discriminating female beauty has so often been called in question, and I have so frequently been told, that it matters not to me, whether a*woman be handsome or not, that a few words in explanation may not be mal-apropos.
In this respect as well as under other circumstances, where my power of obtaining a knowledge of external things is limited by the deficiency of that which, Addison tells us, is
“ the most perfect and most delightful of all our senses,” imagination fills up the hiatus.

When introduced to a lady, if I find her conversation sensible and refined, and. her opinions expressed in an agreeable tone of voice, I immediately assume that other qualities, more or less, harmonize, and that her personal attractions may also be pleasing. Imagination now commences, and finds no difficulty in heightening the picture so as to paint her even as beautiful, since we naturally wish to make the object we admire as -perfect as possible. It, however, on the contrary, there is a harshness of voice, a want of graceful and correct diction, or vulgarity of ideas, my inferences are proportionately unfavourable; and were she actually beautiful as an angel, no such impression would be excited in my mind.

It is true I am liable to much error in forming opinions from such data; but if, in addition, an opportunity is afforded me of feeling the hand, and touching, ever so lightly, the features of the face, I fancy that I can, from their softness, delicacy, or contour, arrive at

conclusions so certain, that I am vain enough to imagine they have not often proved erroneous. The service which was performed in the church, did not appear materially to differ from the regular service, except in the addition of the ceremony of blessing and distributing the palms, for which there was a most pious scramble. When they had received them, each person lighted a small wax taper, which he either attached to the palm-branch or held in the same hand with it, so as to leave the right hand at liberty for making the sign of the cross, which was frequently done, as well as numerous bows, often so low ‘as to strike audibly the ground with the forehead. The next morn ushered in Palm Sunday and Passion Week, the whole of which is, by the Greek Church, devoted to the performance of religious duttes, and held as so rigid a fast, that no religious person will even eat fish, partaking only of sufficient farinaceous food, oil, and vegetables, to support the necessities of nature: nay, some, I am assured, will pass the entire week without eating. The sick
and aged, however, are exempt from these observances.

This season is known by the name of the “ Terrible Week,” and while it continues, no shops are-allowed to be open, except 4 few, by express permission, for the sale of provisions. Visiting is generally interrupted. I had the honour, however, of dining with two families during the week, in one of which the lady of the house, without any apparent reason, begged my pardon. I afterwards learnt that it is customary at this time, for individuals to ask forgiveness of their friends for all previous offences that might have been committed, or imagined to be committed.
On Good Friday the people assembled, at two in the afternoon, in the different churches, to witness a representation of the burial of our Saviour.

On Easter morning, immediately after the midnight hour had struck,.all the bells in the city, including the great Ivan-Veleki, burst forth their summons to the inhabitants to repair to the different churches, to hear the y a

service preparatory to the supposed resurrection. Towards the conclusion of this service, the whole congregation, with the priests at their head, bearing the cross and incense, and each holding a wax taper in his hand, march three times in procession round the church,’ as if they were: looking for our Saviour. While this is passing, the image of our Saviour is removed from the tomb, where it had been deposited on the Friday, to the front of the altar. After the lapse of a few minutes, the doors of the sanctuary are thrown open, when the priests come forth, exclaiming, three a times, “ Christ is risen!’ The people now eagerly advance to kiss the cross, at which time each presents the priest with an egg, or @ piece of money, whichever suits his means or inclination. This concluded, the whole retire to their réspective homes.

At six o’clock the morning service commences, when eack person brings with him a cake and a quantity of curds, the latter made into a pyramidal form, and marked with one or more figures of the cross. These, at the end of the service, are blessed by the priest, who

either takes off a portion of the cake for himself, or receives a small piece of money in lieu of it. With the consecrated food, the pious Christian ther returns home, and enjoys his breakfast, after which he is at liberty to make any compensation to his stomach which he pleases, for the rigidity of his previous fasting. The lower orders avail themselves so freely of this permission, that the results not unfrequently prove fatal.

The above is the only service of this happy day, the remainder of which is devoted to pleasure and enjoyment, visiting their friends, and driving about the city with every variety of equipage: even the tinker and the tailor sport their carriages on the occasion, The bells are ringing the whole of the day, while groups of people animate the streets, presenting eggs of various kinds ana colours to their friends, and saluting them with the joyful tidings of, “ Christos voskos,” “ Christ is risen,” answered by the equally gratulatory response, “ Voustinno voskos,” “ truly he is risen.”
Whet adds to the brilliancy of the day is,

that the middle and lower classes appear in new clothes, and the servants in their gayest liveries. Marriages, however, are not allowed to be solemnized until the following week ;— but every one appears happy enough in. all conscience; and such an addition might be incompatible with the weakness of a mortal brain, and crack it with excess of joy.

-On this occasion I attended‘the seryice of the reformed church, and then occupied the remainder of the day in visiting and congratulating my Russian friends; nor did I forget the customary salute on the hands of the ladies, which was returned by a kiss on the cheek or forehead. I believe, however, this ceremony is not expected from foreigners ; but I was anxious to show the utmost respect, as well as my readiness to-conform with the manners and customs of the country. Perhaps it is a question as yet undecided; whether the traveller in e foreign country should observe his own national peculiarities, or submit them to thosé of?the people amongst whom he may be sojourning.

the whole week, during which time the lower orders amuse themselves with wooden hills, and exhibitions of various kinds, which are held on the Boulevards at the Padnavinsky. Among other ‘curiosities to ‘be seen at this place, during the present season, was & mermaid, represented on the outside of the booth, as swimming in the sea; but, on entering, you were surprised. to find a wooden body, with wings attached to it; that part which most appertained to the fish, made of tin, worked in the manner of scales; while the head, body, and arms, were covered with wax, and the face well rouged.

On the Monday after Easter, business returned into its ordinary’ channel, with this. exception—that, during the first three days, all the various remnants are collected together in the respective shops, and sold at a low rate. :
On. this day I had the» pleasure of being introduced to Dr. Lyall, a gentleman whose literary productions relative to this city have since excited so much attention and jnterest.
On Tuesday, the Ist of May, (O. §,) there

was a promenade, in carriages, in the Sakolnika Wood, with a great display of beauty and fashion. On this occasion, you see large parties dining in their tents, attended by military and other, music, with gypsies dancing, and a variety of other entertainments. This promenade is said to have originated from an " entertainment given by Peter the Great on this day (according to a German custom) to his foreign artificers, who were chiefly of that nation, when the nobility and populace were attracted as spectators. In time, it became a regular annual promenade.* ~

At this time. Moscow was agitated by the horrid report of a woman, who had been apprehended for eating (as it was said, by her own confession,) twenty-four children. We afterwards were informed, that the report was only a tub thrown out to divert the minds of the people, during the period, of casting a large’ bell, intended for the town of Cazany a super-
* Sakolnika, in the Russian language, signifies hawk, and from there being an imperial hawkery near the above wood, just without the city gaté, both these places have hence derived their names.
Stitious opinion prevailing, that the bell cannot be properly cast if public attention is at the time directed to. it!

It may here be worthy of remark, that mothers and nurses in Russia do not like to have their children admired too much: this is what they call casting an evil eye upon them. On this account they will often, before allowing you to see them, desire you to turn from them, and spit three times on the ground, with a view of ejecting the evil spirit;—or if you happen to have seen them without this precaution, the motuer turns her head aside, and, performs the operation instead of you.

There are few people in the world more influenced by superstitious feelings than the Russians, either as respect their religious con- - stitution, or the more ordinary occurrences of private life. Of this characteristic tendency, the above anecdotes, as well as a variety of other instances that have been related in these pages, are illustrations: I shall, however, avail myself of the present opportunity of entering into farther details on the subject.

a parallel, except in the fanaticism of the disciples of Joanna Southcote:—About three years since, a girl, thirteen years of age, commenced digging with her hands under a tree near the church. of the village of Goo- .seiver, in the neighbourhood of Moscow, in consequence of communications said to have been received in various dreams, that she would find, in the first instance a candle; secondly, a post; then an image, which was ‘to be placed in a niche of the church left purposely for it; and, lastly, a spring of water, that would become the source of a mighty river. The nature of this supernatural tommunication becoming known, immense crowds flocked to the spot, to witness the results of her labours; amongst whom were many sick people, who expected to ve relieved from their infirmities by drinking, or washing their sores with the muddy water that collected during her operations, the ground being composed of argillaceous strata, with much moisture from rain. In the course of her proceedings, the candle and post made their appearance ; but the police then interfered, and prevented the VOL. I. 8

‘continuation of the farce, in consequence of the discovery of collusion between her parents and the priest and clerk of the village, who had devised this extraordinary mode of giving celebrity and wealth to a poor country church. It is generally thought that the affair terminated in all the parties, including the priest, being knouted and banished to Siberia. Another instance of the superstition of the Russian peasantry occurred about the same time. The Countess Bobrinski having directed the felling of an old oak tree on her domain, the workmen, after a few blows upon its trunk, observed, to their astonishment, a reddish liquor flow out. This they conceived to be blood; the report soon spread throughout the neighbourhood, and thousands flocked to the spot, who, regarding the phenomenon as a miracle, proceeded to hang the tree with garlands and images; the sick were brought to it to be healed, and va~ious portions of the wood.carried away as sacred relics. The countess persisting, notwithstanding the sanctity of this venerable oak, in her determination to have it prostrated on the ground, the

peasants (fcr superstition will give courage even to slaves) determined to oppose the -execution of her orders 3 and it was not until a body of soldiers were called out to disperse them, that the tree was cut down, and tranquillity restored to the neighbourhood. 1’ In their worship, the Russians profess not to address any image that is carved or graven, but only such as are painted in oil-colours on wood, the artist lying prostrate on his face .while engaged in the divine occupation. There is something very ludicrous in the mode of obtaining a saint from the manufacturer; they do not purchase him, but Call it making an exchange, or buying the gold and silver with which it is ornamented; these holy personages, however, are regularly exposed like other wares of trade. The manner in,which the affair is conducted is as follows: The person who wants a saint, after making his selection, Jays on the counter what he thinks an adequate sum, which, if the manufacturer does not consider sufficient, is put back to him: he then, from time to time, makes additions, until the other is satisfied.
Such ts the requisition in which these images are held, that no apartment, not even a stable, is- without its patron saint.

Much deference is paid to omens. The Russians having their lucky and’ unlucky days, few of them will commence a journey, or undertake any business of importance, ‘on a Monday. Friday is also with them a black day. If, on leaving home, the first person a Russian meets happens to be a clergyman, it is ten to one but he turns back, to obviate. the ill luck of passing him; or, if he happens to have passed’ previous to seeing him, he immediately turns round, and spits three times on the ground..

If a hare crosses his path, or a pigeon flies - athwart his window, it is an ill omen. Many families will not allow ‘salt-cellars upon the table, lest the salt should«be spilled, but have the latter placed on the cloth in a pyramidal form. I discovered this omen one day at dinner, by finding my bread very salt.
On a Russian changing his residence, he assembles his family and servants, when they all sit down in a circle, and rise at the

same instant: this is considered as taking leave of the house. On entering into possession of a new house, or on returning to it after a long absence, his friends send him a present of bread and salt, as a welcomé: nay, even the governors of provinces are in this way received on taking possession of their governments. A friend of mine one day, after a sumptuous dinnef, was, during the dessert, invited to partake of a black loaf, which was placed on the table, with a saltcellar upon it: he naturally declined ‘so uninviting a morsel; but his host insisting on his compliance, he was agreeably disappointed by finding under this form, a delicious spongecake that had been sent by the landlord of the house to his tenant, in conformity with the above custom.

On the 21st of’ May the weather was so fine and warm, that we were enabled to dine in the open air. This is a gratification to which one strong objection exists in Moscow during the summer time—the great abundance of gnats, whose bites are venomous. The cantharis, or blistering-fly, is also sometimes

seen in Moscow, when the wind has been long blowing from the south. It is very common in the Ukraine, so as to constitute an article of exportation. Russia abounds also with many of the serpent tribe, but few of them are venomous.

So many detailed accounts have appeared respecting the highly important part this city was destined to sustain during the late invasion of the French, that little additional information remained for myself to glean relative to this interesting subject.

What most impressed me, however, was the wonderful confidence with which the minds of the people were inspired by the ingenious bulletins of the governor, Count Rostopchin, and which were admirably calculated to operate wpon their feelings and prejudices.
The following can scarcely fail to be read with interest.
“ BULLETIN. “ Head Quarters, between Gjat and Mojaisk.

“ Our van-guard is at Gjat; the situation occupied by our army is exceedingly strong, and there His Serene Highness the Prince intends to give the enemy battle. We are now equal in numbers, and within two days we shall be further reinforced by twenty thousand men. Our troops are all Russians, of one religion, subjects of one Emperor, defending the temples of God, their wives, their children, and the graves of their fathers. The enemy; on the contrary, fight for their subsistence, and die in the act of plundering. If they lose but one battle, they will all disperse, and their names wil] be forgotten.

“ You know that I am informed of every thing that passes in Moscow. Yesterday there was something improper done, and which certainly deserves reproof. Two Germans, who came ‘to exchange money, were fol'owed, beaten, and received so much injury from the people, that one of them nearly lost his life. They took them for spies, which ought to have been examined into; but that was my business, and you know I would not in such a case spare my own countrymen. Where is the merit, for a hundred of you to beat a meagre Frenchman, or a perriwigged, smoked German? What inclination have you to thus dirty your hands? Those who act in such a manner, wHl not defend themselves in case ‘of need. When you think you observe a spy, then bring him to me, but do not strike him, and thus bring a reproach upon your country. We must annihilate* the French army, not bruise the eyes of such poor wretches. The wounded have been brought hither; they are placed in the Palace of Golovin; I fave seen them; { have given them to eat and to drink, and put them to bed. They have fought for you, therefore you-must not neglect them, but visit and comfort them. You feed criminals,

* The original word signifies literally ‘ to bury in the ground without ceremony,” as if the body was that of a brute animal, but these are the Emperor’s faithful servants, and our friends.—How can we refuse them our assistance.
‘Two couriers, dispatched from the field of battle, have brought from the Commander- | in-Chief of the army the following intelligence,

“Yesterday, the 26th, was fought a very hot and bloody battle. The Russians, with the assistance of God, did not retreat a single step, notwithstanding the enemy fought against them with desperation. Trusting in the Lord, and the sacred relics of Moscow, I hope tomorrow to fight them again with renewed vigour. ‘

“<The losses of the enemy are incalculable; their. orders were to take no prisoners, (none whateyer,) and that the French must either conquer or perish, If we to day, with the assistance of God, once more repulsé them; then the wretch, and his wicked followers, must ‘perish by hunger, fire, or sword.’
* T send to the army four thousand men of our new recruits, ammunition for two hundred and fifty pieces of cannon, and provisions.

" My true believers, be not uneasy ; the blood of our brethren flows for the deliverance of our country ; we ourselves are ready to reinforce the army if necessary. God will strengthen us, and a grave awaits our perfidious enemy in the fields of Russia.

“ His Serene Highness, the Prince, in order to unite earlier with the troops marching to join him, has passed Mojaisk, and posted himself in a strong situation, where the enemy canno. suddenly attack him. Forty-eight pieces of cannon, with ammunition, have been sent tohim from hence. The Prince declares that he will defend Moscow to the last drop of his blood, and that he will continue to fight the enemy in the streets. “Do not, my friends, regard the shutting of our courts of justice for the present: we ‘must close those proceedings, that we may settle our accounts with the enemy. If the trial should come, I may stand in need of our youths, both of town or country. My signal will be given two days prior. At present it is not necessary; I am therefore silent. A hatchet will do very well; a hay-fork also will not be amiss; but a three-pronged fork will be best of all. A Frenchman is no heavier than a sheaf of rye. To-morrow afternoon I shall bear the image of the Virgin Mary of Iviria to the wounded soldiers at ‘Catharine’s Hospital; we will there consecrate the water, and they will soon recover. One of my eyes has been disordered, but I now see with both.

“ Brethren! our forces are numerous, and ready to lay down‘ their lives in defence of their country. We will not suffer these miscreants to enter Moscow, but we ourselves must agsist and do our duty. It would be a heavy sin to abandon our countrymen. Moscow is our mother, she has nourished and enriched you.

“ I call upon you, in the name of the Blessed Virgin, to defend the temples of the Lord, Moscow, and the Russianempire. Arm yourselves, each with what he cap, both horse and foot ; take with you bread only for three days. Go with the cross; take also, the sacred banners from the churches ; and with these ensigns assemble immediately on the three hills. I will be with you,-and we will together destroy the enemy, Glory in the highest to those who | persevere—fame immortal to those who fall— but, woe at the day of judgment to those who excuse themselves.

Another contrivance for amusing the minds of the inhabitants at this critical moment, was the preparation of an immense balloon, under the direction of a Dr. Schmidt, which it was reported would infallibly destroy the French

. army. To ‘carry this measure into effect, a requisition was made of more than a hundred milliner girls. The French army, however, made its appearance before this wonderful machine could be got in readiness. It has generally been imagined that the preparation of this balloon was a mere pretext, under cover _ of which the different arrangements for setting fire to the city were expedited. This surmise

-is evidently confirmed by the proceedings of the court-martial held by the French, upon the persons who were taken up in the act of spreading destruction throughout the city; and which also leaves no doubt of the act being the result of a preconcerted plan, on the part of the Russian government.* ‘
After the occupation of the city by the enemy, his foraging parties were from time to time so

harassed by the Cossacks, and other Russian troops, that little or no supplies could be obtained from the surrounding country. Considerable resources, however, still remained within the city, derivable from the public and private stores, as well as the many well stocked fishponds and vegetable gardens in its immediate vicinity; these at length beginning to fail, recourse was had to the immense number of pigeons and crows, with which the city abounds; the former being regarded as sacred birds, and therefore especially protected by the inhabitants. At length they were com- 'pelled to commence their retreat; an ‘event which was communicated by the following bulletin :— r “The enemy, pressed and daily routed by our troops, have’ been compelled to evacuate Moscow, on the 1]th of October, (O.8.) yet in flying he meditated to wound, by new insults, the pious Russian people, destroying by -mines the Kremlin and churches wherein repose the bodies of saints. But God is wonderful in -his works! though part of the walls of we

the Kremlin, and nearly the whole of the buildings have been blown into the air, or destroyed by fire, yet the cathedrals and churches containing.the sacred relics remain entire and uninjured. A mark of, the mercy of God towards the Emperor and the Russian empire. * Moscow, October 12th, (O. 8.) 1812.”

- On this memorable occasion, many individuals are said to have realized considerable sums, by purchasing from the soldiers of the invading army; the plunder which they had appropriated to themselves; as immense bundles of Russian bank-notes, which were gladly exchanged for coins of any description.
I shall not attempt an account of the aggravated sufferings they afterwards sustained, since these are well known to every reader.

The exemplary military qualities displayed by the Russian army during this invasion of their country, as well as in the subsequent campaigns, has not only effaced all previous stigma or prejudice with respect to it, but elevated its reputation to a height of glory
scarcely surpassed by any other nation in the World.’

Independent of the enthusiasm excited on all hands, to repel an unprovoked and apparently overwhelming invasion, this high character of the Russian army may in great measure be ‘attributed to the manner in which its soldiers are levied, and which places in its ranks, only a choice selection of the peasantry of the country. The following is the mode in which their levies are made.

The number of men wanted being divided amongst the different governments, its various subdivisions and villages, the whole are taken by lot, upon the principle of our militia ballots. After the ballot, however, the intended recruit is rejected unless, on inspection, he is found of proper stature, aud perfectly sound in every respect; these péints being ascertained, a tuft is immediately cut off from the fore part of the head, which is the sign of approbation; otherwise he is shorn in & similar way behind, and Started off without a word, as unworthy of the honour of being “ written a soldier? The service is at first very obnoxious to the new

ballots; but they soon not only become reconciled, but attached to it; for although the pay is small, many advantages accrue to them; in the first place they become free at the moment of enrolment, and render free any woman they may choose to marry, and after twenty-five years service are allowed to retire as freemen. Their sons are, however, attached tothe army as soldiers. —
The pay of the lower ranks of the army is as follows :—, Roubles. Copecks.

A cadet serving for the rank of officer.. 12 444 do.

They are allowed in addition, one pood, or thirty-six pounds (English) of flour, and about three-sixteenths of an English bushel of buck wheat per month; ammunition and clothing once in two years; canteens, buttons, and other brass and tin materials, once in eight years ; two pair of boots, with two pair of spare soles, and eighteen arshines of linen‘ every year.

The officers are obliged, to commence their services in the ranks; after which they ad- ’ vance according as they may possess interest, or extraordinary merit. As military title is in this country the only ground of precedence, it becomes desirable for all who aim at public distinction to obtain. this rank; it can, however be acquired by civil as well as military occupation; so that, all the first civilians are generals; this, however, gives no standing in the army itself, to attain which the due gradations of military service must have been gone through.

A major-general of infantry receives in net pay only, two thousand one hundred roubles per annum, equal to eighty-seven pounds ten shillings English money: he has, however, for table money fifteen hundred or two thousand roubles more; and is allowed eight soldiers as servants, for whom he receives flour from the crown. He is entitled also to military quarters; and if he happens to attain the command of a regiment, has many perquisites, which materially improve his income, Independently of these advantages he Fas the

chance, in the event of distinguishing himself, of obtaining an arrende, or grant of an estate, either for a term of years, or in perpetuity, the lease of which, in the former case, is generally renewable to his family, or at least made so without much difficulty.

The pay of a colonel is one thousand two hundred roubles, and of a major eight hundred ; and which, as arrendes are not granted to officers of these ranks, is very inadequate to their.necessities. Occasionally, however, a colonel becomes the commandant of a regiment, in which case his advantages exceed those of a major-general without a regiment.
Military men in Russia, cannot be arrested for debt,—but a portion (one fifth) of their pay, may by a tedious process, be appropriated for the benefit of their creditors.

Officers have no half pay, although they occasionally receive pensions. At the end of awar they may quit the service, and return to it, if they please, at the commencement of a new onc, with their former rank.
There is in Moscow an institution for the benefit of the poor widows of officers; which
is under the patronage of the Dowager Empress, and the more immediate direction of M. Narishkin, a senator of the city, who makes it his study to promote the happiness of its inmates.

The building accommodates three hundred widows with their children, and has gardens attached, which afford an ample supply of vegetables, as well as agreeable promenades. There are also three hundred out pensioners, who receive each one hundred rubles per annum. Fifty of the residents are permitted to study medicine, when after a year’s attendance at the hospital, they undergo an examination, which if satisfactory, entitles them to receive a gold cross, and licence to practice as upper nurses, under the title of Sceurs de Charité, the emolument from which is entirely appropriated to their own advantage. These members of the institution are held in extraordinary resptct, set at a separate table, and provided with four dishes.at dinner instead of three.
