vantage, although they are provided with cloathes, board, lodging, and every other necessary free of expence.
The children are educated with every possible care, until the boys attain the age of nine, and the girls that of twelve; they are then obliged to seek occupation, or an asylum, elsewhere.
The qualification necessary for admission is, that the husband of the candidate must have held the rank of an officer for more than ten year’s.

On Saturday, May 3ist, I was honoured with a visit from General Fonbrien, accompanied by ‘the interesting traveller Captain Cochrane, whose arrival from ‘Siberia I had been for some time past daily anticipating, and from whom I hoped to elicit a variety of particulars relating to my own proposed journey into that country. Notwithstanding my intention of penetrating into‘Siberia was loudly condemned by my friends, yet my resolution was so deliberately taken and firmly fixed, long before I ventured to announce my determina- -tion, tat T should not have been deterred by
any arguments that might have been urged against it. Ireflected in particular, that what Rad proved practicable to others, might not be impossible to myself.

Before leaving Petersburg I carefully concealed my intentions from my nearest friends, and even when his excellency Sir Charles Bagot, questioned me as to the direction I proposed to take from Moscow, I avoided the mention:of any definite extent to my journey, simply admitting that it would be eastward, in the direction of Cazan ; when he was pleased to offer me his assistance on all occasions. I may add, that his excellency’s opinion served to confirm my own, since he expressed himself convinced, that as a private individual, I should receive every possible attention from the chiefs of the various governments I might pass through; and that he did not consider it even necessary to apply to the minister of the interior for letters of especial protection, as some of my friends had recommended me to do.
When my intention first began to transpire at Moscow, every one made it his business to demonstrate the madness and absurdity of

attempting so dangerous, uninteresting, and disagreeable a journey, in a country where, as respected myself.in particular, nothing -was to be either seen or heard! In short, the name of Siberia, probably from early associations, seemed connected in their minds only with sentiments of horror. Not a stranger to whom I was casually introduced, but made it the first object of his conversation to fish into my plans and endeavour to dissuade me from their prosecution. It was kindly meant, but my determination was inflexible, and these urgencies only produced the trite reply that “ time would shew how far my views were chimerical.”

And, what it may be again asked, by his English reader, could be the object proposed by the author, in thus persisting in views so contradictory to the sentiments of all his friends? J admit that the desire of meeting, with novelty, constituted ene of my leading motives.
‘“« For such the bounteous providence of heaven, In every breast implanting this desire; Of, objects new and strange to urge us on,

_ Those sacred stores that wait the ripening soul In truth’s exhaustless bosom. What need words To paint its power? For this the daring youth, Breaks from his weeping mother’s anxious arms, In foreign climes to rove———.”’

I had formerly visited a great part of southern Europe, as well as the continent of North America, and was desirous of making myself acquainted with the manners and customs of a country, with which the inhabitants of Europe have hitherto had but little communication, and at best a very imperfect knowledge of; a country deemed as yet so barbarous, as to be hardly entering within the pale of. civilization, and in whose tents the stranger could scarce abide with safety. Relying, however, on the general similarity of human nature, its various differences being the secondary effects of early habits or prejudice, I felt no apprehension of trusting myself in the midst ef such a people, convinced that a conformity with their manners and customs, and an avoidance of ridicule and opposition to their prejudices, would conciliate their,eelings, and ensure their protection.
J was farther stimulated by a desire to prove to the world, that notwithstanding my personal defects, I was capable of overcoming difficulties which to them might appear impossible. os

On the following day, June Ist, I had the pleasure of accompanying Captain Cochrané to both the commandant, and the governorteneral of Moscow, the latter of whom informed me, contrary to thé expectations of Captain Cochrane, that it was not necessary for me to obtain any especial protection, or licence, from the minister of the interior, to enable me to penetrate into Siberia, since the Siberian governments were, as related to these points, conducted on precisely the same prine« ciples as those in other parts of the empire: and when I stated, in reply to his inquiry as to the proposed extent of my journey, that I wished to take out my licence for post horses to Irkoutsk, ‘fhe gave me to understénd that I might there obtain an extension in any direction I pleased, an assurance which.set my mind at ease in this respect, and which I deemed a sufficient authority to act upon.

Captain Cochrane had been accompanied from Kamschatka by an interesting young lady, a native of that country, to whom he was happily united in the bonds of matrimony ; and as he was anxious to shew her the wonders of this great city, I had the pleasure of attending her, with another lady and gentleman, to the Kremlin, where we mounted the tower of Ivan« Veleki. We naturally expected that she would have expressed het admiration with. much warmth; she appeared pleased with what she saw, but not at all surprised. Ina day or two after we attended her to the theatre, the amusement of which it was conceived she would be enabled to appreciate, from her being well acquainted with the Russian language. She paid much attention, and seemed interested, particularly with an entertaining vaudeville, named the Parrots, at which she laughed heartily ; but although this was thé first regular dramatic représeniation she had ever witnessed, we did not notice that expression of astonishment which we had anticipated.
This lady, who was represented as very handsnme, although a native of so distant a

country, and only in her fifteenth year, was by no means unpolished or awkward in her manners ; she possessed, it is true, much diffidence, which’ served only to render her the more interesting; in short her parents had been conversant with the more civilized parts of the empire, and had educated her according to their customs.

+ On the 6th I accompanied a party to the Prison, named the Ostrog, which is constructed on the plan of Howard, and kept in admirable order. At this time it contained within its walls about four hundred and fifty prisoners, but occasionally the number is much exceeded. The more general punishments resorted to in this place, are knouting, and banishment ta Siberia for life, unless strong interest, or some imperial act of grace shartens the period of exile. We examined the knout, and the mode of using it, and its effects demonstrated on a a plaster wall, when each blow uniformly brought forth a portion of the composition, The handle of this instrument was about two feet in length, and divided in the middle by a leathern joint, so as to allow the one half to

swing backward and forward with the lash. This latter part was about four feet in length, having a.ring of three inches in diameter attached to its extremity, to which was added a thong of hardened leather about the size of a gaiter strap. With this instrument, I am assured, the executioner, (who is always a reprieved criminal,) seldom fails to take a portion from out of the victim’s back at each blow. ‘

Horrible as this appears, the situation of criminals, both as respects their prison treatment and the severity of punishment, has been materially ameliorated ‘during the presentemperor’s reign. Nor are any of the exiles now sent off without adequate supplies of clothing.

On the evening of Sunday, the 8th, after dining at a friend’s in the country, we visited the pleasure gardens of Prince Dolgorouky, at Petrofsky Rasamoffsky. To this venerable gentleman, now eighty years of age, and his daughter, the Princess Gerchikoff, we had the honour of being introduced. I had here, for the first time, the gratification of hearing the

fine national horn music, the softness of which exceeded every idea I had preconceived with respect to it, The tones which were produced could only be compared to, but at the same time greatly exceeded, the most melodious notes of the organ. The prince’s band consisted of twenty-two musicians, each playing three notes; the bands of this kind of music, however, more commonly comprise from forty to sixty horns, each being confined to a single note, The summer was now rapidly advancing, and the weather had become extremely warm, although still variable, particularly towards evening, when we generally experienced a heavy thunder storm, which contributed mate- ‘rially to cool the air. I had now got shrough al) the troublesome forms, required by the police, to enable me to take owt my licence for post horses to Irkoutsk, and determined to abridge as far.as possible ‘my further stay in Moscow. For this licence, to travel a distance of five thousand three hundred and fifty versts, equal to three thousand five hundred and sixtyseven English miles, I was charged about nine pounds sterling, or two hundred and fourteen roubles, being at the rate of four copecks per verst for two horses; and I was afterward charged at the respective post houses ten copecks per verst for this number of horses; to which the charge was limited, notwithstanding the driver put three, and frequently four, into the carriage.
I had travelled from St. Petersburg to Moscow in the diligence ; but I found this mode of conveyance did not extend farther into the

‘interior, and that the only government substitute was the telega, or post cart, a small; light machine upon four wheels, and without springs. I was induced, however, to prefer travelling in my own equipage, and was on the point of purchasing a britchka, when Captain Cochrane arrived, and maie me an offer of the equipage which he had brought new from Cazan, where he was compelled to abandon his sledge, in cone sequence of the snow roads having disappeared, and to whom it now became unnecessary, as he proposed taking’ the diligence to St. Peterse burg. I also engaged the same Tarta~ postillion as had accompanied him from Cazan, and was thus at once nearly fitted out for my journey. :

Dr. Lyall, for whose friendly attentions I. shall ever feel indebted, did’ me the favour to assist in procuring a stock of medicine, not only with a view to my own relief, should sickness invade me in a country where medical aid might be sought for in vain, but also to enable me to be instrumental in affording assistance to others; an expectation in which I was not a little encouraged by the smattering of physic which I had acquired during my~ residence at Edinburgh, several of the medical classes of whose excellent university I had studiously attended.,
My next arrangement was important; the necessary one with my bankers, who paid the kindest attention not only to my pecuniary arrangements, but also to every other comfort.. ¢
The money I took with me was principally in five rouble notes. I had, however, various bags containing coins of different values; for instance, No. 1, one hundred one rouble silver
picces; No. 2, one hundred eighty copeck ‘pieces; No. 3, one ‘hundred ‘ forty copeck pieces, and No. 4, one hundred twenty copeck pieces; these latter being of the value of two pence English..

In the event of supplies being required, my kind bankers made such arrangements, that I had only to write from any town, and whatever sum I wanted would immediately be forwarded by post, on my paying a trifling per centage for government security.

I was provided also with tea and sugar for the whole journey ; six bottles of brandy and as many of French wine, and always took care, at each town, to lay in sufficient bread and meat to serve until our arrival at the next; and thus, having also with me a tea-pot, cups, &c. &c., [ was quite independent of the accidental and inadequate entertainment the posthouses could furnish, with the exception of hot water. “
Nothing now remained but to bid adieu to the kind friends from whom I had been receiving the most unbounded hospitality and attention during my residence in Moscow, and

these, I have the highest gratification in boasting of it, were so numerous as to’ occupy a great portion of my time. To the whole of them cullectively, I now beg to repeat the unabated expression of gratitude, with which my heart was then, and ever will be, actuated, by an experience of their warm and disinterested friendship, to one whom they were led to consider as a helpless and unfortunate stranger.
“ Tho’ keen is the sorrow and sad is the tear,
From the scene of our joys when we part;
And cast a last look on the friends that are dear, Ur the still dearest friends of our heart.
But ah! what a desert that bosom must prove, That knows not the feelings of friendship and love.”
. Berore I take leave of Moscow, I must present my readers with a brief description of that celebrated city.
The city of Moscow is situated upon the river Moskva, in the same latitude as Berwick-upon- Zweed. It occupies three distinct ridges on

* the left bank of the river; on the right bank, also, it has various streets containing many fine private habitations, and which altogether bear much the same proportion to the town in general, as Southwark does to London.
The river, as it approaches the town, makes a fine sweep along the base of the Sparrow

_ Hills. -It is at the wooden bridge three hundred and forty two feet in breadth; its ordinary height in summer seven feet; in the spring floods, however, it generally rises to nearly four times that height, and in the year 1808 to even thirty-two feet; the height of the bank on the city, or north side, is twenty-seven feet, while on the south side it is only twentythree. :

Moscow dates its origin in the twelfth century, and is said to have been founded by Jouri Vladimerovitch. The old chronicles describe it as a village where that prince képt his favourite mistress. This induced him to build a house there, which example many of his courtiers following, the result was an immense city, destined to become the great entrepét of European and Asiatic commerce iw the north.

Following the line of the outer rampart, Moscow nearly equals ‘London in circumference; the district, however, between the *uter and inner ramparts is chiefly taken up with gardens, and but thinly covered with houses. The population has been estimated by
some at four hundred thousand, but this is probably an exaggerated account; it perhaps, may more safely be estimated at half that number.

That part of the town which is termed the Kremlin is its more important division, and the object of the most reverential feelings of the Russians. It was the nucleus round which the bulk of the city was formed ; it is also the depository of the imperial diadems, and the crowns of many conquered kingdoms, — in short of every thing connected with the historical illustrations of the empire. Here the rites ° of the Greek church are celebrated by its chiefest dignitaries in the great national temple, open alike to the emperor and the meanest of his slaves. In it repose the bones of temporal sovereigns and spiritual patriarchs, (scarcely in their time less ‘powerful,) and not a few of the undecomposed corpses of these saints still remain, as standing miracles, for the establishing of faith and the confounding of scepticism..
~The Kremlin is surrounded by a high crenated wall flanked by lofty towers; it has four principal gates, over each of which is an

elevated tower or spire of modern date, not very unlike some anomalous Gothic steeples which are to be met with in England. Asa fortress, it might have served sufficiently to resist the incursions of the Tartars; but could
_make only a weak defence against the cannon shot of an European army.

On the eastern side of the Kremlin, is the Khitai-gorod or Chinese Town, surrounded by a wall, and flanked at moderate distances by towers. Here the greater part of the commerce of Moscow is conducted. There is an
‘immense bazaar, consisting of extensive piazzas in the style of the Burlington Arcade, but infinitely inferior to it in elegance. This market, as it is termed by the English resi-

‘dents, is situated on both sides of the great street leading from the Holy Gate, and here the carriages of the nobility, who come to purchase the commodities of the place, are ranged jn -lines, and dccasionally so confusedly jammed together, that the Cossacks in attendance, are hardly able to restore order, even with the free application of their whips.

As these shops ate narrow and roofed over. with glass, they are very cold even in summer, and from this cause it is said the shopkeepers are extremely unhealthy. It is an-° noying to a stranger to enter this bazaar, for no old clothesman of Monmouth-street, or Rag-fair, was ever more troublesome or impertunate in his solicitations for custom than the _tradesman of this place. He perseveres in trying you at all points, in hopes of discovering that you want something. On évery side you are overwhelihed with encomiums on the excellence of.the various wares. In the boot and shoe shops, the customer is induced’ to purchase on the assurance—made doubly sure by an invocation of God and all his saints to witness its truth ;—that the Caloshee, Sapoghee, and Bashmakee, are all Nemetskirabote; that is of right German make, although it is ten to one that not a pair of. that quality is contained in the whole shop. Few occurrences are more painful to an .Englishman in Russia, than to enter a shop to purchase even the smallest article, he is sure

to be cheated unless he is- indeed a hnowingone ;—for instance, if he enquires for a piece of cloth, the shopkeeper will shew, in the first : place, the worst he has, and exert all his rhetoric to persuade him that it is the best ever made ; on rejecting it, he rings a.variety of changes on other pieces of increasing qua- - lity; until at length he is forced, as it were, to produce what is really the best. Now comes the second contest, the battle of prices. “ Pray, sir, what is the price of that piece per yard 2” “ Thirty roubles at a word,” replies the shopkeeper. The customer shrugs up his shoulders, and muttering “ dorrago othchen dorrago,” (dear, very dear) prepares to leave the shop, which the other observing, offers to let him have it, as a great favour, at twenty-five roubles. The gentleman, however, still shakes his head ;—“ Well, then what will you give sir?” ‘“‘ Eighteen roubles.” “ How can you offer me such a sum 2” rejoins the shopkeeper. “I vow to God, I myself paid more for it.” “I ar very sorry I cannot offer you more.” «“ Well, then twenty-three roubles at the last

word.” No, sir,”—* then twenty.” « No, sir.” “ Good bye” but just on leaving the door the honest tradesman shouts out— please sir to take them.” The purchaser returns and receives the.cloth, when it behoves him to be careful that it has not been changed, while he has turned his back; after this he walks off with compliments and thanks showered down upon him in profusion.

The nobility chiefly inhabit what is termed the Beloi-gorod or White City, so called from the whiteness of the houses, which, although built of brick, are stuccoed. It is situated without the Kitai-gorod, within the circuit of the first ditch, which has lately been converted into public walks or boulevards. In these two last divisions of the tuwn, the houses must all be built of brick, and roofed with vast iron;’in the more outward towns, the inhabitants are permitted to build with wood, and roof With the same material if they please; formerly the roofs of the houses _ were painted black, but ‘the emperor aLout five years since, noticing the sombre appearance this made, gave orders that in future
they should ‘be. painted of a green, red, or - grey colour.
Beyond the boulevards lately mentioned, is the Tartar Town surrounded by a ditch, and without the latter, an immense space occupied by houses and gardens.

Havine now visited the two chief cities of this empire, St. Petersburg and Moscow, and been for many months conversant with the manners and customs of the Russian people, I shall, previously to setting out for Siberit, venture upon a few. observations respecting these points.,
It is not, however, to be-expected that a limiced intercourse with the metropolis of an

empire, constituted like that of Russia, can enable the traveller to enter minutely or correctly, into the various traits and shades of its * national character ; since the latter must necessarily, in such.a situation, be materially influenced by a variety of artificial and accidental causes, dependant upon the reigning - modes of fashion and politics, which finding here a luxuriant soil, give a monstrosity, or rankness of growth, that disguises, or even occasionally obliterates, its genuine and natural features.

The Russiahs,. generally, are possessed of much natural quickness of mind and sensibility of feeling, which gives them the appearance of being a cheerful, amiable, and open hearted people; but alas! under this exterior are concealed so much disingenuosness and artful policy, as to aiminish materially, on closer acquaintance, that estimation ta which they would otherwise be justly entitled. How lamentable it is, that the noble mind of&man should be led by the meanness of artifice, to violate the principles of honour and honesty.

Although some of the highest classes are not altogether exempt from a tincture of this discreditable principle, yet it is among the lower orders that it operates most actively, so as to degenerate into the lowest cunning, meanness, and perfidiousness, and cast a shade of obloquy.over the various transactions between man and man; in short, they hesitate at no breach of moral duty, so that they can accomplish their darling object of acquiring money.
*“ And conscience, truth, and honesty ate made, To rise and fall like other wares of trade!” , , ‘

The only excuse that can be offered for this want of proper feeling is, that education is in this country so generally defective, that few of the ‘sound principles of religion or morality are instilled to inculcate better conduct. Indeed these people are so little aware of the nature of human-justice, that a former writer, adverting to this blemish on their character, observes, that “ in whatever they do or perpetrate, they think they are acting right; and as tliey seldom look back on the past, or anti-
cipate the future, they derive little advantage in the culture of their moral principles from experience.”

In further extenuation it may be urged, that the system of slavery authorised by the government, necessarily tends to depress the nobler feelings, and degrade the character of the population of this country.

The following are illustrations of the ingenuity and cunning of the lower classes of the Russian people, the occurrences to which they relate having been communicated to me by persons on whose veracity I can rely.

A tub of butter was one day offered for sale to a gentleman, apparently so excellent in its quality, that he was induced to purchase the whole of it, weighing fifty-two pounds. On using it, however, with hot toast on the following morning, it was found so combined with water, that the bread was literally soaked with that fluid, which had been, in the making, ingeniously rozen into it in such quantities, that when separated, little more than half the proper quantity of butter remained.

a man in the streets, a number of pots of fine carnations, at the same time agreeing with him to bring more on the following day ; and to insure his punctuality, she only paid him half the price of her first purchase. On proceeding to transplant them into a flower bed, they were all found to be without roots! The man had, notwithstanding, the assurance to make his apptarance the next morning, when, on being threatened with committal into the hands of the police, he solemnly protested his innocence, but, what was inconsistent enough, prostrated himself on the ground, and abjectly solicited forgiveness. After keeping him sometime in suspence he was suffered to depart. «

A gentleman who had received an invitation to a ball, at a merchant's house, on ascending the staircase, met-a man passing down with @ number of fur pelisses over his shoulder, and who offered to place his with the rest; an opportunity of disposing of it which he was glad to avail himself of. When the party broke up, he, as well as other gentlemen, sought for their

30-4 AMUSING ROBBERY. great coats in vain, the supposed servant proving to be a thief, who had thus ingeniously contrived to carry them off. There is a proverb in Russia, that “there cannot be thieves from without, if there are not some within.”

An amusing robbery of the master.of the police himself, took place some time since at Moscow. A nobleman waited upon this officer to say that the Countess K. see him on the instant, and pressed, him in was anxious to order to gain time, to avail himself of the equiprage he had himself come in. On his arrival, the servant who had accompanied him took off his pelisse, when he was ushered into the drawingsroom. After some conversation, it came out that the lady had not sent for him. Nothing remained but to return home; when, to complete his astonishment, it was discovered, on passing into the anti-room, that the servant, pelisse, and equipage had all disappeared. It proved that the nobleman had laid a bet, that he would have this important gentleman’s pelisse stolen from off his back, and had made
use of this stratagem to win his wager. Of course his pelisse was afterwards returned to him.

Perhaps, for ingenuity, the following trick would not ‘be surpassed in London or Paris. A respectable looking man fell senseless in the’ street from a fit, when a person in the crowd started forward exclaiming, “ Oh, my master! my poor master !” He now very coolly transferred the contents of the unfortunate gentleman’s pockets into his own, not forgetting his watch, and then, with all the concern imaginable, requested the persons near him to watch his poor master, while he ran to procure an equipage to convey him home. On being observed to spass a coach-stand without stopping, the cheat was detected ; but it was too late, for he contrived to get clear off with his booty.
To compensate these darker shades of cha-.

*racter, the Russians are possessed of many estimable qualitics, Their hospitality is unbounded, and, perhaps, from the palace to the cottage, equals that of any other people in the ‘world. The stranger, particularly if destitute or in distress, requires no other passport to
their benevolence, and may tiavel from one extremity of this vast empire to the other, and receive the most disinterested succour and comfort, without being deemed either intrusive or burdensome.

In private life this virtue shines most conspicuous; so that a person who has oncé secured an introduction into a family, is, without the ceremony of an express invitation, afterwards regarded as a welcome visitor, whenever he feels disposed to avail himself of the privilege 5, nay, a remissness in this respect often receives a friendly reproach. 2

Another virtue amongst this people is a disinterested principle of charity, scarcely equalled in any other country. I shall “have various occasions for illustrating this point; the following example, however, will suffice for the present. A friend of mine observing a tradesman, at whose shop he was making a purchase, give money to an ‘intoxicated woman, inquired his motive for relieving a person fn her imptoper state. “She begged,” he replied, “in the name of Jesus Christ, and I could not refuse her; if she does not inaker

right use of what I gave, the fault rests with herself, not me.” It is by no means unusual for the merchants and shopkeepers to send bread and other necessaries to the prisons and hospitals, besides relieving privately many other objects of charity. It is remarked that beggars are much more numerous in Moscow than at St. Petersburg; and you frequently there see parties of peasantry going about, under the sanction of the police, to collect money for re-building their villages that have been destroyed by fire.,

The population of Russia may be divided into two classes—the nobility, and the peasantry ; the former comprising such only as have attained military rank, together with their descendants; the latter, the great mass of the people.

The nobility have again been divided into two orders—the higher, and lower nobility ; the distinction between which is arbitrary and undefined :—the only actual difference appears to consist in the greater or lesser opulence of the individual; so that here, as under all other more ordinary circumstances, he who
has the greater command of worldly advantages, is deemed the greatest.

The dress of the Russian nobility, while resident in the capital, is both elegant and expensive; in the country, however, less attention is paid to this point. The gentlemen follow the fashions of London, the ladiés those of Paris; and many of their tailors and marchandes des modes, according to the vocabulary of our English artists, give undoubted evidence of high scientific taste.

Nothing-can be more fascinating than a . Russian ball or dress party, where the ladiés exhibit all the taste of our Gallic neighbours, and which, it must be confessed, on such occasions, surpasses that of our fair countrywomen. The latter, however, transcendantly outrival all other women in the world in their morning costume: in short, it is in the neatness and simplicity of her dress at the breakfast-table, that the English lady evinces a degree of propriety and elegance, to which no parallel can be found. The ladies of Russia, indeed, ray so little attention to their personal appearance,.that, throughout the morning, tue hair

is generally scen in paper, and the body jnelegantly enveloped in 4 loose robe, sans corset. The Russian ladies are not generally considered handsome; nor is this the mere invidious observation of a stranger, for the Russian gentlemen themselves are disposed to admit the superior charms of other females ; and I have.frequently heard them speak, with rapturous delight, of the beauty of their Polish neighbours. ‘To assert, however, that there are no handsome womert in Russia, is a libel not to be credited; at all events, the exceptions are most numerous; and if they are. not all beautiful, they are generally amiable, ‘frequently fascinating, and possessed of many. of the virtues that adorn the female sex. There is one habit attached to the ladies of this country which, in my opinion, detracts materially from the interest they would otherwise excite in the eye of an Englishman—the disgusting custom -of taking snuff, and for which I can imagine no reasonable excuse. They are also more intensely devoted to cardplaying than is rational, or consistent with mere amusement. I knew a married, lady,

with a young family, who had such a passion for these occupations, that the cards or snuffbox were scarcely ever out of her hands. I also heard of an instance, where a priest came to confess-a lady while engaged at cards, when he was requested to wait until she had finished her game.

The richer nobility keep an extraordinary number of servants, who, as sufficient occupation cannot be found for them, become indolent in the extreme. Count Vladimer Orloff, it is said, retains not less than eight hundred domestics in his family. And yet, pne day, when I had the honour of dining with him, he related to me that he had rang his bell” several times before it was answered,* although he had nine servants exclusively attached to his person, and whose business it was to wait in the anti-room. Each was ready with his excuse: one. had been to the housekeeper, another cleaning a pair’ of shoes, a third brushing a coat, &c. It was evident, however,
* Bells are not very numerous in the Russian houses, and I have frequently heard the master of a Russian family summon his servants bya whistle or a hollea.
that they had, most of them, been asleep, " The count terminated the affair by assuring them, that if the neglect was repeated, he would make them beat each other into a proper sense of their duty.

It is usual, at the door of every nobleman’s house, to have a servant called the suisse, dressed in the family livery, with a broad embroidered sash around his waist, or a belt hanging across the body from one shoulder, and a gilt-headed staff in his hand. This man receives cards, and takes charge of the hats, great-coats, &€é.

The upper servants imitate, as far as they can, the dresses of their masters and mistresses; the men have their hair cut short, and are clean shayen, and the women plait their hair into a long string, which js then coiled up like a@ snake, and secured at the back of the head with a comb; the fore part is divided in the eentre, each division lying behind the ear, and terminating in a curl.
The other servants are dressed in the family liveries of their respective masters. The coachinan, however, cuts the smartest, figure

of the group. In summer, he wears a hat with a low crown, the upper part of which projects to about half the external circumference of the brim; the body is surrounded with a robe, that reaches to the ancles, and is secured around the waist by a silk sash of various colours, made expressly for the purpose, and about ten inches broad; the beard is worn long, and without a cravat. In winter. the costume differs, and consists of a wadded fur cap, with a broad flat top,and ornamented with a gold tassel. Under the ordinary summer robe is worn a sheep-skin shoub, to protect from cold; and on the feet are double worsted stockings, with white shoes; the latter are made of wool and a glutinous substance, beat up together, which composition is then moulded. over a form, and dries very hard; it is then extrémely effectual in keeping out cold.

Some of the nobility, in order. to employ their servants, have them instructed in music and theatrical pursuits; so that they have both their family band and company of comedians attached to their establishment. Indeed, in their domestic orchestras the number of performers is occasionally so superabundant, that each, musician plays only a single note, as is particularly instanced in their peculiarly | national horn music. This system becomes the more necessary, as it is the custom never to employ the in-door servants in agriculture, or other out-door occupation.
The following is a detail of the general manner of living amongst the Russian nobility.

The first breakfast is taken at seven or eight, in the private apartment of each individual; this, however, only consists of a crust of bread or a biscuit, with a cup of coffee, accompanied occasionally, on the part of the gentleman, by a pipe or segar. Between eleven and one they ordinarily take a dejeuné a la fourchette.

The usual time of dining is from two to four; but the party generally assemble sdme time previdusly, and occasionally -sit down to cards until it is announced. The . dinner is almost always preceded by caviare, dried fish, butter and cheese, or some other
similar relish, to whet the appetite; as also wine, brandy, or liquors.
In some families the ladies sit together at “one end of the table, while in others they mix indiscriminately with the gentlemen.

The dinner is generally cooked and served according to the French or German fashion, or a mixture of both; the former, however, is considered the most stylish. To an English eye, the table presents a singular coup a’eil, being rather covered with fruits, cakes, sweetmeats, &c., than the more substantial viands, the latter being carried round in succession to the company; and to prevent delay, the same kind of meat is generally served at different parts of the table at ‘once. The ordinary French wines, Madeira, and decan-. ters of water, are placed on the table; you are, however, occasionally presented with a varjety of other wines of the first quality, and the repast always concludes with a glass of - Malaga, when the dessert is served up. This last part of the entertainment is brought forward as a continuation of the dinner ;

and after it is concluded, the company immediately retire to the drawing-room, where coffee is instantly presented to them. The company soon after ‘disperse, although some few, occasionally, remain to play at cards or billiards.

In the evening, about seven or eight o’clock, the party re-assemble, when cards, chess, and conversation, contribute to amuse ‘them until supper is ready; cards, however, constitute the more favourite amusement with the Russian nobility, who occasionally play very high. The most fashionable games are whist, Boston, acarté, and patience; they are also fond of fortune-telling.

It is customary here, as in some parts of England, to pay for your cards at, the rate of five roubles for two packs, which leaves a profit of about cent. per cent. for the servant that furnishesthem. In marking the game, a piece of chalk, formed like a crayon, is used, with which the number is written on the cloth; to remove this, when an alteration {s required, a small brush, made for the purpose, lies upon the table. "

So great is the passion of the Russians for card-playing, that many of them spend a large portion of their time in the occupation; even in the forenoon they may frequently be seen playing at patience, or telling fortunes ;, and I am assured, that with respect to the latter,

- when amarriage is on foot, they notonly try the - cards themselves, but request their friends to do the same; and even occasionally consult a professed fortune-teller to declare their future destiny.
About eleven o’clock supper is announced, preceded, however, like the dinner by caviare, &c.’; after which, on rising from the tablo, the party immediately retire.

The Russians hurry over their meals so fast, that there is seldom much time for conversation. I have frequently had my plate taken away while I rested my fork, in the act of addressing some one or other of the party ; but there are so many servaats in attendance, that it has no sooner been carried away on one side, than another has been substituted in its room on the other, so that ignorant of the change, when about to recommence eat-
ing, I have been much surprised to find nothing on my plate.

On rising from the table the Russians always cross themselves over the breast, making the sign very small and quick; the ladies are said to be particularly graceful in performing - this ceremony, always turning themselves. to the image in the room.

The Russians ‘rarely visit by’ a formal invitation as we do in England.. I once dined with a family where no one but myself was expected ; and the table was only laid for ten visitors; just before we sat down two or three others came in, and announced the intention of more coming to partake of their friend’s dinner, and in this way the party accumulated until there were not less than four and twenty. The table was necessarily enlarged, but no other apparent alteration made, and yet the dinner was as plentiful as if the whole had bren expected; it is one adyantage of the French mode of cookery, that many of their dishes admit of being made up extemporaneously, as it were, during dinner cme.,

‘As a substitute for formal invitations, the Russians are very particular in calling, dining, or supping, with their friends on their respective names-days. For this purpose they have only to look into the calendar, as soon as they rise in a morning, and as most of these people bear the name of some saint or other, the‘. arrangement for the day is readily made out; those, however, who have a very extensive _ circle of acquaintance, keep a memorandum book, for the purpose of-recording the namesdays of their friends. The birth-day is made of no account, and may be entirely overlooked without giving offence.
The peasantry of Russia, may also be divided under two heads. The merchants and tradesmen; and the slaves or serfs.

The merchants and tradesmen have all originally been slaves, who, having accumulated money sufficient to commence mercantile pursuits, and perhaps’to purchase their freedom, then constitute what may be onsidered, as virtually, a distinct order of the community. They differ from each other, chiefly according to their respective degrees

of opulence; so that while the lower tradesmen are little above the level of slaves, the first and richest merchants, in a degree, approximate to the nobility, or rather imitate them; for the two classes are ever kept at a distance that forbids thern entering into any thing like contiguity, or competition, as is the case with the more elevated merchants of England.

The merchants, with the exception of some few of the more refined ones, universally wear beards and fur caps. Their dress, in summer, is a long coat or caftan, with a girdle, and long boots; when they go out in cold weather, they wear a fur shube, with warm outer boots.
I have already, when treating of St. Petersburg, as well as in different parts of the work, described the habits and mode of living of this part of the Russian people.

The system of slavery, in which the lower orders of the Russian people are kept by their government, and which is certainly widely opposed to the happy liberty of the correspondent ranks of our countrymen, can “searcely fail to impress a British besom as

unjust, oppressive, and derogatory to the dignity of man; but yet it is a question, whether as matters at present:stand in this country, the system is not the one best adapted to promote the happiness and interests of the individuals concerned ; who, if presented with the divine boon, would neither know how to appreciate its value, or controul the dangerous licences it might lead to; population must have materially increased, the various orders of society be more amalgamated, and the principles of sound morality and education more generally diffused, before the word of emancipation can be sent forth with advantage; these must be the works of a future age, and can only be brought about by a series of progressive changes. Nor is the condition of the lower peasantry so degraded or pitiable as has been generally imagined. With all its exertion of arbitrary power, the government is sufliciently-paternal to adopt generally, the most excellent measures to promote their best interests. It is true, the serfs are much exposed to the caprices of their more immediate lords, who occasionally exer-

cise the privileges they possess with a rigidity, amounting to despotism; but they Jhave advantages, which, with industry, will generally enable them to break through the fetters of indigence, attain wealth, and enjoy the pleasures and luxuries of life, as far as the constitutioa of their minds admit of it. One circumstance, however, has often excited a most painful feeling in my breast, a feeling amounting.to indignation; the manner in which persons, who possess rank, make use of the whip, to stimulate the peasants to exertion; a fact that I have frequently been sensible of, at the various post-stations, which I have made on my journey. It is true, that this is part of a system, which custom has - rendered familiar, if not necessary; and in consequence, it appears not to gall the mind, however much the body may suffer from it; and at all events, it excites none of that ° warmth of injured feeling, or spirit of retaliation, that would instantly burst forth in the ~bosom of an Englishman, subjected to similar treatment. Each slave pays a poll, or capitation tax to VOL. I. Y

the government, and which is always levied from the, lord, whether the number has increased or diminished, according to the’ last census. Peter the Great was the first monarch of this country who caused a census of his subjects to be taken; it included, however, only the male population; since his time: there — haye been six more taken; the last in 1815, when Alexander caused the females also to be numbered. In the event of a slave.being sold to a new master, the former proprietar continues to be charged with the capitation tax until a new census is taken; the payment of which is of course considered in the deed of contract.
The following is a literal translation of a letter from a peasant to a Russian gentleman, * requesting him to purchase himself and famfly,

“To your high nobility, Augustus, the son of Charles, and to your ‘wife, and to your children, we wish yous health, and we bow to you all, and we for ever thank you for your goodness. We,beg of you, Augustus, the son of Charies, of the government of Witepsky, the

town of Lutin, the estate of Rudini. Mr.S—— who asked your goodness in the autumn, about the freedom of Jacob Serentief, the baldheaded ; his family is four souls, the son is eleven years old, the daughter is twelve years old, and the ‘gentleman asks for the two married souls six hundred roubles, and besides to pay the capitation tax; but when your goodness will please to think of us, then we are your servants for ever; when your goodness will send us the price, then we shall live. Augustus, son of Charles, do us this favour ; we reckon on you as on God ; $0 if your goodness should, then write to us back in a quick hour. With this letter I remain alive, in health; and for the future rely on God.
“ 1823rd year, the month of May, the 9th date.”

The dress of the lower peasantry corresponds with that of the merchant, except that it is made of coarser matetials; instead of boots, however, the legs and feet are sur- . founded with coarse cloth, secured by a cord made from the bark of the lime-tree; they wear a'so sandals, made with the sam3 mate-

rials; the hands are protected by double mittens, the inner ones being of worsted, and the outer ones of leather. The women, besides the under garments generally used by the sex, wear a sheep-skin shoub, similar to that of the men. ° :

The ancient Asiatic costume is rapidly giving way in all the larger cities, and is chiefly confined to the merchants, shopkeepers, labourers, and peasants. Servants, barbers, tailors, and many others, now shave, and adopt the common European dress.
The general mode of living amongst the peasantry is much the same as has already been detailed at St. Petersburg.

The females very seldom employ themselves with needle-work, or domestic occupations within doors, except of the coarser kind, as cooking, cleaning their apartments, &c. &c. When not thus engaged, some few employ themselves in knitting and’spinning, but sleeping is more congenial with their feelings.
In some of the villages the young women assemble in the evening at each others houses, and arause themselves with spinning and sing-
ing. On these occasions they seat themselves in a circle, with a torch of pine wood burning
_in the centre, and which it is‘the office of one of them to superintend, so as to keep it constantly lighted.

AT nine o’clock in the morning of June 12th, I went to the diligence-office, where I found Captain Cochrane already seated’ in the carriage, and in the act of driving off for St. Petersburg. I was just in time to shake him by the hand, and wish himself and companions a bon voyage; I then returned to my lodgings, to prepare for my own departuré, and at ten o’clock, after taking an affectionate leave of the few friends who came to gee me
off, commenced my long anticipated journey into Siberia.

My situation was now one of extreme hovelty, and my feelings corresponded with its pecyliarity. I was engaged under circumstances: of unusual’ occurrence, in a solitary journey of several thousand miles, through a country, perhaps, the wildest on! the face of the earth, and whose inhabitants were scarcely yet accounted within the pale of civilization ; with no other attendant than a rude’ Tartar postillion, to whose language my ear was wholly unaccustomed. And*yet I was supported by a feeling of happy confidence, with a cali resignation to all the inconveniences and risks of my arduous undertaking; nay, I even derived a real inward gratification, in the prospect of retirement from the eternal round of pleasure and social enjoyments of which I had been participating to 4 degree of satiety that began to be oppressive ; again and again interested myself by contrasting tmHy voluntary exile with the constrained banishment of the numerous unfortunate wretches who have been doomed to languish away, in the inhos-
pitable wilds I was about to traverse, the remnant of a protracted existence, aggravated by an eternal separation from all the blessings that they have deemed most dear to them in life. F

I was soon, however, roused from my reveries by finding that our postillion had lost his way. It had been arranged that I should call at the country-seat of a gentleman not far distant from the city, and my friends had directed the postillion accordingly. It was in vain that he attempted to elicit any information from myself, for his words were quite uninteltigible ; and how long our embarrass- ~ ment would have lasted I know not, had not a young gentleman rode up, who was able to converse in English, and who, it was singular enough, proved to be a nephew of the lady of the family I was proposing to visit. This gentleman offered to conduct us, and of course, I congratulated myself on being now in the right way; but no! we were still doomed to disappointment ; our new guide actually found himself lost, and after leading us from one toad to another, at length fairly admitted, that

he knew not where to go: we were’ at this time in the midst ofa wood, with roads branching in all directions. At length, after rambling about for some time, we stumbled upon a peasant, who directed us to the main road and the house we were in quest of, and which I had passed close by at least two hours before. We were here heartily welcomed by our friends, who amused themselves not a little with our adventures in the wood ; chiefly, however, at the expence of their young relative.

After dinner I recommenced my journey, and at length arrived at the’ end of the first station, where I had the mortification to be informed that there were no post-horses to be procured, although I was given to understand I might engage horses from the peasants of the place. As I should have had to pay a considerable extra demand for this accommodation, I felt forcibly impressed by the belief that the post-master and peasants were in collusion, to make their advantage of me; I, therefore, for a time, determined to appear indifferent, and resist the imposition, and declared my intention of waiting until

horses might arrive. I therefore, as it began to rain hard, covered myself up in my pavoshka,* with every appearance of resignation; but reflecting that time was more precious than money, I at length determined to avail myself of the peasants’ horses, and proceed to a manufactory, which belonged to the gentleman whose house I had so lately dined at, to pay him a visit, also with the hope that he would be able to assist me in making an arrangement for my farther progress; but on my arrival, | had the misfortune to find that he had just left, and must have passed me on the road. Thad no remedy but to make the best of my way to Coparna, a village, adjoining to which I knew there resided a countryman, Mr. T manufactory, the property of Prince Usupoff.
On my arrival, this gentleman was greatly astonished to see me, and could hardly be brought to credit the account I gave of inyself ;

however, be immediately invited me to spend the night at his house, and was kind enough to promise to see me provided with horses in the morning. I had the pleasure of passing an agreeable evening, and the gratification of enjoying, for one night more, a comfortable bed, which I had no right to expect after quitting Moscow.

In the morning, after breakfast, I set off, with peasants’ horses, for Boghorodsk, a small town, distant about fifty versts from Moscow. Here I again reccived the unpleasant intelligence that no post-horses were to be had, and had no alternative but to wait an indefinite time, or to take peasants’ horses again, of which a plentiful supply was offered to convey me forward to Vladimer. For this, however, they demanded what I knew to be an exorbitant sum, and therefore I determined to appear indifferent, manifesting my intention to wait for post-horses, and taking out my provisions, with which I began to occupy: myself. Viewing this, the peasants lowered their prites; and at length finding, by repeatodly sounding the post-master, that I had little

encouragement on his: part, I agreed with them to carry me on to Vladimer, a distance of ninety-seven miles, for thirty-one roubles, equal to twenty-six shillings. This, however, was more than double what the ordinary posting would have cost me.

We now travelled all night, and this without making any rapid progress, for the stations were long, and the roads bad, particularly one that was made with trees laid transversely across the path, and which, every instant, gave us such intolerable jerks, my equipage being without springs, that I was fain to get out and walk: in short, no position within the carriage was tenable, and the shocks it gave my brain so excessive, that it felt every instant ready to burst out of its tenement. This dreadful road continued for several versts. :

We arrived at Vladimer at three o’clock in the afternoon, when, having a letter for the ‘governor, I drove first to his house, in the hope of learning where I could obtain comfortable que@fters. He was, however, unfortunately, from home. Disappointed iere,

KINDNESS OF THE GOVERNOR. 333 my postillion and driver conducted me to what they were pleased to designate as good lodgings, where, however, on examining my apartment, I found nothing to entitle it to such an appellation. It contained but an old table, two wooden chairs, and a wooden frame to sleep upon. I was anxious to ascertain whether the ancient city of Vladimer did not afford some more comfortable accommodation for strangers, and at length had a man brought to me, who was supposed to know something of French; the only information, however, I could derive was, that the lodgings which had been offered me were excellently good ones, and that I could not have any better; nor was this comforting intelligence imparted, until I had answered a variety of impertinent enquiries concerning my rank, and more particularly whether I was a baron or a captain. In the evening I repeated my visit.to the governor, whom ‘I had now the pleasure of finding at home. He received me very politely, and kindly sent a servant to my quarters, to see the most comfortable arrangement possible made for me; so that on my —

return, I found every dispositionsto treat me with attention, as well as a straw mattress and pillow for my night’s repose; and on which I contrived, after my jolting bout for the preceding day aud night, to sleep as soundly as if I had lain upon the finest bed of down. -

_ IT spent the next morning in visiting this venerable city, once the capital of all the Russias. It contains, at this time, a population of only eight thousand souls. I had afterwards the honour of dining with the governor, in the company of an agreeable party. The following anecdote respecting a medical man was here related by himself. He stated, that when attached to the army, he had the misfortune to fall into the hands of the Turks, who, sharpening their knives, removed his handkerchief, preparatory to taking off his head. At this juncture, he recollected a Turkish prisoner having recommended him, ~ under such circumstances, ‘should they ever befal him, to repeat two Turkish words, which signify, “ I am a medical man.” He had the happiness ifmmediately to find their efficacy ; for the enemy not only desisted fron. their
butcher-like purpose, but restored him to his property and liberty.

After dinner I accompanied a gentleman, in his carriage, to the cathedral, where there is a fine painting of St. Vladimer, by Tonchi, an Italian artist, We then proceeded to examine some other interesting buildings, and afterwards went to the public walks, I then took tea with this gentleman ; and on returning to my lodgings, having procured post-horses, recommenced my journey at eight in the evening, being provided with a letter from the post-master, which I found useful in procuring — me horses without delay at the differerit post-

Our ‘progress was, however, much impeded by the bad state of the roads; and, on the following morning, J was detained at one point for two hours, by the necessary repairs of ny equipage. In the early part of the day we traversed heavy sandy roads, leading through forests. At the station where I took my dinner, J met a stupid kind of medical man, who was on his way to Irkoutz, where he had received a government appointment

as dccoucheur. Had he possessed more intelligence, I might have been happy in him asa companion; but, there was another objection to our proceeding together, that he was hastening to his point with all possible celerity.

In the evening I reached the town of Murom, distant about two hundred miles from Moscow, and one hundred from Nijni Novogorod. About midnight, we crossed the river Oka, on a perrevost, or stage-raft; a machine frequently used in Russia, as a substitute for bridges. After leaving Murom, I found the postmasters and drivers much more civil and attentive, which may be attributed to the diminished demand for horses, the country becoming now less populous.

At the station before reaching Nijni Novogorod, we met the governor of Cazan, on his way to Moscow, for whom [ had a letter of introduction; which, with much trouble, I ferretted from out of my packages, and presented to him. He was so kind, as to express his regret that his absence would prevent those attentions, he should otherwise have been happy to have shewn me at Cazen; but

to compensate it, he would write to the vicegovernor, on the subject. After partaking of refreshment with him, we proceeded on our respective journeys; and between three and four in the morning, I arrived at the city of Nijni Novogorod.

As I proposed spending a day or two at this place, my postillion drove me to a lodging-house, where they gave me a room, containing a mere wooden frame, on which I could lay the travelling mattress with which I had fortunately provided myself, at the suggestion of Dr. Lyall, whose experience had led him to duly appreciate the necessity and advantage of such an article. After this, I called at the governor’s, for whom J had a letter, but was disappointed in finding both himself and his lady from home; nor was their return expected during my stay in this city. I had, however, another letter for Captain G » whosé residence I at length had the satisfaction of making out, notwithstanding my attempts were nearly baffled by the obstinacy and sulkiness of my Tartar, who was always averse to incur trouble when he VOL. I., / £

could possibly avoid it. The captain, being from home, and not expected to return until the evening, I went back to my lodgings, where [ found ‘the Siberian accoucheur, with whom I made an arrangement to dine. “In the evening I repeated my visit to Captain G a gentlemanly intelligent man, well conversant with both the French and English languages, advantages which it may be believed, , whom I had the pleasure of finding

Nijni Novogorod has experienced a rapid improvement of late, in consequence of the great annual fair of Macarief, having been transferred to it. The principal streets, which were. previously covered with wood, have _since been paved ; and the foundation of new assembly rooms, upon the principle of the English cluhs at St. Petersburg and Moscow, has just been laid by the Prince of Georgia; many other buildings are also in progress. The town itself, is situated on an elevated spot, at the confluence of the Oka with the Volga, and commands many delightful views of the surrounding country.

On the 19th I crossed the Oka, to visit the buildings belonging to the fair, which is held on the opposite bank of the river. These buildings have been erected on a low tract of ground, in many places, originally, more than twenty feet below the present level; the surface having been artificially raised by soil transported, partly from a hill at some distance, and partly from:an island of the river. This island lies immediately in the line of communication between the fair and the town, and which communication is established by temporary bridges of pontoons, that are removed to a place of security, after the business of the season has terminated.

The fair consists of various buildings, or ranges of shops, &c., laid out in regular streets, the whole comprising an oblong square; the three sides which are unprotected by the Oka, are surrounded by a canal, that is supplied by a lake in its vicinity, the waters of which are brought a distance of fourteen versts from the river Pira; this canal, which is from ninety toa hundred and forty yards in breadth, can beevacuated at pleasure, by means

of a subterranean culvert that opens into the Oka. It is in contemplation to make another canal, communicating with the Volga, and which will admit of merchandize being brought. up to the very doors of the warehouses.

The front of the fair towards the Oka extends about three hundred and fifty yards, and the. whole isdivided into two equal parts, by a main street running longitudinally through its middle to double that extent. Inthe centre of a square, formed at the nearer end, is situated the governor’s house, the sides of the square being occupied by public offices. At the farther extremity of this principal street is a church, flanked on the right and left by: buildings in the Chinese style of architecture. Payallel with the main ‘street are ten lesser ones, and the whole are intersected at right angles, by various transverse streets. There are also numerous buildings for cooking, and other accommodation of the visitors; but which, in order to obviate the risk of fire, are placed at a considerable distance from the proper fair, on the outer side of the canal.

The expence of this immense undertaking, including the canal, was’ not less than eight millions of roubles. It returned, however, in the year 1822, a rent of six hundred and seventy thousand roubles; and it is supposed, that three hundred thousand persons of different nations attended the fair. The above income arises from the rent of the various shops, &c., for which a fixed price is taken; each article of merchandize having its respective situation. The rent is much higher than for- ‘merly, when the fair was held at Macarief, and many of the people express their dissatisfaction, not only on this account,’ but at the change altogether; and they particularly urge the danger of being overflowed by spring floods; an accident, however, which the engineers employed, have apparently taken every necessary precaution to guard against. When the admirable arrangements, not only of buildings, but of every other measure, which has been adopted both for safety and convenience, are taken into consideration, no disinterested person can question
the preferable situation of the present, as compared with the former establishment.

The original fair at Macarief, was the property of the Prince of Georgia, who received a rent for the various shops, proportionate to the value of the commodities sold in them; and whose income must have suffered materially by the government having taken the fair into its own hands.

The business of the fair when held at Macarief, during the year 1817, was more extensive than usual; the quantity of merchandize’ brought forward, however, materially exceeded the sales, in consequence of the high prices demanded. This was more particularly - the case with respect to Asiatic produce, which arrived in great abundance, under the charge of no less than three thousand merchants.
