At eight o’clock in the evening, I pursued my journey to Cazan, thinking it preferable to travel during the cool of the night. By this arrangement I was no loser in other respects, as I was just as well able to make my observations on the face of the country as in the day time; and as to the picturesque, I am willing to relinquish this point to some future Dr. Syntax; this I do with the less regret, as during the earlier part of my life, I saw enough of the sublime and beautiful teenable my imagination tocreate the most delightful pictures. at pleasure; I shall not, however, attempt to delineate these ideal representations, which, I apprehend, would scarcely excite the same interest in the minds of my readers.

The only incident worth noticing during this night, was a violent quarrel between two drivers, which, however, terminated without either blows or bloodshed. At nine in the morning we arrived at the village of Liskova, the residence of his highness the Prince of Georgia, a descendant, of the former sovereigns of that
country, and to whose mansion, having letters of introduction from his sister, the Princess Bores Galitzin, I immediately drove.

I was here received in the kindest and most cordial manner by the prince and his amiable daughter. The former was much surprised to see me, as he had, only a few days before, noticed, in the Petersburg Journal, a statementof my being a visitor in that city. His intelligence in this respect was also no small matter of surprise to myself, as it was the first time of my being aware of any notice having been taken of me by the publications of this country. !

After a princely dinner, my noble host’seldest son, a very amiable officer, who happened to be at home on leave, did me the honour to take me in their barge, which had about twenty oars, to Macarief, where the fair was formerly held, and which I felt desirous to visit. After rowing down & small river for a mile and a half, we entered the Volga, and soon reached the point of debarkation on its opposite bank. Oncommencing our journey, I remarked, that the men tossed up thei oars,

and was informed, that this constituted part of a ceremony, the object of which was to implore the protection of the Almighty on their voyage ; the remaining part of this ceremony consisted of taking off their hats and devoutly crossing themselves..

We landed at a spot adjoining the Monastery of Macarief, and were received by some of the monks, who conducted us over the more interesting parts of the building. In one of the rooms, a party of these holy people were occupied at the very grave game of nine-pins, but played in a manner distfnct from what I had before witnessed. The ball was suSpended over the centre pin by a cord, long enough to allow it to sweep the pins, and being taken out to its fullest distance, was then propelled upon the latter in such a direction as the science of the game prompted. We afterwards repaired to the apartment of the superior, who, notwithstanding the great defalcation of their revenues in consequence of the removal of the fair, which used to bring them many a good donation from the rich and pious merchatits who attended it, entertained us with

excellent wine, preserved fruits, tea, &. We were informed, that the great reduction of their income had compelled them to a proportionate diminution of the number of their brotherhood, a point of information which, I must admit, excited litthke commiseration in my bosom, as I felt assured, that their talents might be better employed in the more active pursuits to which they would be obliged to resort. I ought to feel grateful for the personal attention they. paid myself; on leaving they accompanied us to the water side, and presented me with a print of their monastery.*

The buildings where the fair was formerly - held, were constructed of wood, and at the time of my visit, had nearly all been removed. A greater part of them, however, were destroyed by fire, about seven years since.
About sun-set we recrossed the Volga, amidst scenery, which the young prince described, as beautiful in the extreme.
The following day was very stormy, with frequent thunder and lightning, so much so

as to deter the young princess and her friend, the Princess of Chercass, from joining the family party until tea-time, when I ventured to rally them on their timidity, and which they bore with the greatest good humour. I have frequently remarked the apprehensions of the ladies of Russia in this respect.

The prince, who is a widower, has only this one daughter, now about twenty-five years of age, and so remarkably fond of retirement, that it is said, she will neither marry nor enter into fashionable life, although, from her personal attractions and her elevated rank, she is entitled to the highest pretensions in both these respects. Her chief amusement and occupation is in reading, and instructing two young females, whom she has taken under her protection ; she is also the Lady Bountiful of the neighbourhood. Although she prefers retirement on the banks of the Volga, and shuns society from. home, her manners are by no means reserved ; on the contrary, her conversation is animated and agreeable, and she appears to take a peculiar pleasure in paying all possible attention to her father’s visitors.

On Sunday, the 22d, I accompanied the family to the village church, where the choir of singers were all domestic servants of the prince, who has himself a considerable taste for music, and an excellent bass voice, with which he frequently accompanies them.

After dinner I had the pleasure of attending the young princesses in a ramble to their gardens, beyond the village. In our way, they stopped to converse with a poor woman, who was sinking rapidly under that painful disease cancer. The amiable princess regretted that her knowlege of medicine was too limited to allow her to administer to the relief of her villagers as she could wish; a circumstance she the more regretted, as the family had been for some time without a medical man. In England we should say, that here was a good opening for a son of Esculapius, as the village contains a population of not less than six thousand souls with male bodies attached to them; many of whom are reputed to be very rich, in consequence of their extensive traffic in grain.
Soon after midnight I took leave of this
charming family, and proceeded on my journey not, however, without carrying with me additional and substantial evidences of their hospitality, in the shape of provisions.
They also did me the honour of ‘pressingly
inviting me to make them a longer visit on my return, which gratified me much, although
I had but little expectation of passing that way again.

About nine o’clock in the morning, when about a mile from the town of Vasali-Soursk, my ears were saluted by the sound of my fore-axletree breaking down, succeeded by the ominous “ Stoe, stoe!/” (stop, stop!).of the postillion. I was consequently detained two hours before a temporary axletree could be procured, to enable me to reach the town. I congratulated myself, however, that the accident did not occur in the middle of a stage, in a dark night, and with the agreeable accompaniments of- thunder, lightning, or of rain.”
We were provided with a spare axletree, in contemplation of an accident of this kind, and which, after we reached the town, was attached with all possible expedition. In the

mean time, I went to the river side, to endeavour to ascertain, whether any water conveyance was to be met with from hence to Cazan} as this town is one of the ports, as they term it, where vessels put in for shelter or trade. My enquiry, however, proved abortive. 1 !! On my return I found the pavoshka ready, and immediately set forward, but had not proceeded many yards when the other axletree gave way. This was truly provoking, as I had no second spare one with me; and soon found that the good people around me were disposed to make the most of my misfortune. At length, I had the luck to meet with a decent person, who could speak French, to whom I expressed my determination to bundle myself and broken-down carriage into a boat, and proceed by water. He replied, what I well knew before, that there was no boat in the port, but that he would talk to the people, and get my repairs done as reasonably as possible. I assured him, however, that, sooner than submit to imposition, I would wait until a boat arrived, or, selling my carriage, proceed by a post telega. At

length, he bargained with them to put me on a new axletree, for about double the sum it would have.cost at Moscow; this, however, detained me until six o’clock, at which hour I had the pleasure of setting off in the rain, that continued throughout the night, and made the bad roads still worse.

About seven in the morning we arrived at the town of Tchebocsar, said to have been - built by a robber of that name,’situated in a deep valley, close to the Volga, of which it is a principal port, and containing about five thousand inhabitants. The Russian merchants of this place carry on an extensive trade with the neighbouring tribes of the Tschuwashes and Tscheremishes, who inhabit villages peculiar to themselves, being a distinct race of Finnish extraction, and not Tarfars, as some have represented them. ‘The chief commodities they supply, are corn, honey, wax, and the bark of the lime-tree, which is made use of to cover houses and kabitkas, as well as for other purposes. They also trade largely in the skins of animals, particularly of squirrels, whick they shoot with light guns, made at
Toula for the purpose, and which carry a single shot, about the size of a. pea. This place is also celebrated for its excellent bricks, which are exported to various places on the Volga.

Although I had been disappointed in my previous attémpts to find a water conveyance to Cazan, I did not give up the point; and notwithstanding my Tartar showed himself averse to it, determined to prosecute my enquiry at this place; and at length, through the medium of a gentleman whom the Prince of Georgia had wished me to call upon, I found a boat belonging to Simbirsk, which was returning empty, after discharging a cargo of salt higher up the river, and which I ascertained to be just wide enough to receive my equipage. I agreed with the captain of this vessel to land me near the mouth of the Cazanka, a distance of a hundred miles, for eight roubles. At one,in the afternoon we commenced our voyage, having a very fine day, and a fresh breeze, which, towards evening, sunk into a calm, so that we were obliged to take to our oars, with which eiouiNs ALTERCATION. 355 we proceeded merrily enough, the crew sing? ing, as they advanced, their ‘national airs in concert, so as to remind me forcibly of the Canadian boat-song. ;

Our harmony was, at length, interrupted by an occurrence which, for a time, excited some apprehension on my part. About midnight I perceived our crew leave off rowing, and commence a violent altercation, which, at first, I imagined arose from the wish of a part to go on shore for spirits. At length, however, the dispute increasing, my imagination began to operate, and to. suggest the possibility, that I might be’the subject of -contention, and that they were deciding my fate} for I well knew that they would make little scruple of sacrificing me, could they derive any profit by it, and do it with impunity. I determined, therefore, to put myself on the guard. In taking my place on board, I had preferred the seat of my pavoshka, as being the most comfortable situation in the vessel ; this served me as a kind of entrenchment, and having my: postillion’s pistols by my side, I put myself on the gui vive, prepared to mark

‘one or more of them, should any attempt be made to molest me; and which I hoped, in the event of the affair proving fatal to myself, might lead to their discovery and punishment. It can scarcely be wondered at that my apprehension should have been excited to this pitch, when it is recollected that this ‘river was formerly the scene of the most horrid acts of piracy, and that such crimes’ are still occasionally perpetrated, particularly during the season of the fair of Nijni Novogorod.

Fortunately, however, my suspicions were groundless: After the squall had continued about an hour, it blew over; I was afterwards informed it was occasioned by a dispute respecting the division of some money they had made. When it concluded,,the parties betook themselves to rowing and. singing, as, before. About seven in the morning I was landed, near the confluence of the Cazanka and the Volga, at the port of Bakalda, distant only six versts from Cazan. I here took horses, and arrived at the latter place about, nine o'clock.

My accommodations at Cazan were of the same kind as J had now become accustomed to, namely, a room, with a table, wooden chairs, and a frame to Jay my mattress upon; in addition to which my apartment was freely ventilated by a ‘deficiency of glass in the window, the replacement of which I urged in Vain.
My first occupation was delivering my letters ‘cf introduction, particularly the one

directed to the governor, whom J had met with near Nijni Novogorod, and who had returned it to me with an addition of his own, and which I lost no time in presenting to the vicegovernor, who, through the medium of his aid-de-camp, informed me that he would order. one of the police to attend me wherever I might wish to go, and which appeared rather a novel mode of shewing civility to a stranger, especially as I could derive no information from him, in consequence of my being wholly unable to conyerse with a Russian. Independent of this, f felt myself treated by this gentlemen with much less respect than I had been accustomed to, as he received me in an outer room, ard kept me standing during our interview. I could not avoid ‘entertaining a suspicion that this behaviour had its motive, the more particularly as my letter was from no less a person than the governor-general of Moseow. This surmise was afterwards cons firmed by my finding that this officer’ and the governor, to whom the introduction was addressed, were at variance, in consequence of the latter having rendered himself obnoxious
to the nobility of his government, and which "was the reason of his journey to St. Petersburg.

I had no further communication with the vice-governor during my continuance at Ca-* zan; but was fortunately provided with other letters of introduction, and amongst the rest, one to his excellency the senator, General Simanoff, who had been sent by the government to enquire into the misunderstanding before alluded to; this gentleman I found a sensible, friendly man, and his wife and family very amiable.

Thad the gratification of spending the evening with Mr. Fuchs, who had on this day been elected rector of the University of Cazan, and who introduced me to several of the professors, who were assembled at his house on the occa-. sion; in such society I could not fail to spend an agreeable evening.

Mr.F. presented me with a letter which had been forwarded to his address, from a friend in Moscow, and which detailed the various opinions of my acquaintance in that place, relative tomy journey ; some anticipated, that sickened by experience, it would terminate at Cazan;

while.others, who knew me better, believed that I should accomplish all that I had proposed; I was happy to confirm the latter opinion, by expressing the satisfaction I had thus far derived, and assuring them, that I had met with less difficulty than I had cons templated.
Thursday, June 26t, I spent most of this day in exploring the town of Cazan, accompanied by M. Jobard, the professor of Greek at the university.

Cazan contains a population of about forty thousand, including the Tartars, who inhabit a separate part of the town, and are distinguished by their own customs and religion; the latter being Mahometan. During the, winter time, the society-of the place is said to be highly polished; at the time of my residence, however, most of the, nobility were living at their country-seats ; none remaining except those who were compelled to do so by professional avocations.
On the following day 1 accompanied Mr. Fuchs and his family to a promenade, held on account of Trinity week, which is kept, as a

festival throughout Russia. The amusements consisted of rope-dancing, horsemanship, light,, amusing comedies, and buffoonery. According to the report of superintending officers, the lower orders of people assembled on this occasion consumed fifteen hundred gallons of brandy, and five thousand of beer.
The spot were these amusements were held, was once the scene of a bloody battle, fought between the impostor, Pugatchef, and the
Russians, commanded by General Michaelson, in the year 1774, and which terminated in the defeat of the former. :
“ This extraordinary man was born’at a village on the banks of the Don. He was a common Cossack, and served in the wars

| against Prussia and the Turks; after which, © being refused his discharge, subsequent to the siege of: Bendor he deserted. After wandering about in different parts of the empire, he was taken, and sent to Cazan, for treasonable conversation; from whence he made his escape, and not long afterwards
. appeared in the character of Peter the Third,
at the head of numerous insurgents composed of Cossacks and dissenters. - _

“Tn the month of July, 1774, he advanced towards Cazan, burnt the town, murdered the principal inhabitants, and besieged the citadel, — whither the governor, and some of the nobility, had taken shelter, until he was forced to raise the siege, by the approach of Colonel Michaelson, at the head of a considerable body of troops, when after repeated engagements during three days, he was forced to retire across the Volga, with a chosen band of Cossacks, where he was again reinforced by numerous troops of Cossacks, as well as by numberless discontented peasants.

“ After various successes and defeats, ha was at last betrayed by some of his most confidential followers, from a promise of pardon for their treachery, and delivered up to a body of troops under the command of. General Suvaroff, stationed on the banks of the Yaik, which is now called the Ural; from this place he was conducted to the commander-in-chief, Count Panim at Simbirsk, and then to Mcuscow, ,
where, after his trial and confession, he was executed, on the 21st of January, 1775. Thus terminated the rebellion of the fifth and last impostor that had assumed the title of Peter the Third.”,

On the 28th I dined with the senator Simanoff, in company with all the principal government officers, and also of the governor of Viatka, whose daughter was married to the vicegovernor of Cazan. After dinner I visited the monument lately erected in commemoration of the taking of this town from the Tartars in 1552. Jt is of a pyramidical form, with a church in the centre of its base, and is situated on an elevated spot of ground, where the Russian warriors who fell in the contest were buried.

The following day, being Sunday, I spent chiefly with Mr. Fuchs. In the evening I visited the admiralty, established by Peter the Great, on the: Cazanka, at a distance of three versts from the city, where smaller vessels are built for the protection of the Caspian _ sea trade. The works admit of the building of si.ty-four gun ships if required. Peter shewed his usual sagacity in the selection of

a dock-yard at this point, for it is in the midst of the finest growths of oak timber which this empire posseses, and which is cut and trans~ ported to the water side in the winter by a class of men named Lashmas. These people’ are chiefly Tartars, and in consequenee of this duty, exempted from military service.

At this place I went on board a yacht, built at Tver, which name it bears, by the order of Catharine the Second, to allow herself and court to navigate the magnificent Volga. She had been ship-rigged, and measured one hundred’ feet in length, sixteen and a half in breadth, and five’ deep in the hold. This interesting relic, which is now materially decayed, is about to undergo some reparation, in order to preserve her from falling to pieces.
I occupied the Monday and Tuesday in visiting the cathedral, fortress, and other interesting parts of the town.

Cazan contains a celebrated university, which holds under its inspection the public schools of no less than sixteen governments. Its chief officer, or curator, resides at St, Petersburg; there are, however, two resident

sub-curators; the one devoted to its economy, and named the director; the other to science, and named the rector; the latter department being divided into four faculties, at the head of each of which is a dean. These again comprise twenty-six professors, with twelve adjuncts, who teach all the various branches of human philosophy. The number of students are, at this time, only a hundred, which is to be attributed to the circumstance of the sons of the nobility being almost entirely brought up to the army, and those of the class below them to the navy and public offices; so that the poorest gentry only embrace the-literary profession ; besides, those who can afford it, prefer giving their sons private educations. The sons of the Russian clergy are all, ex necessario, priests, and brought up in the universities established exclusively for that purpose, and which are termed academie spirituales, of which there are four principal ones; namely, at St. Petersburg, Moscow, Kief, and Cazan, with minor ones in each bishopric. ” There is a bishopric attached to every thrce governments.

On Wednesday I went to a Tartar school, where, before being permitted to enter, my shoes were taken off, after which I was seated ona low box, with a pillow placed uponit. The molla, or superintendent of the school, who is also the priest of the parish to which it belongs, called up several of the boys, who repeated passages from the Koran, chanting them out with a strong nasal tone. This school con- - tained about fifty boys.
It may not be uninteresting to enter into some details, illustrative of the manners and characters of thé Cazan Tartars.

The traveller, who visits Cazan, cannot fail to be impressed with the observation that the Tartars, generally, are a more civilized people than their Russian masters. The Tartar who is unable to read and write is held in very little estimation by his countrymen; and hence it is a leading consideration with the fathers of families, to- send their children to school at an early age, with a view to their being instructed in reading, writing, and the principles of religion; and to promot these points, every mosque has its proper school attached to it. :
The expences attendant on these schools are defrayed in an unusual manner: some — rich Tartar charges himself with jhem for the

* current year, and which he deems a service acceptable to his God; thus. practically looking for his reward in heaven. There are eight mosques, and consequently eight school~ houses, in the Tartar Town of Cazan, each of which accommodates its masters and pupils with lodging and board. They are always under the supreme direction of the clergyman of the mosque, with subordinate masters or ushers under him, who receive no fixed stipend, but content themselves with the donations of the friends of their pupils, consisting chiefly of corn and other necessaries of life, with some little money, and, on great holidays, the occa-_ sional present of a robe.

The books employed in the instruction of the boys are ranged on shelves against the walls, and interrsingled with various implements of trade; and such is the spirit of industry, that the masters may be often ob-
~served, at the same time that they are in-

structing their pupils, occupied in mending their shoes. ; Children are generally admitted between the ages of seven and eight, and continue at least five years;.and those who are devoted to the church, or the sciences, much longer.. The system of education commences with reading abridged sentences of the Koran: this is followed by books of Tartar poetry, explanatory of the sacred volume, and afterwards by the study of a work entitled Mourhamid Essendi, which contains a variety of commercial precepts in the Arabic language. Many aiso learn the Persian language, either with a view to commercial relations, or as a matter of taste. It is not a little singular, however, that few become acquainted with the Russian, notwithstanding the intimate connexion that must exist between the two people. The reason they assign for this is by no means honourable to the latter, as they assert, the party who acquires that language is sure to become worthless. The scholars generally take their lessons fs.

: VISIT TO A MOSQUE. 369 seated on their beds, with their legs crossed under them, and read in a singing tone of voice, which is both plaintive and disagyeeable. They have one common pot for boiling their provision, into which each puts his portion, one being appointed to superintend the cooking. Each individual is at liberty to eat when he pleases, although the more usual hour of breakfast is eight in the morning, and of dinner six in the evening.
The females receive a similar kind of education, under the superintendance of the wives of the priests. :

On Friday I took an opportunity of visiting a mosque during divine service, this being the chief day of the week when it is performed, My shoes were here also taken off at the entrance. The service did not last more than half an hour, during which I noticed that the people were in great agitation, occasionally jumping up,eand then sitting or lying down, as the molla read particular parts of the Koran. Women, of course, are not allowed
“to attend. : The Tartars observe four feasts in the year : VoL. I. 2B

Two of them are national; one intended for the men, the other for the women. The former takes place in the spring, and lasts a week ; during its continuance the people enjoy themselves in wrestling, which is their favourite amusement, and consists in each combatant taking his opponent by the sash, and in this way endeavouring to overthrow him; also in races, both on foot and horseback. The latter feast appears chiefly intended to congregate the sexes, with a view to matrimonial speculations, and consists of dancing, singing, and music. It is held in summer, and lasts one or more weeks.

The first ecclesiastical feast is the Ramazan, which is preceded by a fast of twenty-eight days, no one eating or drinking, except in the night time. At the conclusion of the month, the feast commences, and is characterized by a compensating indulgence in good living for three days. On the first ef these days, the men all go out into a plain near the town, and, at the rising of the sun, perform their devotions, while lying on their faces.

TARTAR ENTERTAINMENT. 371 in about two months after the former. It lasts only one day, and chiefly consists of a sacrifice in commemoration of Abraham’s obedience to God. Every master kills, with his own hand, some animal: for instance, a sheep for one man; @ cow, Ox, or a camel, for seven men; such parts of which, as are ‘not consumed by the family themselves, are distributed to the priests and the poor. In killing the animal, its head is turned towards Mecca, the man who performs this office using an Arabian expression, signifying that the sacrifice is made “ in the name of God.” The people then dip their fingers into the first blood’ that flows, and mark ‘with it the forehead, nose, chin, and cheeks; this they imagine protects them from the devil.

A friend, who had been dining by invitation at the house of a Tartar merchant, favoured me with the following description of his entertainment. On the party arriving at the house, the host, dressed in a linen robe that hung down to his heels, came to the outer door to receive them, and conducted them, with an-
~easy nolitencss, into the dining apartment. ‘He now, with his own hand, proceeded to

place a variety of dried fruits, cedar-nuts, &c: on the table, which was covered with a Persian cloth, grotesquely worked. The merchant’s wife then made her entrée, when the lady visitors rose and embraced her. Dinner was next brought in, and the party sat down to it, with the exception of their hostess, who retired behind a curtain in a corner of the room, to dine by herself, it being the custom of the women never to be seen eating by the men. The first dish was soup, strongly flavoured with onions and vinegar, and having small oblong cakes, filled with minced-meat, floating in it, and which was eaten with wooden spoons, those made of any other material being forbidden. After this came a grilled fowl, with salted cucumbers, and which was succeeded by the remainder of the dinner. As soon as dinner concluded, tea was introduced, served up with brandy and rum instead’ of milk; the Tartar himself, using the rum only, in consequence of brandy having been interdicted by Mahomet. Sweetmeats and Don’ wines were drank by thé guests, both before and after tea. The merchant proved

himself an agreeable, intelligent man, answering all the questions submitted to him respecting the customs and commercial relations of his countrymen, in an unreserved and satisfactory manner. On taking leave, the party found a sledge provided for them; and his son, as a mark of ‘particular respect, drove them home, singing, en the way, a variety of Tartar songs for their amusement.

The Tartars, without exception, sleep on feather-beds, which renders their skin more delicate and tender than that of their Russian neighbours; they consequentiy are unable to bear the baton or knout without greater injury; and have such horror of these punishments, that, to avoid them, they will frequently abjure their religion, and become Christians, a conversion which is accepted in mitigation of their sentence. This people, however, very seldom commit any of the higher crimes, as murder, or such as subject them to the knout; notwithstanding, they have no objection to stealing when a favour-
~ able onportunity offers, and particularly horses, to the flesh of which, as a food, they are ex-

tremely partial. They are also, many of them, very ingenious in the forgery of banknotes, or any written documents, which they imitate so exactly with the pen, that the deception can with difficulty be detected.

The commerce of Cazan is chiefly carried _ on by Tartars, many of whose merchants are excoedingly rich, and have relations with all the principal cities of the empire. The-trade consists of soap, leather, potass, skins, wax, tallow, &c. The quantity of soap manufactured in the place is from two hundred to two hundred and fifty thousafid poods per annum; the soda used im making it being the produce of the neighbourhood, and the oil brought from Astracan. Even the Tartar princes do not deem it derogatory to enter into trade; and it is said that the best soap is manufactured by the Prince Samanoff, and has his name stamped upon it. Tartar princes, however, are not to be ddemed of equal importance with those of Europe. The Czar Alexie advanced to this dignity all who embraced Christianity ; a stratagem which procured him many thousand prosclytes. Strahlenberg says, that he

saw in one village, eighteen such noble families, who all lived by tillage and husbandry, There is also at Cazan a manufactory of gunpowder, that supplies all Siberia; and another of cloth for the army, belonging to Mr..Osokin, and which ‘has been in existence since the time of Peter the Great. It employs a thousand workmen, and can produce a hundred and thirty thousand arshines of cloth annually, and which sell to government for three roubles and fifteen copecks per arshine, The wool employed is the growth of, the governments of Orenburg, ‘Simbirsk, and Cazan. Many sheep are, brought te Cazan from the former province, which are remarkable for their Jarge fat tails. A friend af mine, who kept some of these sheep at this place, found their tails degenerate, probably in consequence of the change of living, and the want of the nourishing food of their native plains. They have also been observed to lose the bulk of their tails when driven a long journey, the fat being absorbed in conse- -quence of the increased circulation which is excited. This variety of sheep is of large

size, with long hanging ears, and the wool of a brown colour, bordering on the nature of hair, and very long. They soon become unhealthy at Cazan, the marshy ground in - _ its neighbourhood exciting disease of the lungs. :

On account of the extent of marshy ground around it, and which is frequently overflown, Cazan is by no means a healthy situation. Agues, rheumatism, scrofula, scurvy, and diseases of the skin, are prevalent; and the latter are frequently extended amongst the lower classes by the communication afforded in the warm baths, which are indiscriminately. resorted to.
The government is much infested by mosquitos, gnats, bugs, beetles, rats, mice, and innumerable snakes.

On Saturday, July 5th, it was communicated to me that Captain Ricord the late governor, of Kamschatka,y had arrived at Cazan, in his way from that country. This induced me to defer my departure a day longer, in order that I might avail myself of the opportunity an invitation F had to:meet

him at dinner would afford, of eliciting information respecting my - future projects. I had the pleasure of finding him an intelligent gentleman, well conversant with the English language. He acquainted me with the death of the father of the lady of ‘Captain Cochrane, and a variety of particulars respecting that gentleman’s marriage and residence in Kamschatka.
After spending the whole evening in the company ef Captain Ricord, I took leave of my friends in Cazan, and resumed my journey for Siberia. :

I had hastened my departure, ineorder to avoid being present at a grand ceremony that was to commence on the following day, consisting of a procession of the clergy and an immense concourse.of the people, of all descriptions, many of whom had travelled more than two hundred versts from the country to be present thereat.» On this occasion, the “ Image of the Mother of God of Smolensko” is brought
‘to Cazan from the Monastery of Semiosernoe, distant about eighteen versts, and where it is kert during eleven months of the year, pre-

' ceded by flags and images from the various churches, and which are carried out to invite her ladyship into town. On arriving in the city, her ladyship is first conducted to the cathedral, where she remains three nights; after this she visits, in grand procession, all the other churches, spending one day and night in each parish, which period is almost wholly occupied in making calls upon its inhabitants, a- greater or lesser time being spent in each house, in proportion to the respectability of its owner, or the grateful liberality with which he repays the favour conferred upon him. In each house she is received with all possible respect and veneration, the rooms and passages being strewn with carpeting, matting, or boughs. She is conducted, on entering the house, to the apartment where the patron image is kept, and placed on a table, in an upright position, with wax candles in front of her. Prayers are now said in her presence, after which the attendant priests proceed to regale themselves with tea, brandy and wine, or, according to the time of the day, with dinner, or more substantial refresliments.

During the period of paying her visits, the bells are continually ringing, accompanied by every other demonstration of joy on the part of the inhabitants. One day is occupied with visiting the gates of the town, in commemoration of her having, in the year 1654, arrested a plague, which was proving very fatal in the city. The period of her annual residence in Cazan is one month, and the money collected on the occasion about twentyfive thousand roubles: this is the perquisite of the priests of her monastery.
There is another feast whith takes place in this city on the 8th of July, in honour of the image called the Mother of God of Cazan.

I err Cazan at midnight, and was detained for nearly half an hour at the gate of the city, by some explanations between the soldiers and my postillion, the nature of which I could not comprehend. The follow:ng day, July 7th, proved very fine, but extremely hot and dusty. About two o’clock I arrived at a Tartar village, where I expected to have procured a dinner, but in vain; so that I was compelled to von-

tent myself with dry bread and quass. This was truly a contrast to the enjoyment of the preceding day, when I had partaken of all the luxuries of an opulent city, in the society of its great and learned; I now was doomed to. eat my humble fare in solitude, at least without a soul to whom I could communicate a sentiment. And yet I smiled at my crust, and reflected how little man required, provided his mind was content, and so constituted ag to bend itself to circumstances. Perhaps there was not a better subject to philosophize over than adry crust; so I indulged my ¢houghts freely in their lucubratjpns, and when my hunger was appeased, recommenced my journey, with the anticipation of a better dinner on, the morrow.

Theroad was rough and hilly, and the villages chiefly inhabited by Tartars, whose children occasionally followed us with wild strawberries for sale. This reminded me of the gypsy children who run after the coaches near Shooter’s Hill, and in other parts of Kent. I could not
. fail to remark throughout this journey, that the Tartars appeared far more advanced in civili-

zation than the Russians, were more expert in what they attempted, more civil in their attentions, more tractable in their manners, and from their villages I uniformly found myself accommodated with the best horses and drivers.

On Tuesday, the 8th, the day was hot, but the roads much improved, although dusty. I was again disappointed in my dinner, as neither fish, flesh, nor fowl were to be procured, with the exception of horse flesh, which they did not presume to offer me, or I certainly should have ventured upon an experiment with it. ¢f again, therefore, smiled over my bread aid quass, and hoped for better times. The reader will, perceive that I had been unlucky enough to leave Cazan without my usual travelling stock of provision, which was attributable to two.causes — negligence and modesty. The latter quality is one which experience had long taught me that a traveller is better without, and yet I, some how or other, in the present instance, allowed it to interfere with my comforts. The fact was that I had taken my usual precaution, at Cazan, of yequesting a friend to lay me in the necessary stores;

he had purchased them, but imagining I should not set off at the time I had fixed, had neglected ordering them to be dressed. The friend with - whom I had supped, aware of my deficiency, most kindly urged me to take some of the remnants of his feast; but this I resolutely declined, affirming, that I should certainly meet with supplies at the different post-stations ; and I believe my friend did not doubt but that this would be the case.

About five o’clock I arrived at the town of Malmyche, in the government of Viatka, where, after taking my tea, and while preparing to set off, I was accosted, by a man, who with difficulty made me understand that a gentleman would soon arrive who could speak French, and who shewed great anxiety to have me stay until he came. Thinking I might gain from this person some information respecting the country I was travelling through, I was induced to accede: to the request, and accompanied him into his house, which adjoined the one at which I had been taking my tea. As
~s0on as I was seated, he almost forced me to take. wine with him, which I bore with all poso8t MYSTCRIOUS OCCURRENCE.
sible patience, expecting every instant the arrival of his friend. Time passed away,

+ however, without his appearance, during which I frequently heard my entertainer, with apparent anxiety, looking out of the window; and when I showed a disposition to move, he ex: claimed “ sechas! sechas!” which means “directly.” Atlength, in about an hour, and to the satisfaction of both, the gentleman arrived, who, after a conversation with the other, shook, me heartily by the hand, and laughing immoderately at the same time, began to talk to me in the German language, and I had the mortification of finding that he could not converse with me in French; so that I had been Josing my time in waiting for him. I therefore, after a few more hearty shakes of the hand from my laughing acquaintance, who was a tall, stout man, again prepared to recommence my journey.
I afterwards received an explanation of this mysterious proceeding from a gentleman whom I met in Siberia, and who had his account from the man himself. <
The person who was so anxious for my ¢om-

munication with the gentleman who was to speak French, had charge of the post-station of the place with the title of expeditor; and very sagaciously, in consequence of my not looking him in the face when he spoke-to me, took it into his head that I was a spy, and although he was informed that I was blind, observed that it was impossible a blind person could be travelling in the way I appeared to travel. He was so convinced of the correctness of his:surmise that he lost no time in sending for the laughing gentleman, who was a brandy distiller, and who really was able to converse in Frenth—in.a morning; but had most unfortunately so muddled his organ of Janguages by the vapour of his stills, or perhaps some more immediate application of their contents, that no other resource remained to make himself understood than what his superior knowledge of the Russ or German languages afforded. : About ten versts from this town we crossed the river Viatka, on a raft, after which the roads te the next station proved very heavy and sand;"; they improved, however, on the fol- VOL. I. 20

lowing day. I was again obliged to content myself with bread and quass for dinner ; but I felt in excellent health, and my mind was so deeply interested in my present and future proceedings, that I merely felt anxious to - satisfy the cravings of nature. Besides I had always the power of preparing myself a refreshing cup of tea. In the afternoon we reached the town of Okhane, situated near the fine and rapid river Kama, which, about three miles after leaving this place I crossed on a raft, in company with various other carriages. This river abounds with the sterlet ; but they are not so fine, or of the samé colour, with those caught in the Volga.

On Thursday, the 10th, I arrived at the city of Perm, and immediatly drove to the residence of the governor, for whom I had letters, and who received ine in the most friendly manner, anticipating my request to be recommended to good quarters, by offering me the best in the town—at his own house. In the evening I accompanied a gentleman to visit a coppet manufactory in the vicinity of the city, where.the various processes of sfelting
and cleaning the ore, and forming it into bars, are carried on.

This copper manufactory, named Molovitche, belongs to the crown, as well as another (Tugovski) at the distance of thirty-five versts from the city. The copper of this government is, excellent, and highly esteemed for its malleability ; about twelve thousand poods are produced annually, three thousand workmen being occupied in the various operations connected with: its mines, a great proportion of them in cutting down wood and preparing it for the use of the furnaces: the wages of these people remind one of olden times, being, exclusive of provisions, only about a halfpenny a day. :

There are, beside these government works, various private manufactories scattered throughout this government, particularly on the Ural Mountains, where the ore is procured. There*are also many iron-works belonging both to government and private individuals.

salt wells exist, the property of Baron Strogonoff, the Princess‘of Charovskin, and others, ~ the water of which is drawn up from a depth of forty sagenes, or two hundred and eighty feet, by means of spiral pumps, and afterwards exposed to evaporation; the salt is then transported to Nijni Novogorod in vessels that carry from fifty to sixty thousand poods.

On the following day, I amused myself with exploring the town, the streets of which are not paved. There is a pleasant promenade on one side, a mile in length, and which is called the boulevard, and was made a few years since by_a late governor.

There is a grand procession on this spot, on the 13th of May, which in the year 1819 was attended in sledges, a heavy fall of snow having occurred on the previous evening, a circumstance very unusual so late in the season. _
The governor being fron: home, I dined téte a téte with his nephew.
Soon after noon on the following day it began to rain heavily, accompanied by loud
thunder and vivid lightning, which proved fatal to two persons in an adjoining village, and materially injured five others.
The town-of Perm is well situated, being built on an acclivity from the eastern bank of the Kama; its climate, however, is very variable, and generally much colder than Cazan.

At this place a military hospital has lately been erected; and like all other government towns in Russia, it possesses a gymnasium, as well as some minor schools established by the present governor, on the Lancasterian plan.
On Sunday, July 1, after dinner we visited the house of a Danish medical gentleman, who

_ had dined with us at the governor’s, and who regaled us with melon and coffee, and shewed us his neat garden and hothouse.. He informed ‘us that Kotzebue had rested in this house when on his way to Tobolsk.
On our return I recommenced my journey, after taking leave of my kind host, Governor Kriegner. This gentleman is a Livonian, and a married man, although his lady does not
~reside.with him; having, much to his regret, declited accompanying him to Siberia. He

has proved himself particularly attentive 16 the interests of his government, the emperor having, in acknowledgement, presented him -with one of the more respectable orders of knighthood. He has in particular madé great _ improvement in the road and posting arrangements, his government being, in these respects, perhaps, the best regulated i in the empire.
The governor is particularly fond of music, and often amuses himself with his viol @’amour, a large violin with seven strings, on which he plays delightfully.

On arriving at a Tartar village, the first post-station after leaving Perm, we found some of the iron work of the wheels of the pavoshka broken. This in the course of an hour the Tartar blacksmiths repaired. The remainder of this and the following day proved windy and rainy, which rendered the roads very heavy, and in the middle of the night one of my axletrees broke, and ‘was replaced by a spare one which I had with me. At dinner time I arrived at a post-station a hundred and sixty versts from Perm, and two hundred from Ekaterinburg. At this point the Ural \foun-

tains afe said to commence, although for some distance nothing more than slighter hills, or undulations of ground, are perceptible ; little occurs worthy of the name of mountain until you arrive at Bilinbaefskoi, within fiftytwo versts of Ekaterinburg.

On the 15th the weather was fairer. I was now crossing the Ural Mountains, which separate Europe and Asia, and my heart bounded with joy that I had accomplished so considerable a part of my journey, and was entering, as it were, upon a new world, a world of strangers, with Providence only as my guide. I had now succeeded in what had been, for many years, one of the most ardent objects of ‘my wishes, but which I had little expectation of realizing—a desire of visiting the fourth quarter of the globe. The satisfaction I felt is indescribable, and served to animate me with increased zeal to perseverance in my future projects. » I almost imagined that a supernatural power was imparted to me, and that I had only to wave my wand, and will it, and every obstacle, every difficulty, would give’ way before me. With my mind thus
enthusiastically interested, L arrived at Ekaterinburg.

Before entering this place, which is situated at the commencement of the declivity of the Asiatic or eastern side of the Ural Mountains, I was sensible of a material change in the atmosphere, which had become colder by many degrees; this, however, as there had been much rain previously, and the weather had now cleared up, was probably to be attributed to an increase of evaporation, or other accidental causes.

I had three letters of introduction, on which I depended for securing the best accommoda-. tions thé place would afford, and I immediately addressed myself for their delivery. The first was to the civil commander of the place, who received me with politeness’; but, as he only spoke Russ and German, I could not explain my wishes to him. The second was to a gentleman who waz ill in bed, and, consequently, unable to see me. The gentleman to whom my last letter was addressed was -fortunately at home, and could speak English. | He kindly offered to accommédate

me in his own house, an opportunity I thankfully availed myself of, there being no respectable public accommodation in the place. ° This gentleman, a German, and_ superintendent of a government manufactory of marble vases, was entertaining a small party of friends at supper, sonte._of whom understood French, so that I was enabled to collect some information from them. Among’ other points, my observations of the greater coldness of the climate here were confirmed, it being stated, that during the last winter the thermometer stood, at Ekaterinburg, at forty degrees of frost, equal to sixty-eight degrees below zero, of Fahrenheit. -

On the following day, having letters for Mr. M——, an English gentleman who.re- | sided in the country, at ten miles distance, I drove over ta see him. I was ushered into the presence of -three ladies, who in vain attempted to converse with me in the Russian and German languages; Mr. M——, however, soon entered the room, and pressed me in so
. Warm @ manner to spend a few days with him, thav I could not deny myself the gratification.

This gentleman, who has resided many years in Russia, is possessed of great mecha+ nical genius; and, as a remuneration for his services to the government, has received a grant of the fine tract of land and- village which he now occupies, on the condition of - his establishing there a manufactory of cutlery, and instructing a certain ‘number of government slaves in that trade.

The estate comprises about two square miles, and the village, which is named Istock, ‘is most delightfully situated, being excellently - watered by different rivers, and abounding with wood, game, fish, and the most luxurious verdure. :
Mr. M—— had, for some years, been much occupied by government in putting up steamengines in this part of Siberia.

In this happy retreat I had the pleasure of spending several days, during which I enjoyed frequent walks in the country: and neighbouring woods, in company with the ladies of the family; a part of the time was rainy, and these days were agreeably passed away in Mr. M——’s library, which contained a choice

selection of English books, and which an English lady, who had been a companion td his daughters, was kind enough to read to ° me. The society of this lady was truly valuable td me, although she had the misfortune to be extremely deaf. - The family of Mr. M—— consisted of his ludy and two daughters, and his son, a boy of eight years of age. It is singular that neither Mrs. M—— nor the young ladies had any knowledge of English ; and, what is still more burprising, Mr. M—— was unable to converse. with his own daughters in any language! During my residence in this neighbourhood, General Simanoff, whom I have before mentioned, as being at Cazan during my stay in that place, arrived at Ekaterinburg, to inspect the mines in its vicinity, but, perhaps, more particularly to examine into the nature of a kind of sand, lately discovered in this country, and which has become a new source of great wealth to the government, being richly loaded with gold: in short, since its ~ discovery, the former gold mine has been diseontinued working, a measure which, how-

ever, had been long anticipated, as its produce was scarcely equivalent to the expences. * The value of this sand was first detected by a German of the name of Herman, who, coming into this country on some special commis: -sion, and being informéd that some boys had found large pieces of native gold in the sand; ‘near the surface of the earth, went to the spot, and ascertained that its sand contained many particles of gold. The discovery, however, was neglected until the year 1816 or 1817, when, on farther research, a still richer sand was found, -which could be collected at the - rate of three roubles for every zolotinck of gold; whereas the gold procured from the Berezooskia mine was at the comparative expence of ten roubles., ¢ The sand is found in strata of from six inches to three feet in thickness, sometimes lying close to the surface, at other times at the depth of a fathom from it; or at any intermediate depth, but generally underneath a bed of clay; and occasionally two or three strata are found. Masses of native,gold, nearly a pound in weight, have been found in

it, and it is generally combined with quartz; it is not improbable that the sand is formed from decomposed material of this kind. ° The gold is separated by washing the sand, for which purpose it is spread upon inclined wooden planes, over which a gentle stream of water is passed, the sand being kept in continued agitation; by this means the sand is carried off, while the more ponderous gold remains behind. Mr. M——, however, has lately invented a mode of washing, by which the process is effected with a tenth of the labour of the old process. The proportion of gold contained in the sand varies from three zolotincks to a quarter of one in every hundred poods, which are equal to three thousand six hundred pounds weight, English.

It is evident that the gold thus found in combination with quartz, is the result of the decompositions of the neighbouring mountains, the alluvia of which has been washed down into the plains below, and thus disposed into strata. All the specimens found on
In Anson’s voyage, gold is said to have been

discovered in a similar manner in the mountains of Brazil, near Rio Janeiro: “ great quantities of it were ‘annually washed from the hills, and left amongst the sand and gravel which remained in the valleys, after the runming off or evaporation of the water.”,

There is at Ekaterinburg a. considerable manufactory of copper money, producing annually coin to the value of about half a million of roubles, which are chiefly.sent to St. Petersburg. I did not’ examine this mint, as the workmen, on my return from Mr. M.’s, were occupied in getting in the hay-harvest, for which purpose they are allowed twenty days every summer,,
It may be interesting to offer a few remarks with respect to the unfortuate exiles and prisoners who are doomed to work at the mines and manufactories of Siberia..

The annual average of the new convicts is about six thousand, or about a hundred males and twenty females weekly, who pass through Ekaterinburg, the former every Tuesday, and the latter every Friday morning, into the more distant parts of Siberia. The rate of ‘their
" progress is from fifteen to twenty miles a day, excepting on Sundays and other great holidays. Houses are built at every station for ’ their reception.

Their fatigues and sufferings, on so immense a journey, must, it may be conceived, be very great; if, however, they become foot-sore, or really ill, the peasants are compelled to forward them in telegas; and occasionally, when dangerously ill, they are left behind on the road, and not unfrequently relieved, by the friendly hand of death, from future misery. The females who survive’the journey are generally so far broken down by its hardships or disease, as to be incapable afterward of bearing children; and thus the intentions of government, of adding to the future population of the country; are frustrated by the want of some better arrangements for the transferring these poor wretches to the scene of their banishment. The wives and, families of the convicts are permitted to accompany them, if they wish it.
‘In the summer time many of the male convicts elude the vigilance of their guards, and

" escape into the woods, where they contrive to subsist for a time, either on the wild fruits which nature offers them, or by the plunder of the neighbouring peasants and villages. As winter approaches, cold and hunger invariably compel them to surrender themselves, when they are punished accordingly.

A few years since, sixteen of these runaway convicts collected together in the woods near Ekaterinburg, and committed exfensive de- _ predations on the town and neighbourhood. They not only plundered for provisions, but,. Roman-like, carried away women, whom they compelled to live with them; a body of soldiers, however, at length dispersed them, and secured several of them.

A singular attempt at robbery took place about a year before my visit to this place. Three men, designing to plurder a miller’s house, which was’ situated near his mill, at two or three- miles distant'from the main road, procured a carriage resembling a post equipage, under the disguise of which they took the opportunity of the miller.being absent, to get admitted into his house. They

found the miller’s wife and another woman ° only within; the former, they immediately directed to take them to a certain room, where , they supposed the miller kept his money. Instead, however, of obeying them, the poor woman fainted away through fright, during the bustle ogcasioned by which the other woman contrived to escape. The robbers now put the wife into a large chest, and proceeded to rifle the house. Before they had satisfied themselves, however, a number of workmen from the mill rushed in and secured them; the female who had made her escape having given the alarm. It is needless to add, that the rogues got knouted and sent to the mines. One of them proved to be a butcher, in good circumstances.

On the day previous to leaving Ekaterinburg, I had the honour of dining with the Senator General Simanoff and his amiable family, comprisiag his lady, two sons, and as many daughters. Madame is a very pious woman, but yet, as it ought to be, very cheerful and agreeable in her manners and conversation. The general himself is an accomyoL. 1. 2p *
plished gentleman, and, from his knowledge of mineralogy, well calculated for the business he is at present occupied with.

-Madame Simanoff expressed great ‘anxiety to contribute to the comfort of my ensuing journey; and although I assured ‘her that every requisite provision had been made, would persist in contributing something. At length it occurred to me, that, as the heat of the weather would not permit my recently-cooked meat to keep-more than a couple of days, an addition of some salted provision would be acceptable; when she appeared highly gratified in ordering a couple of tongues and some smoke-dried sausages to be sent to me. These I found very serviceable, and they lasted until my arrival at Irkontsk.

Previous to setting off, 1 had my pavoshka put into good repair, and in particular two new wheels attached to it,« which cost me only twenty roubles, and proved so good, that 1 afterwards travelled two thousand five hundred miles with them, without the least necessity for repair.

Ekaterinburg, founded by Peter the Great, and so named in honour of his empress, contains about twelve thousand inhabitants. Perhaps a duller town for a traveller cannot be found. Its more respectable population consists of government officers, attached to the mines and manufactories ‘in its neighbourhood. It has a post from St. Petersburg only once in the week, which is seventeen days on the road, and which, of course, anticipates all the public news, so that little information,’

except of a private nature, can be gleaned from the traveller who makes it in his route. The town contains seven stone churches and a nunnery, besides some excellent stone houses, where the merchants principally reside: one of these, occupied by the senator, is almost worthy of being a royal residence. The streets are not paved, and consequently very dirty after rain; from the situation of the town, however, they soon hecome dry again, particularly in summer; so that the chief inconvenience is felt at the commencement and breaking up of
On the evening of Saturday, August 9, I. e

took my leave of Ekaterinburg, and proceeded to the country residence of my friend Mr. M., where [| rested for the night, and in the morning bade adieu to his amiable family, who showed the most gratifying interest in my future ‘happiness and safety: in short, the sensibility they éxpressed on this occasion almost overpowered my feelings. Nothing, however, could divert me for a moment from . the gratification I felt in prosecuting my journey, to which my imagination began to set no: limit, otherwise than by completing the circuit of the whole globe. "In the, evening, without any event of particular interest occurring, I arrived at the town of Camichlof, distant a hundred and one versts from Ekaterinburg. At three in the afternoon of the next day, we reached a station where no post-horses,were to he met with, in consequence of a General, who was on his way from Tobolsk tc St. Petersburg, having taken them all.

I not only found this station without horses, but without postmaster or blacksmith. -There is indeed only one postmaster to every four ; TUMEN. 405 stations, between Ekaterinburg and Tobolsk;" while from Tobolsk to Irkoutsk the number is still further diminished. This is a great in-’ convenience to those travellers whose rank does not give them authority to inflict corporal punishment on the negligent or insolent drivers; besides, where the postmaster is wanting, ‘you generally find the want also of a Sama-— var, or cther convenient vessel to boil your water in.

My occasion for a blacksmith was not very urgént; but on arriving at the next station, the town of Tumen, we were detained nearly an hour in repairs, notwithstanding [ had left Ekaterinburg so lately, in what was considered a perfect state.

As I sat in my carriage during these operations, an unfortunate exile addressed me in French; and began to pour out his tale of woes. He informed me, that he had held a respectable situation in the service of this’ country, from which he had been removed into exile, without having the slightest know-
_ledge of the nature of his offence. Of course I cannot vouch for the authenticity of his
“story. [dropped a few words of condolence, and drove off.

Tumen is the first town in the government | of Tobolsk, and about midway between that city and Ekaterinburg, being two hundred miles from each; it was also the first town built by the Russians in Siberia. The inhabitants are principally Roscolnicks, a numerous " sect of dissenters from the Greek church. They will neither enter a Greek church, nor ‘permit one of-its priests to enter their houses; the consequence is, that they’ are obliged to fee the latter for abstaining from this exercise of their duty, and blessing their. habitations on certain festivals, when they have a privilege of doing so; hence where _ there is an abundance of these dissenters in parish, its pastor thrives better than in the midst of a pure flock of his own. These people are possessed of great industry, and are very regular and sober in tkeir habits, and therefore, as relates to temporal affairs, are generally prosperous.
There are several large brandy distilleries in this neighbourhood, and the town itself is
of much consideration, being well situated for | commerce on the river Tuma, in the midst of populous villages and a fertile country.
On leaving this place we crossed the Tuma, and proceeded to the next station, through a hilly country and along indifferent roads.

On the 12th, about one o'clock in the day, we crossed the river Tobol, and soon after arrived at a station distant a hundred and seventy versts from the city of Tobolsk. The postmaster. here was particularly civil and attentive, the accommodations of his house being superior to what are generally met with in this part of the world.

The roads were now very rough and hilly. At eight in the evening we arrived within ‘three stations from Tobolsk, at a Tartar village, where there was much difficulty in procuring boiling water. The postmaster and his wife were both absent, and their daughter, a girl of fifteet., unable to furnish me with any thing except a few berries. My postillion set off into the village, amongst his Tartar brethren, and at length returned with water, which, however, he stated, he had procured
“with great difliculty. I suspect that his laziness, or wish to make much of his services, were the principal sources of this difficulty.

After much detention; throughout the night, eithér‘at the post-houses, or in consequence of the badness of the roads, we at length arrived in the immediate neighbourhood of the celebrated capital of Siberia, the city of Tobolsk. When within half a mile of it we crossed the river Irtish, ona raft; on landing on the opposite bank, my passport was examined, after which we were allowed to procced into the city. ‘ ;

On arriving within the city of Tobolsk, I drove to the house of a gentleman for whom Thad letters. His lady received me with the most polite attention, and immediately sent for her husband, who was from home. When he arrived, they insisted upon my taking up my residence with them. The lady was well acquainted with the French language, and acted as my interpreter with Mr. R——, who VOL. 11. K

only knew Russ and German. Through this medium I found him a very worthy gentleman, and shall ever retain a grateful sense of the kindness and hospitality which.I experienced both from him and his lady.

After dinner ] accompanied my new friends to spend the evening at the post-director’s of all Siberia, where I had the honour of meeting the governor-general of Western Siberia, to whom I had a letter of introduction. This gentleman at first treated me with cold reserve; but after reading the letter, addressed me ina far more courteous manner; and we entered into a long conversation, the chief object of which, on his part, appeared to be to ascertain the motives for my journey; and which J only admitted to be undertaken from fancy, and under an impression that Siberia was a more interesting country, and less dangerous to the traveller, than it was generally. represented. He afterwards made a few common-place remarks, as some great Men are used to do when they wish to shew their condescension.
I had the pleasure of meeting, at this party,

two other interesting persons: one a countryman, Mr. S——, who was engaged in the Russian service, and had just returtied from an extensive inspection of posts in the eastern parts of Siberia. [had a letter of introduction to this gentlemen from Captain Cochrane ; -and it afforded me no small delight to meet a countryman at such a distance from home.
‘« And as the sparks of social love expand,
So the heart opens in a foreign land,
And with a brother’s warmth, a brother’s smile, The stranger greets each native of his isle.”

The other gentleman alluded to, was an officer in his imperial majesty’s guards, whom I had known at St. Petersburg, and who paid me much attention during my residence in Tobolsk. Ue f{ntroduced me to a brotherofficer, who had travelled over the greater part of the south of Europe, and who, on comparing notes, I found was at Rome and Naples at the same time with myself.

Our host and hostess appeared to be very amiable people, and had assembled at their house this evening nearly the whole fashion of Tobolsk, so that it proved a very agreeable introduction for me. ‘here was, how-

ever, a great scarcity of ladies, the latter being only in the proportion of one to four gentlemen. The amusements of the eveniig were cards and conversation, with billiards in an adjoining room. The governor-general and a few others retired early, but the greater part of the company remained for supper.

On the following day, Mr. S—— and one of the governor’s aid-de-camps, dined with us. I found a number of letters waiting my arrival at this place, many of them from my friends, in England, which, it may be supposed, in my present situation, in the heart of Siberia, were no trifling gratifications to me.

On the 15th I accompanied Mr. R--— and Mr. S—— to dine with the governor of Tobolsk, whom I found a very agreeable man, although I was compelled to converse with him through the medium of my countryman. This gentleman had previously been director of the posts of all Siberia; in the course of which duty he had hospitably received our missionaries under his roof, when théy were. on their way to the eastern parts of Siberia, with a view of converting the Mogul Tartars to Christianity.

On the 16th, after occupying the day in writing letters to. my friends in England, I passed the evening at the house of a gentleman who was intimately acquainted with the most distant parts of Siberia, and who gave me much interesting information respecting them. This gentleman had discovered a considerable island in the Frozen Ocean, which, with the permission of the emperor, he named New Siberia. He had ‘accomplished the \ hazardous task of making a circuit of this island, which he effected in sledges drawn by dogs. I examined at his house various skeletons of the heads of an unknown animal, which had been brought from the shores of the Frozen Ocean; I afterwards learnt that they belonged to the sea-cow. He had also some curved horny substances, about two feet in length, which he could not determine whether they were the claws or horns of an incognitum; I was decidedly of opinion they were the latter.
The entertainments of the evening at this gentleman’s consisted, as usual, of tea and supper, with cards and conversation. I noticed

one peculiarity, which was the introduction of punch immediately after tea;' most of the gentlemen partook of it. It was prpared: without lemons, which are, probably, too scarce to be procured in this country. -The ladies, and many of’ the gentlemen, refreshed themselves with differerit kinds of preserved fruits, which stood 6n a table in the middle of the room, and which were eaten by each person with the same spoon, a circumstance I was at the time ignorant of, but which 1 afterwards ‘learnt was a common custom throughout Russia. On finishing the supper, the company immediately began to disperse, although, where there is much etiquette observed, it is usual to stay until the servants have cleared the table.
Having passed nearly a week in this city, in which I found nothing very interesting, except its society, | began ‘to think of pursuing my journey eastward, [| met with

one gentleman who was anxious to detain me longer; this was the medical man who attended the family of my kind host, and who very confidently assured me, that for the trifling expence of ten roubles, he could, in the course of six months, restore me to sight, He added, however, that if I thought well to make him an additional remuneration, he should not refuse it. These terms were indeed very liberal, but my former experience had exy hausted my faith, and I was further prepossessed against him, by his declaring that eye which every other medical man had considered the most hopeless, to be the one that would be first recovered. Besides he was too much of an egotist to allow me to give him credit for any real superiority of talent. His plan of cure was to give internal medicine, and subject the eyes locally to the action of electricity.

The time I passed at Toboisk did -not give me any very favourable opinion of its climate; for although it was the middle of August, we found it frequently cold and rainy. This is, probably, in great measure.the consequence of its situation, in the midst of water and ex-

tensive marshes ; and hence, when much warm weather is experienced, the miasmatic exhalations occasion fevers, agues, and other diseases. The winter is excessively severe. Game and water-fowl are in great abundance: there are numerous migratory birds, as swans, geese; ducks, &c., and also the double snipe. The rivers abound with the finest fish, particularly the sterlet and sturgeon. The gentlemen of Tobolsk have a singular mode of fishing as soon as the rivers are closed in winter. A hole is cut through the ice in the deepest part of the river Irtish, where the fish assemble in numbers, and are then taken in the usual manner in great abundance, so as to afford a supply for the whole winter.

The city of Tobolsk has few public buildings; the handsomest is the one appropriated to the post department, built of brick, and stuccoed. There is another, named the Arsenal, which I visited; my imagination, however, could scarcely acknowledge it as a place of arms, but rather depicted it as a stable, the floor being very irregular and every where strewed over with hay. Here was exhibited

the portrait and armour of Yermack; the former a miserable daub; the latter consisting chiefly of a chain shirt, so heavy that one cannot wonder at his going irretrievably to the bottom, when, in his last: battle, he stepped ' short of the Tartar king’s galley, and fell into water. Whether the history of this banditti leader be fabulous or not, it is at least interesting; and tradition has now established the present Cossacks of Siberia’as descendants of | his followers; and from the different native tribes to the exile, all hold them in terror. Their children are necessarily all soldiers, and expected to serve from the age of sixteen to sixty. They are valuable troops, so that it is said Siberia would be lost without them. These troops, officered from among themselves, are at the free disposal of the government, who call them out in their turns, those who are not on duty being left at home to cultivate the lands allotted to them, and which constitute the sole remuneration for their services, as they receive neither pay nor clothing. Two regiments of these troops are stationed at
Tobolsk, two at Irkoutsk, one at Tomsk, and one in the government of Crasno-Yarsk.

The streets of Tobolsk, ave almost entirely laid with planks. For this purpose, trees are Sawn longitudinally in two, and placed lengthways, with their convex surfaces downwards; the consequence of which is, that when the edges are a little worn, the wheels of the carriages break through them, and sometimes get broken thereby.,

I had proposed taking my departure on the 20th, but was unable to» procure post-horses, in consequence of the governor-general having quitted Tobolsk on that day, and without its being known what direction he had taken. This is his customary manner of proceeding, in order to keep his government on the quz vive. In pursuance of this plan, he had arrived quite unexpectedly at Tobolsk. This officer has the character of being extremely zealous in the discharge of his duty; but too rigid to please his subordinates. He has, however, received many tokens of the approbation of the emperor. The governor of Tobolsk is equally strict in

his office, and more generally liked; but, unfortunately, the governor-general and himself do not accord well together; so that he had applied for, and was expecting to be removed to, some other government.

On the evening prior to my,departure, I called upon this latter gentleman to take leave of him; on which occasion he took the opportunity of enquiring into what parts of the world I had already’ travelled. When, amongst others I named St. Helena, he exclaimed, that he had a drawing of it, and immediately brought it out from an adjoining room, to enquire whether I thought it a correct resemblance. This is only one of the many ‘instances, in which persons with whom I have been in conversation, have forgotten my want of sight, and presented objects for my inspection, or for me to take from them; and occasionally they have only had their recollection recalled, by some unexpected movement of my hand overthrowing what they offered, as for instance, a cup of tea. Others, recollecting that I am suffering from some deprivation, mistake the sense, and begin to shout at me as if I were
hard of hearing; in short, this feeling is. so general, that almost every one who is not intimately acquainted with me, elevates his voice when in conversation.

When I am desired to give my hand to examine any thing by the touch, they take it as if my sense of feeling were deficient, squeezing it rudely, and pressing it forcibly on the subject of examination, as if I were about to ascertain the condition of a bird or beast; whereas my sense of touch is most delicate, and all that I require is to”pass the hand lightly over the surface of a body, and then the result is both pleasing and satisfactory.

Another circumstance, which was somewhat ludicrous, occurred during this visit, While the governor was gone into the adjoining room, to fetch his drawing of St. Helena, I was induced to enquire from my friend, who accompanied me, what extraordinary animal it was that was making the singular snoring, or breathing noise, on the other side of him, and. which had for some time attracted my attention. Unfortunately it was one of the principal counsellors of Tobolsk, who had a pecu-

liar obstruction in his nasal organs, which produced a singular wheezing noise ; besides the gentleman was of a very diminutive stature, so that his head was not much above the level of that of a good sized Newfoundland dog, and I really mistook him for some, non-descript Siberian animal. This proves how cautious we ought to be in speaking in the dark!”

My residence at Tobolsk was too brief to authorize me to say much respecting the general state of its society. That which I fell _ into was of the most respectable kind and truly _agreeable; in short, I shall never cease to recollect the great hospitality and marked attention I received, particularly from my kind friend Mr. R who, in every possible manner, studied my , and his amiable lady, happiness and comfort. The first society of the place is, of course, composed of the government Officers and their families; there are, however, some rich merchants who are permitted to associate with them, and join in the public assemblies. ;
Tobolsk was formerly the capital of the whole of Siberia. The country has, however,

lately been divided into two districts, Eastern and Western Siberia, and Tobolsk is now only the capital of the latter, including the government of Tomsk and Omsk; while Irkoutsk has become the metropolis of the former. Each of these divisions has its own. governor-general.

Tobolsk carries on a considerable trade in native furs, and also with China; but Irkoutsk so far rivals it in both these points, that the commerce of the city is now greatly depressed, although, from local advantages, it must always be considerable, whether we refer to its geographical position, or to the circumstance of its being the channel through which the trade, between Europe and the more eastern parts of the country, chiefly passes.
